Save $5,000 in 26 paydays, starting Fri Oct 23. Here's the whole plan.

1. Pick a separate place for it, away from everyday spending, and give it a name.
2. Set an automatic transfer for payday: $192.31, or your own pace.
3. Write down your finish-line date. On this plan it's payday 26: Fri Oct 8, 2027.

The math: 25 paydays of $192.31, then $192.25 on payday 26 = exactly $5,000.00. Halfway is payday 13 (Fri Apr 9, 2027).
Not $192.31 for you? $100 a payday gets there in 50 paydays. $250 gets there in 20.
A sample plan, not real results. Same amount every payday, no windfalls. Miss one? We'll show the catch-up math.
Every second Friday at 12 pm ET: the progress bar, one real-number lesson (Canada and US) and one move for that payday.

posts.caption:
Get up to $2,000 for your kid's school, free. Here's how to claim the Canada Learning Bond.
🇨🇦 Canada series: rules below are for Canada.

1. Get your child a SIN (Social Insurance Number).
2. Open an RESP, a school savings account, with a provider that offers the bond. No deposit needed.
3. Ask for the bond when you open it. Already have an RESP? Ask if the bond was requested.

How much: $500 for the first eligible year, then $100 for each later eligible year up to age 15. Maximum $2,000. ESDC also pays $25 to help cover the cost of opening the RESP.
Who: kids born in 2004 or later from lower-income families. One eligible year is enough for the first $500 (Jul 2025 to Jun 2026: 1 to 3 kids, adjusted family income $57,375 or less).
ESDC estimates about two-thirds of those born in 2004 or after are eligible for at least $500. It only lands once someone asks for it.
Turned 18? You can apply yourself until the day before you turn 21. It applies in Quebec too.
Can you add $500 a year? The education savings grant adds 20%, plus 20% more on the first $500 if family income is $58,523 or less (2026).

Send this to a parent, or to anyone 18 to 20.

Source: canada.ca · Rules as of Oct 2026

General education only, not financial advice.

#resp #canadalearningbond #personalfinancecanada #parenting #moneytips

Reach more of your goals: write one if-then plan tonight.

Pick a cue you can't miss: "When I sit down with coffee at 7:30..."
Name the first move: "...then I open the draft and type one line."
Plan for the obstacle: "If my phone buzzes, then I flip it face-down."

Why: across 94 independent tests, if-then plans had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals (d = 0.65). It was the only one of 5 famous focus rules we checked that fully held up. Habits took 18 to 254 days in the classic study (not 21), and one missed day didn't derail them.

Baby hates tummy time? Try it on your chest.

1. Lie back, propped up a little, wide awake.
2. Lay baby tummy-down on your chest, face to face.
3. Talk, sing or just let them look at you. A minute or two is plenty to start.

Tummy time can start from birth. Only do it while baby is awake and you're watching.
The WHO suggests at least 30 minutes a day, spread through the day, for babies who aren't moving around yet. It adds up a minute at a time.
Feeling sleepy? Lay baby on their back in their cot or crib.

Send this to a new parent.

Sources: WHO guidelines on physical activity, sedentary behaviour and sleep for children under 5 (2019) and NHS tummy time advice (Berkshire Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust) · As of Oct 2026

The car repair is today. Payday isn't. Build a small buffer so surprise bills don't land on a card.

1. Open a separate savings account.
2. Name it "Buffer".
3. Set an automatic 25 a week into it, and use it only for surprises.

Example: 25 a week is 1,300 in a year, before any interest. Any currency. Same math.
The catch: cash grows slowly and prices rise, so a buffer is for surprises, not for investing. A common rule of thumb is to start with 1 month of spending, then build to 3 to 6 months.

posts.caption:
Know what's normal in your first 72 hours home, and when to call.

Watch 3 things, every day:
1. Wet diapers. By day 6, expect 6 or more in 24 hours.
2. Bleeding after birth. Call your care team if you soak 1 pad in an hour, twice in a row, or pass clots larger than an egg.
3. Baby's skin and eyes. Worried about yellowing? Call your care team. Don't wait it out.

Also common: many babies lose a bit of weight in the first few days and gain it back by around 2 weeks. Lots of crying, tears out of nowhere a few days in, and bleeding for up to 6 weeks are common too.
Still feeling low after 2 weeks? Talk to your doctor. That goes for both parents. Partners can get postpartum depression too.

Save this for your first night home. Send it to whoever's driving you home.

Source: Public Health Agency of Canada, Your Guide to Postpartum Health and Caring for Your Baby (canada.ca) · As of Oct 2026

General information only, not medical advice. Talk to your doctor, midwife or public health nurse.

#newborn #postpartum #fourthtrimester #newparents #firsttimeparents

posts.caption:
Your freedom number is your yearly spending × 25. Work yours out tonight.

Spend 30,000 a year: 750,000. Spend 40,000: 1,000,000. Spend 60,000: 1,500,000. Any currency. Same math.
Why 25? It's the 4% rule turned around: 1 ÷ 4% = 25. It's a rule of thumb from US market history research in the 1990s (William Bengen, 1994; the Trinity study, 1998).
Expect a pension or state benefit? Take its yearly amount off first. Spend 40,000 with a 10,000 pension: 30,000 × 25 = 750,000.
The catch: it's a rule of thumb, not a promise. Many planners use a lower rate to be safer (at 3.5%, it's about × 29), and it's before tax and fees.

Save this, then send it to the friend who says they'll never retire.

Source: Bengen (1994) and the Trinity study (1998), example math · As of Oct 2026

General education only, not financial advice.

#personalfinance #retirementplanning #investing #moneytips #financialindependence

Money can make its own money. It's called compounding, and it works like a snowball rolling downhill: the bigger it gets, the more snow it picks up.

Invest $10,000 at age 30. If it grows 10% a year, the first year earns you about $1,000. Leave it alone until 60, and in that final year it earns about $18,800, with nothing added. The whole thing grows to about $198,400, and most of that growth shows up in the last 10 years.

The honest part: markets drop some years, sometimes a lot. This is for money you won't need for 10+ years. Your emergency fund stays in savings.

Do this today: open your banking app and check what your savings earned last month. Near $0? Your snowball hasn't started.

Money Foundations is a series. Part 2 tomorrow: the cheap coat that costs 5 times more.

Send this to your "I'll start next year" friend. Save it for later.

"I'll start Monday" isn't just an excuse. It's a real effect, and tomorrow is Monday.

Why it works: researchers tracked visits to a university gym. At the start of each week, the chance of a visit jumped by about a third. It went up at the start of each month and after birthdays too. A new week feels like a new chapter, so last week's mess feels like it belongs to the old one. They call it the fresh start effect.

Do this: tonight, open your calendar and book one hour tomorrow for the thing you keep putting off. One hour, not a whole new routine.

Send this to the friend who always starts on Monday.

Still feeling low, weeks after the birth? You're not failing, and you're not alone.

Feeling low, teary or anxious in the first days is very common. It's called the baby blues, and the NHS says it usually passes within 2 weeks of the birth. If it lasts longer or gets worse, it might be postnatal depression. It's common, and it's not your fault.

Do this: still feeling low after 2 weeks? Call your doctor or midwife this week and tell them how you feel. You don't need to have every sign to ask.

In crisis, or thinking about harming yourself? In Canada, call or text 9-8-8, any time. In an emergency, call 911.

Send this to a new mum you love.

General information only, not medical advice.

posts.caption:
Your newborn is talking to you long before they cry. Here's how to hear it.

HUNGER COMES IN 3 WAVES (NHS feeding guidance):
1. "I'm hungry": stirring, mouth opening, turning their head to search (rooting).
2. "I'm really hungry": stretching, wriggling more, hands to mouth.
3. "Calm me, then feed me": crying, agitated movements, going red.

WHY IT MATTERS: catch wave 1 or 2 and feeds start calmer. By wave 3, a very upset baby often finds it harder to latch, so you soothe first (skin to skin, gentle rocking, your voice) and feed second.

THE BONDING PART: every cue you answer is a tiny conversation. Baby "serves" (a stir, a little mouth open), you "return" (you pick them up, you talk to them). Child-development scientists at Harvard call this serve and return, and it's how a baby's brain starts building its wiring. Feeds are comfort and closeness too, not just food.

Bottle-feeding? Same cues, same conversation. Hold baby close and upright, look at them, and let them set the pace.

DAY 1 → WEEK 1 → MONTH 1: on day 1 you'll miss most cues (everyone does). By week 1 you'll spot the head turn. By month 1 you'll know your baby's own "I'm hungry" face before anyone else in the room.

Do this: next feed, watch the face for a minute. Mouth opening or head turning? Feed then. Missed it and baby's crying? Calm first, then feed.

The rule that stays: answer the whisper, not the scream.

Send this to someone expecting.

General information only, not medical advice.

#newborn #breastfeeding #bonding #newparents #responsivefeeding

posts.caption:
New baby, new mortgage: which life insurance? Here's the difference in plain words.

TERM LIFE covers you for a set time, like 20 years. If you die in that time, your family gets the full amount. If you don't, it ends. Average price for a non-smoking 30-year-old, $500,000 for 20 years: about $20 a month for a woman, $28 for a man.

WHOLE LIFE covers you for your whole life and builds some cash value inside the policy. That costs more: the same 30-year-old woman pays about $50 a month for just $100,000.

Why term fits most young families: you need the most cover while the kids are small and the mortgage is big. Every year, the mortgage shrinks, the kids grow, and your savings grow. A 20- or 25-year term covers exactly those years.

The part people miss about work coverage: most group life pays 1 to 2 times your salary, and it usually ends when you leave your job.

Do this tonight (10 minutes):
1. Open your benefits portal (or booklet) and find "Life insurance". Write down the amount.
2. On paper, add up: your mortgage balance + the years your kids would need your pay.
3. Big gap? Get 2 or 3 term quotes for that gap, for as many years as the kids need you. Ask each one: "Is this price fixed for the whole term?"

The rule to remember: cover the years people need you.

Send this to your partner.

#lifeinsurance #termlife #newparents #personalfinancecanada #moneyfoundations

posts.caption:
Every ping costs you more than time. Here's the 2-minute setup that fixes it, and why it works.

THE SURPRISE: in a UC Irvine study, 48 people wrote work emails while being interrupted again and again. They finished a little faster than people who weren't interrupted, and their work was just as good. But their stress and frustration went way up. They were racing to make up for lost time. Interruptions don't just steal minutes. They wind you up.

THE SETUP (do it once, use it every day):
1. Turn on Do Not Disturb for one hour. iPhone: Settings > Focus > Do Not Disturb. Android: Settings > Notifications > Do Not Disturb (names vary a little by phone).
2. Allow 2 or 3 people only: your partner, your kid's school, whoever looks after a parent. Everyone else waits an hour.
3. Turn on repeated calls. On iPhone, a second call from the same person within 3 minutes rings through. On most Android phones, "repeat callers" does the same within 15 minutes.
4. Text the people who matter, once: "I silence my phone 9 to 10 each morning. If it's ever urgent, call twice."
5. At the end of the hour, check everything in one go.

WHY BATCHING WORKS: in a University of British Columbia study, 124 adults spent one week checking email only three times a day and one week checking whenever they liked. In the three-times-a-day week, they felt less stressed.

IF YOU SLIP: caught yourself checking? Don't write off the day. Put the phone back, turn Do Not Disturb on again and finish the hour.

WHAT CHANGES:
Day 1: it feels weird. You'll reach for the phone and find nothing new.
Week 1: in that UBC study, one week of batching was enough to feel less stressed.
Month 1: one quiet hour every day that nobody else gets to spend for you.

The big idea (it runs through Indistractable and Deep Work): you don't beat distraction with willpower in the moment. You set it up once, ahead of time, so there's nothing to resist.

The rule that stays: urgent calls twice. Everything else can wait an hour.

Send this to the coworker who answers every ping in ten seconds.

#focus #worklife #productivity #stress #deepwork

Up to $2,000 for your child's education, and you don't have to put in a cent. Part 2 of baby money.

Yesterday was the 20% grant you get when you save. Today is the one you get without saving: the Canada Learning Bond. The government puts it straight into your child's RESP.

WATCH IT GROW (if your family qualifies every year):
• First year: $500
• Age 5: $1,000
• Age 10: $1,500
• Age 15: $2,000 (the maximum)

WHO QUALIFIES (July 2026 to June 2027): children born in 2004 or later, in families with 1 to 3 children and an adjusted family net income of $58,523 or less. The limit is higher for 4 or more children.

THE PART NOBODY TELLS YOU: it's retroactive. If you qualified in past years and never asked, those years can still be paid. Parents can ask until the day before the child turns 18. After that, your child can ask for it themselves until the day before they turn 21. Only about 4 in 10 eligible kids had it in 2022.

3 STEPS AND 1 HABIT:
1. Get your child a SIN (in Ontario you can ask for it when you register the birth).
2. Open an RESP. No deposit is needed for the bond. Ask for one with no fees.
3. Ask your bank or RESP provider for the Canada Learning Bond. They have the form.
Then the habit: file your taxes every year, even with little or no income. That's how the government checks if you qualify again.

Do this: this week, call your bank and say: "I'd like a no-fee RESP with the Canada Learning Bond." Have your child's SIN and yours ready.

The rule that stays: no deposit, just the account.

The cheap coat can cost you 5 times more. And the difference can grow into something big.

You buy a $60 coat on sale. By February it's pilling, and you're done after 6 wears. That's $10 every time you put it on. Your friend paid $240 for hers and wears it all winter: 120 times in 3 years. That's $2 a wear.

It's called cost per wear: the price, divided by every time you use it. The price tag is today's cost. Cost per wear is the real cost.

Why sales fool us: a sale shows what you save today. It hides how soon you'll buy it again.

The 60-second check, before any buy over $50:
1. Guess honestly how many times you'll use it this year (look at how often you used the last one).
2. Divide the price by that number.
3. Do the same for the cheaper option. The lower number wins.
Still unsure? Put it in your cart and wait 48 hours. If you've forgotten about it, you didn't need it.

The honest part: pricey isn't always better. Check the seams, the reviews and the return policy. A $240 coat that never leaves the closet is $240 a wear.

Now watch it grow. Canadian households spent an average of $2,739 on clothing and accessories in 2023 (Statistics Canada). Buy half as often, and about $1,370 a year stays yours: $114 a month. Invest that $114 a month at 10% a year:
After 1 year: about $1,432
After 5 years: about $8,828
After 10 years: about $23,352
After 20 years: about $86,568
After 30 years: about $257,696
Same closet, fewer trips to the till.

The mindset: books like The Millionaire Next Door describe the same quiet habit. Many people who build wealth buy good things, look after them and use them for years. Wealth is often the money you didn't have to spend twice.

The rule to remember: divide before you buy.

Money Foundations, Part 2. Part 3 tomorrow: index funds, in plain words.

Send this to your sale-loving friend. Save it for your next shopping trip.

One sentence more than doubled how many people exercised. Here's the sentence, and how to write yours.

THE STUDY: 248 students in the UK were asked to exercise more over two weeks. One group did one extra thing: they filled in a sentence, "I'll exercise on [day] at [time] in [place]." Two weeks later, 91% of them had exercised. In the other groups, fewer than 4 in 10 had.

WHY IT WORKS: you make the decision once, ahead of time. When Tuesday at 7 comes, there's nothing to decide and nothing to argue with. The time and place become the trigger, so you just go. Researchers call these if-then plans, and across 94 tests they clearly helped people reach their goals.

HOW TO WRITE YOURS:
1. Pick ONE task. Not "get my life together". "Chapter 4" or "the budget sheet".
2. Name the exact time: "Tuesday, 7 pm", not "this week".
3. Name the exact place: "kitchen table", not "at home".
4. Put it in your calendar with an alarm, using the same words.

PLAN B FOR BAD DAYS: add one more if-then for the thing that usually stops you. "If I'm too tired at 7, I'll do just 10 minutes." "If the kids are still up, I'll start at 8:30." A small win still counts, and it keeps the habit alive.

The rule that stays: decide once, then just go.

WHAT TO EXPECT: the first week, you still have to remember. Then the time and place start doing the remembering for you. In a study of 96 people building a daily habit, it took about 66 days on average to feel automatic (anywhere from 18 to 254). Missing one day didn't undo it.

PICTURE A YEAR FROM NOW: one locked hour, five days a week, is about 250 hours. That's more than six full work weeks spent on the thing you kept saying you'd get to.

(This is the idea Atomic Habits calls an implementation intention. Same science, your sentence.)

Do this: tonight, write "I'll work on ___ on ___ at ___ in ___," and put it in your calendar with an alarm.

Send this to the friend who says "I'll go when I feel like it."

AI stopped talking. It started doing.

For three years, AI was a chat box: you typed, it typed back. Now the biggest companies are shipping agents, AI that opens a browser and does the clicking.

July 2025: OpenAI launched ChatGPT agent. It works on its own virtual computer: it browses, fills in forms, builds slides and runs code.
January 2026: Google added auto browse to Chrome. It can schedule appointments, fill in forms and request quotes while you keep browsing.
Anthropic's Claude in Chrome and Microsoft's Copilot Actions do the same kind of work.

Why it's different: a chatbot only reads your words. An agent sees the screen and decides the next click, like handing a helper your mouse.

Why it matters: the research group METR measured how long a task AI agents can finish on their own. It has doubled about every 7 months for 6 years. If that holds, METR says agents could handle projects that take a person a month by about 2030.

The catch: a web page can hide instructions that trick an agent (this is called prompt injection). That's why Google's auto browse never presses Buy or Post for you. Rule to keep: AI clicks. You press pay.

Do this: this week, give an agent one dull errand, like comparing 3 quotes. Watch every step. Pay yourself.

Availability varies: ChatGPT agent is in paid ChatGPT plans; Chrome auto browse launched in the US for Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers.

Send this to someone who still thinks AI just chats.

Hold the dots and slide. Watch one $1,000 double, and double, and double 👀

$1,000 invested at 25, growing 10% a year, is about $28,102 by 60. You never add another dollar. The same $1,000 in a 2% savings account: about $2,000.

The rule that stays with you forever: the Rule of 72. Divide 72 by your yearly growth rate, and you get the years it takes to double. At 10%, about 7 years. At 2%, 36 years.

Why the jumps get bigger: each double adds as much as everything before it put together. That's compounding, and it's why the last 10 years do more than the first 25. Morgan Housel puts it simply in The Psychology of Money: the real secret is time.

Do this: next windfall (tax refund, bonus, birthday cash), put $1,000 in a broad index fund in your TFSA. Then leave it alone.

Baby has a fever? Find their age and follow the line 👉 The rule changes as they grow.

👶 Under 3 months: be seen urgently. Call your doctor right away. If you can't reach anyone, go to emergency.
🍼 3 to 6 months: any fever means a doctor visit. Call today.
🧸 Over 6 months: if they're drinking and playing between fevers, it's often fine to care for them at home. See a doctor if it lasts more than 48 to 72 hours.

Why age matters so much: a young baby's immune system is still new, and signs of a serious infection can be subtle. That's why the youngest babies get checked even when they seem OK.

How to check it right: under 2, a rectal reading is the most accurate; armpit is a first check. A fever is over 37.9°C rectal, or over 37.5°C armpit.

At any age, call your doctor if your child is very sleepy or hard to wake, very cranky, has a rash, a cough or wheeze that won't stop, or anything that worries you. You know your baby.

Never give aspirin to children. Ask your doctor before giving ibuprofen to a baby under 6 months.

Do this: right now, save your doctor's after-hours number and your health line (811 in most provinces) in your phone.

Send this to your babysitter and the grandparents.

General information only, not medical advice.

From 2 minutes to a locked hour. Follow the trail 👉

Most people start a new habit at full size: an hour of study, a 5 km run. Then life happens, they skip, and they quit.

The trail goes the other way:
🌱 Day 1: just 2 minutes. Sit down, open it, stop. You're training showing up, not the work.
🪑 Week 2: 10 minutes, same time, same chair. Add a few minutes each week. The place becomes the cue.
📅 Week 4: 20 minutes. Missed a day? Never miss twice. One slip barely dented habits in the study below.
📵 Week 6: 35 minutes. Phone in another room, and end by writing tomorrow's first step.
🔥 Week 8: 50 minutes. It stops feeling like willpower.
🔒 Day 66: one locked hour, on autopilot.

Why it works: habits form by repeating the same thing in the same context until the context triggers it for you. In a well-known study, that took 66 days on average, anywhere from 18 to 254. So don't panic on day 20.

Do this: tonight, pick one thing and one time. Tomorrow, do just 2 minutes of it. Stop on purpose.

Send this to the friend who "starts Monday".

#habits #atomichabits #focus #deepwork #selfimprovement

What really happens when you ask AI a question? Follow it 👉

✂️ Your words are cut into tokens: chunks of words, about 4 characters each in English (100 tokens is roughly 75 words).
📚 The model learned from huge amounts of text. It isn't looking facts up in a database (unless it's searching the web); it learned patterns of how words follow words.
🎯 It writes the reply one token at a time, each one a likely next piece after the last.
🎲 The catch: when it doesn't know, it may guess, and sound just as sure. OpenAI's own 2025 research says training and testing have rewarded guessing over admitting uncertainty, like a student guessing on a multiple-choice test.
🗺️ Your move: give it context, and ask for sources. Then check anything that matters.

Why the context trick works: the model predicts from what's in front of it. Tell it who you are, what you need and for whom, and the likely next words become your words. Ethan Mollick's Co-Intelligence makes the same point: treat it like a very fast new colleague who needs a proper brief.

Do this: next time, start with "I'm a [role]. I need [task] for [who]. Ask me 3 questions first."

Send this to the friend who thinks AI is magic.

#ai #chatgpt #howaiworks #aitips #hourback

Started investing at 33, not 28? You can catch up. Here's exactly how.

Your friend invests $300 a month from 28. At 10% a year, by 60 that's about $835,500.
You invest the same $300 a month, but from 33. By 60: about $493,700.

Why the gap is so big: her first 5 years of deposits had the longest to grow. Like a snowball that started rolling sooner.

Two ways to catch up:
1. Invest about $508 a month instead of $300, until 60. That's $6,096 a year, which fits inside one year's TFSA room ($7,000 in 2026).
Watch Fix 1 grow: about $61,000 by 40, $270,000 by 50, and $836,000 by 60. Slow at first, then it snowballs.
2. Keep $300 a month and keep investing until 65. You land at about the same $835,500.
Or mix them: a bit more each month, a couple of years longer.

Do this, this payday (5 minutes):
1. Open your bank app and go to Transfers, then Scheduled or Recurring transfers.
2. Find the automatic transfer into your TFSA (no transfer yet? set one up for payday).
3. Raise it toward $508, or whatever you can do today. Every time you get a raise, raise it again.

The mindset: you can't buy back the 5 years, but time still does most of the work from here. Books like The Psychology of Money make the same point: the biggest lever is how long you stay invested.

The rule to remember: late isn't lost. Pay a bit more, or go a bit longer.

Send this to the friend who thinks it's too late. Part 2 of 2.

posts.caption:
AI made people 25% faster. Then it made them wrong.

Harvard Business School and BCG gave 758 consultants GPT-4 for real consulting work. On tasks AI is good at, they finished 12% more tasks, 25% faster, and their work was rated more than 40% higher in quality.

Then the researchers slipped in a task that looked similar but sat just outside what AI does well. The consultants using AI were 19 percentage points less likely to get it right than those working alone.

Why: AI's skills are jagged. It can be brilliant at one task and confidently wrong at the next, and the two can look the same from the outside. The researchers call it the jagged technological frontier. Ethan Mollick, one of the authors, builds his book Co-Intelligence around it.

The rule to keep: you can't see the edge until you test it.

Do this: test AI on work you know cold, where you can spot every mistake. That's how you learn where it slips in your job.

Send this to whoever trusts AI with everything.

#ai #futureofwork #chatgpt #careers #productivity #hourback

posts.caption:
The 5-step game that builds your baby's brain. No toys, no apps, no cost.

Child-development scientists at Harvard call it serve and return. Your baby "serves" (a look, a coo, a point, a babble) and you "return" it. In the first few years, more than a million new brain connections form every second, and these back-and-forth moments help shape them.

THE 5 STEPS:
1. Notice the serve. What is baby looking at, reaching for, pointing at?
2. Return it. Smile, nod, touch, coo back.
3. Name it. "That's a dog! A big brown dog."
4. Take turns, then wait. Count to 5 in your head. Babies need time to answer.
5. Notice the end. They look away or drop the toy? That's the end. Catch the next serve.

WHAT IT SOUNDS LIKE, BY AGE:
• 2 months: baby coos. You: "Ooh, is that right?" Pause. Baby coos again. That's a conversation.
• 6 months: baby says "ba-ba". You: "Ba-ba! You're talking!" Wait. "Ba!"
• 12 months: baby points at a bird. You point too: "A bird! It's flying." Wait for the next point.
• 2 years: "Truck!" You: "A big red truck. Where's it going?" Wait. Let them answer, even if it's just "there!"

DAY 1 → YEAR 1: on day 1 it's eye contact and your voice. By month 3, the coo-and-pause game. By month 9, pointing together. By year 1, every first word gets a reply.

Do this: tonight at bath time, play 2 minutes of serve and return. Follow what they look at, name it, then wait.

The rule that stays: wait for their turn.

Send this to a new parent.

posts.caption:
Which hour should you lock? Not the perfect one. The one that comes right after something you already do.

WHY: a habit needs a trigger. Stanford researcher BJ Fogg's recipe is "After I [something I already do], I will [new habit]." If-then plans like this, tied to a clear when and where, helped people reach their goals across 94 tests. "Sometime tomorrow" has no trigger. "After I pour my coffee" does.

PICK YOUR ANCHOR:
- Office day: after you put your coffee down at your desk.
- Parent: after school drop-off, or after the kids' bedtime.
- Night shift: after you wake up and eat, whatever time that is.
Choose the one you can protect most days, not your dream hour.

MAKE IT STICK:
1. Write it: "After I ___, I work for one hour on ___."
2. Put the note where the anchor happens: on the coffee maker, the car dashboard, the fridge.
3. Book it in your calendar as a repeating event called "Locked hour", so meetings can't land on it.
4. Plan B: "If I only have 10 minutes, I'll do 10 minutes." Starting small still keeps the habit going.

WHAT CHANGES: Day 1, the note does the remembering. Week 1, the coffee (or the drop-off, or the alarm) starts pulling you to the desk on its own. Around two months in, on average, it stops being a decision at all. A year from now: about 250 locked hours.

The rule that stays: anchor it, don't float it.

Do this: tonight, write your sentence on a sticky note and stick it where the anchor happens.

Part 2 of 2.

posts.caption:
Your baby is learning your voice before they're even born.

WHEN: from about 18 weeks, babies start to hear sounds from outside the bump (some jump at loud music). Most people feel the first movements somewhere between 16 and 24 weeks.

THE PROOF: in a classic study, newborns just days old worked harder to hear their own mother's voice than a stranger's. They learned it in the womb.

HOW TO BOND WITH THE BUMP:
• Talk to baby at the same time each day: "Good morning, little one. Today we're going to the market."
• Sing one song every night. The same one. It can become their lullaby after birth.
• Partners: put your hand on the bump and talk too. It's your first hello.

LEARN THEIR PATTERN: there's no "right" number of kicks. Notice when your baby is usually busy (after dinner? when you lie down?).

THE SAFETY RULE (NHS): if your baby is moving less than usual, you can't feel them moving, or the pattern changes, call your midwife or maternity unit right away, even in the middle of the night. Don't wait until tomorrow, and don't use a home heartbeat monitor or app to check. You are never a bother.

WEEK 18 → WEEK 28 → BIRTH: first, sounds reach baby. Then you know their busy times. At birth, the voice they hear on your chest is the one they already know.

Do this: tonight, hand on the bump, talk or sing for 5 minutes, and notice when they move. Save your hospital's birth unit number in your phone while you're at it.

The rule that stays: talk to the bump, trust the kicks.

Send this to someone expecting.

posts.caption:
TFSA or RRSP? One question decides it.

RRSP: what you put in can lower your taxes this year. You pay the tax later, when you take the money out.
TFSA: no tax break when you put money in, but the growth and every withdrawal are tax-free, forever.

The one question: is your tax rate higher now than it will be in retirement?
Higher now (a good salary today)? The RRSP often wins: you skip tax at a high rate and pay it later at a lower one.
Lower now (early career, part-time, a low-income year)? The TFSA often wins: you pay the low tax now and never again.
Not sure? Many people start with the TFSA. You can take money out any time and the room comes back the next year.

2026 room (canada.ca): TFSA $7,000 (plus any unused room from past years). RRSP: 18% of last year's earned income, up to $33,810, minus any pension adjustment.

Do this tonight (5 minutes):
1. Log in to CRA My Account.
2. Find "TFSA room" and "RRSP deduction limit". Write both down.
3. Next to them, write your tax bracket from last year's return. Now you know which account to fill first.

The rule to remember: tax higher now, RRSP first. Tax lower now, TFSA first.

Send this to the friend who asks every tax season. Money Foundations, Part 3 is in today's post.

posts.caption:
For every parent who gets interrupted halfway through everything. Here's the one-minute note that lets your brain put it down.

WHY YOUR MIND KEEPS CHEWING: when you stop a task halfway, part of your attention stays stuck on it. Researchers call it attention residue. So you're feeding the baby while still drafting that email in your head, and doing neither well.

WHAT THE RESEARCH FOUND: Sophie Leroy and Theresa Glomb gave interrupted people a quick "ready-to-resume" plan: write down where you are and what you'll do next. It took about a minute. People who wrote it carried less of the old task with them, and did better on the task that interrupted them.

THE METHOD:
1. Keep one sticky pad in one spot, on your laptop lid or next to the monitor.
2. When the baby stirs, before you get up, write 3 lines:
   Where I stopped: "paragraph 2 of the daycare email"
   What's next: "ask about the October fee"
   What I need: "the invoice from my inbox"
3. Stick it on the screen, and go. You've parked it. Now you can be fully with the baby.
4. Next nap, read the note and start with "what's next". No scrolling back, no "where was I?"

WHAT CHANGES: Day 1, it feels like one more chore. Week 1, every nap starts with a clear first step instead of ten minutes of finding your place. And the bigger win: when you're with your baby, more of you is actually there.

The rule that stays: park it on paper.

Do this: put a sticky pad on your laptop right now, before the next nap.

Send this to a friend with a newborn.

Meltdown in the cereal aisle? Here's what to do, step by step, and exactly what to say.

FIRST, THE WHY: at 2, the feelings part of your child's brain is loud, and the calm-down part is still being built. The NHS says tantrums usually start around 18 months. Your toddler has big feelings and not enough words yet. It's not bad behaviour you caused.

THE 4 STEPS:
1. Get low. Kneel to their eye level. Soft, slow voice. Stay close.
2. Name it. "You really wanted that cereal. You're so cross." Putting a feeling into words helps calm the brain's alarm.
3. Keep the no. "The answer is still no. I'm right here." If you give in, they learn tantrums work. Shouting back won't end it either.
4. Redirect. Once they're a little calmer: "Can you help me find the bananas?"

LATER, THE REPAIR: at bedtime, "That was hard in the store. You were so cross, and we got through it together." This is where they learn feelings pass and you stay.

WEEK 1 → MONTH 1: in week 1 you'll mostly remember step 1. By month 1, "You really wanted…" comes out on its own, and your toddler starts to know what comes next: you get low, you name it, you stay.

Do this: next shop, keep it short and give your toddler one job, like finding the bananas.

The rule that stays: connect, then redirect.

Send this to a parent of a two-year-old.

Picking the winning stock is hard. In 2025, about 8 in 10 professional US big-company funds did worse than the S&P 500 (79%, S&P Dow Jones Indices).

An index fund skips the guessing. It buys a little of every company on a list, like the 500 big US companies in the S&P 500. Think of a fruit basket: instead of betting on one apple, you buy the whole basket, so one bad apple barely matters.

Since 1957, the S&P 500 has grown about 10% a year on average, before inflation.

Now watch it grow. $300 a month into the basket from age 30, at 10% a year:
At 31: about $3,770
At 40: about $61,453
At 50: about $227,811
At 60: about $678,146
You put in $108,000. The basket did the rest.

The honest part: some years it drops hard. In 2008 it fell about 37%. The people who got hurt most were the ones who sold at the bottom. The rule: never sell in the drop.

The silent leak: fees. Pay a 2% yearly fee instead of 0.2% on that same $300 a month, and after 30 years you end with about $200,000 less. Tomorrow at 8:15: the full fee table.

Start in 15 minutes:
1. Open a TFSA at an online brokerage (or a robo-advisor, if you want it done for you).
2. Pick a broad index fund or ETF. Check its yearly fee (the MER): under 0.25% is a good sign.
3. Set an automatic monthly buy for payday. Then leave it alone.

The mindset: books like The Simple Path to Wealth and The Psychology of Money land in the same place. Own the whole market, keep costs low, and let time do the heavy lifting. Boring is the point.

Do this today: open your investing app, search "S&P 500 index" and write down two funds' fees. Just look. No need to buy today.

The rule to remember: buy the basket, keep the fee low, sit still.

Your phone can drain your focus even when it's switched off. Here's the full method, not just "put it away".

THE STUDY: about 800 people took tough brain tests. Some had their phone on the desk, some in a pocket or bag, some in another room. Another room: best scores. Desk: worst, even face down and switched off. The bag was in between.

WHY, AND THIS IS THE SURPRISE: part of your brain stays busy NOT checking the phone, and that uses up focus you need for the task. The researchers called it brain drain. The scary part: people said the phone barely crossed their mind. You can't feel this one.

THE SETUP (2 minutes, before the hour):
1. Turn on Do Not Disturb.
2. Text the people who matter, once: "My phone's in the other room 9 to 10 most days. If it's urgent, call twice." (Turn on repeated calls so a second call rings through.)
3. Put it in a room you'd have to stand up and walk to. Not your bag, not a drawer by your knee. Out of sight isn't enough. Out of reach is.
4. Set a timer on a laptop, oven or watch for one hour.

WHEN THE URGE HITS (it will, usually in the first few minutes): don't fight it and don't obey it. Write the thought on paper ("check the parcel"), then wait 10 minutes. Nir Eyal's Indistractable calls this the 10-minute rule. Urges rise and fall like a wave, and most are gone before the 10 minutes are up.

NEED IT FOR A 2FA CODE? Sign in to everything you'll need before the hour starts. If a code still comes, walk to it, type the code, and walk it back. The walk is the point: it turns a reflex into a decision.

WHAT CHANGES: Day 1, you'll reach for a phone that isn't there. Week 1, five locked hours, each one done. Same time and place: in one study, daily habits took about 66 days on average to feel automatic. A year from now, that's about 250 hours of your best focus.

Honest note: later studies found mixed results. Moving your phone still takes ten seconds.

The rule that stays: out of sight isn't enough. Out of reach.

Do this: tomorrow, Do Not Disturb on, phone in another room, timer for one hour.

Send this to the friend who studies with their phone on the desk.

AI sounds sure. That's not the same as right.

Why it makes things up: AI doesn't look facts up. It predicts the next likely word, like autocomplete on a huge scale. Likely isn't the same as true.

OpenAI's own researchers explain the rest: training and testing reward guessing. On a multiple-choice test a guess might score, but a blank never does, so models learn to guess instead of saying "I don't know".

4 ways to catch it:
1. The source. Ask where it's from, then open the link. AI can invent quotes, links and even court cases.
2. Ask twice. If the answers don't match, neither is safe.
3. Hand it the facts. Paste the real document and ask it to work from that, not from memory.
4. The big stuff. For health, money and law, AI can start the research. A real source finishes it.

The rule to keep: fluent isn't true.

Do this: next time AI gives you a fact that matters, ask twice and open the source.

Send this to the friend who believes every AI answer.

Winter car seat, fixed in 5 swipes 👉 Each swipe fixes one thing.

1. Coat off. Dress baby in thin layers instead: leggings or tights, a long-sleeve top, a thin fleece. In a crash, puffy padding squashes flat and the straps end up too loose to hold them.
2. Pinch test. Buckle up, then try to pinch the strap at the shoulder. If you can pinch it, tighten until it's snug on the chest.
3. Warmth goes on top. Buckle first, then tuck a blanket over the straps, or put their coat on backwards over the harness. Take it off as the car warms up.
4. Keep the infant carrier inside until you leave. A room-temperature seat pulls less heat from your baby.
5. Nothing under baby or behind the straps that didn't come with the seat. Inserts and covers sold separately weren't crash-tested with it.

Why it matters: a harness only works when it's snug against your child's body. Anything thick in between creates slack you can't see.

Do this: tomorrow morning, coat off, buckle, pinch test, then the coat on backwards over the straps.

Send this to whoever does daycare drop-off.

General information only, not medical advice.

#carseatsafety #winterwithkids #newparents #canadianparents #babysafety

Not married? No will? Your partner may get nothing.

In Ontario, if you die without a will, the law decides who gets everything:
Married partner: everything if the estate is under $350,000, or the first $350,000, then the rest is shared with your kids.
Common-law partner: nothing under these rules, even after years together. They may have to go to court for support.
Other provinces have their own rules, so check yours.

The fix is a will. It says who gets what, and who you want to raise your kids if both of you are gone.

Do this week (one evening, together):
1. List your accounts, your home, your life insurance and your debts on one page.
2. Agree on a guardian for your kids, and ask them first.
3. Book a first call with a wills lawyer. Ask: "What does a will and power of attorney cost for both of us?"
4. Check the beneficiary names on your TFSA, RRSP and life insurance while you're at it.

The rule to remember: no will means the law writes one for you.

Send this to your partner. Tonight.

posts.caption:
Two AIs. One admits "I don't know". Which would you trust?

OpenAI tested two of its own models on the same set of hard fact questions. The older one almost never said "I don't know" (1% of the time): it got 24% right and 75% wrong. The newer one said "I don't know" about half the time: 22% right, 26% wrong.

So the guesser got a little more right, and nearly 3 times more wrong.

Why: most AI tests only count right answers, and "I don't know" scores zero. So models learn to guess, and a guess comes out sounding exactly as sure as a fact.

The rule to keep: an AI that admits doubt is more useful than one that never does.

Do this: when AI says "I'm not sure", believe it. And check the confident answers that matter.

The first 2 weeks: protect your bonding bubble.

WHY SKIN TO SKIN: the NHS says holding your baby naked against your bare chest helps steady their heart rate, breathing and temperature. They hear your heartbeat and voice, which calms them, and your body releases oxytocin, the feel-good hormone that helps you bond. Partners can do it too.

HOW: baby in just a diaper on your bare chest, a blanket over you both, their face turned to one side so you can see their nose and mouth. If you start to feel sleepy, put baby down on their back in their own crib or bassinet.

THE VISITOR RULES:
1. Wash hands before holding the baby.
2. No kisses on the baby. A cold sore can pass to a newborn through a kiss, and it can be very serious.
3. Feeling unwell? Visit later.
4. Come with a job: dishes, laundry, a meal. Not "Let me hold the baby so you can clean." The other way round.

DAY 1 → WEEK 2: on day 1, the first hour skin to skin. By week 1, skin to skin is how you calm a fussy evening. By week 2, your visitors know the rules and you've barely let go of the baby.

Do this: today, text your visitors: "We'd love to see you. Wash hands, no kisses, and bring dinner if you can."

The rule that stays: protect the bubble. Visitors help, you hold the baby.

Send this to the family group chat.

General information only, not medical advice.

#newborn #skintoskin #newparents #fourthtrimester #bonding

posts.caption:
Lying awake thinking about tomorrow? Your brain is trying not to forget. Give it paper.

WHAT THE SLEEP LAB FOUND: 57 young adults spent 5 minutes writing before bed. Half wrote tomorrow's to-do list. Half wrote about what they'd already done. The to-do group fell asleep in about 16 minutes, the other group in about 25. And the more detailed the to-do list, the faster people fell asleep. (One small study, so it's a nudge, not a cure.)

WHY: unfinished tasks keep pinging your mind. A specific list tells your brain it's handled.

THE 5-MINUTE SHUTDOWN (Cal Newport's Deep Work makes the case for a fixed end-of-day ritual; here's ours):
1. Open tomorrow's calendar. What's fixed?
2. Write the list on paper, with detail: not "dentist", but "call the dentist at 9:15 to move Thursday, have the insurance card".
3. Close the laptop. Phone on its charger, outside the bedroom if you can.
4. Say one line out loud, the same every night: "Done for today." It's your cue that work is over.

WHAT CHANGES: Night 1, the paper holds it so your head doesn't have to. Week 1, the ritual starts to feel like the off switch. Month 1, bedtime stops being planning time.

The rule that stays: write it, then rest.

Do this: tonight, 5 minutes before bed, write tomorrow's list as detailed as you can.

Send this to the friend who texts you at 1 am.

#sleep #productivity #todolist #habits #bedtimeroutine

SOUND FAMILIAR? You're with them all day, but half on your phone and half on the dishes. They can tell.

THE FIX: Special Time. It's a tip NHS speech and language therapists give parents, and it comes from the same child-led play that child therapists use. 10 minutes. Your child leads. You follow.

THE SETUP:
• 10 minutes, at least 3 to 4 times a week. Same time each day if you can (after dinner works for lots of families).
• Your child picks: blocks, playdough, drawing, cars, dolls. Not screens, and not books or chasing games for this one: you want face-to-face back and forth.
• TV, music and phones off. Sit at their level.

WHAT TO DO:
• Say what you see: "You're building a tall tower. You put the red one on top."
• Copy them: they stack, you stack.
• Praise the exact thing: "Gentle hands with the blocks!"
• Repeat their words: "Big truck!" "A big truck!"

WHAT TO SKIP: questions ("what colour is that?"), instructions ("put it here"), and corrections. Even friendly quizzing takes the lead back.

ENDING: when the timer goes, "Special time is over. I loved playing with you." Stop at 10, even if they beg. That's what makes it something they can count on.

DAY 1 → WEEK 1 → MONTH 1: day 1 feels awkward (not asking questions is hard!). By week 1, saying what you see starts to feel natural. Imagine month 1: a child who knows that every day, for 10 minutes, they have all of you.

Do this: tonight, set a 10-minute timer, put your phone in another room, and say: "You choose. I'll follow."

The rule that stays: they lead, you follow.

Send this to your partner. You can take turns.

The government will put up to $2,000 toward your child's education, and you don't have to add a dollar.

It's called the Canada Learning Bond. It starts with $500, then adds $100 for each year you qualify, up to $2,000 (to age 15).

Who qualifies (July 2026 to June 2027): kids born in 2004 or later, in families with adjusted net income of $58,523 or less for 1 to 3 kids, under $66,036 for 4 kids, or under $73,577 for 5 kids. The limits change each July.

Now watch it grow. Just the bond, invested at 10% a year:
At birth: $500
At 10: about $2,891
At 15: about $5,266
At 18: about $7,009
Free money, plus 18 years of time.

The part nobody mentions: the money only lands in an RESP, a savings account for school. In 2022, about 2.5 million eligible kids had never received it.

Get it in 3 steps:
1. Get your child a Social Insurance Number (free, from Service Canada).
2. Open an RESP with a bank or provider that offers the Learning Bond. Many charge no fees, and no deposit is needed.
3. Ask them to apply for the bond for you. Keep filing your taxes every year so you stay eligible.

Missed it? You can still apply until your child turns 21, and the bond includes the years you qualified.

The mindset: free money only works if you collect it. It's the same idea as paying yourself first, the famous rule in The Wealthy Barber: small, early and automatic beats big and late.

Do this: this week, ask your bank to open an RESP with the Canada Learning Bond. Bring your child's SIN.

The rule to remember: never leave free money on the table.

Multitasking feels fast. It isn't. Here's what it really costs, and the one-block day that fixes it.

THE COST: your brain can't do two hard things at once. It switches back and forth, and every switch costs a little time while it gets back up to speed. The American Psychological Association says those switches can eat up to 40% of your productive time. In a 5-day week, that's up to 2 days.

WHY IT'S WORSE THAN TIME: every switch leaves part of your mind on the last task. Researcher Sophie Leroy called it attention residue: people who jumped to a new task while the old one was unfinished did worse on the new one. (Cal Newport's Deep Work builds a whole argument on this.)

THE ONE-BLOCK MORNING:
1. Close email and chat. Closed, not minimised. Phone in another room.
2. One task for one hour. One document, one tab.
3. A thought pops up ("reply to Sam")? Write it on paper and keep going. It'll be there at 10.

WHAT TO TELL YOUR TEAM (copy this into your status): "Heads down till 10. Urgent? Call me." Then answer everything at 10, so people learn they always hear back.

THEN BATCH THE SMALL STUFF: check email and chat at set times, like 10, 1 and 4, not 30 times a day. In a University of British Columbia study, people who checked email 3 times a day for a week felt less stressed than in a week of checking whenever they liked.

WHAT CHANGES: Day 1, one real thing is done by 10 am. Week 1, that's 5 real hours. Month 1, you stop ending days busy and empty.

The rule that stays: one block, one task.

Do this: tomorrow, close email and chat for your first hour and do one task only.

Send this to the friend with 30 tabs open.

Where do your AI chats actually go? Follow one message.

Step 1: you hit send. Your message leaves your phone and is answered on the company's computers, not yours.
Step 2: it's saved. ChatGPT and Claude keep your chats until you delete them; deleted chats take about 30 days to clear out.
Step 3: it may teach the AI. Unless you switch it off, your chats can be used to train future models. OpenAI, Google and Anthropic all let you choose.
Step 4: a person may read it. Google says human reviewers read some Gemini chats, and keeps those for up to 3 years, even if you delete your activity.

The different one: Apple says requests sent to its Private Cloud Compute are used only to answer you and are not stored, and it lets outside security researchers inspect the system.

Why it matters: training data isn't a chat log you can tidy up. Once something has helped train a model, you can't pull it back out. That's why the choice in settings matters.

The rule to keep: type it like a postcard, not a diary.

Do this: today, open your AI app's settings and decide whether your chats train it. Use Temporary Chat for anything personal.
ChatGPT: Settings → Data Controls → Improve the model for everyone.
Gemini: Keep Activity (formerly Gemini Apps Activity).
Claude: Settings → Privacy → model training setting.

Your paycheque, on autopilot in 5 swipes 👉

1. Pay yourself first. An automatic transfer the day your pay lands, before you can spend it. The Wealthy Barber's rule of thumb is 10% of every paycheque; The Richest Man in Babylon said it 100 years ago: a part of all you earn is yours to keep.
2. Every bill on autopay, set for 2 days after payday.
3. A monthly automatic purchase of one broad index fund. You never have to guess the right moment to invest.
4. Next raise: half goes straight to the auto-transfer. In the famous Save More Tomorrow study, workers who pre-committed future raises to savings went from saving 3.5% to 13.6% of pay in about 3 years.
5. One 15-minute money date a month, just to check it all ran.

Why it works: willpower runs out; automation doesn't. Ramit Sethi's I Will Teach You to Be Rich is built on this: make good choices once, then let the system repeat them.

Do this: this payday, set one automatic transfer: 10% of your pay, the day it lands, into your TFSA.

Send this to the friend who "can't save".

5 minutes a day that build a brain. Hold the dots and slide 👀

Scientists at Harvard's Center on the Developing Child call it serve and return. Your baby "serves" (a coo, a look, a point). You "return" it (a smile, a word). Back and forth. Those moments build the connections in a young brain, and they're the heart of bonding.

Their 5 steps, one a week:
👀 Share the focus: notice what they're looking at.
🙂 Return it: smile, nod, answer back, hug.
🗣️ Name it: "That's a dog. He's fluffy." Words they hear now, they'll say later.
⏳ Take turns, and wait: give them time to answer. The pause is their turn.
👋 Practice endings: when they look away, let them end it.

Missed a day? That's real life. Pick it back up tomorrow. In The Power of Showing Up, Siegel and Bryson put it simply: kids need to feel seen, again and again. Not perfectly.

Do this: tonight, 5 minutes, phone away. Follow their gaze, answer back, name it, then wait.

Send this to a new parent, or a new grandparent.

#bonding #servereturn #newparents #babydevelopment #canadianparents

Every habit has 4 steps. Climb them with one example: reading at night instead of scrolling 👉

👀 The cue: make it obvious. Book on your pillow, phone charging in the kitchen.
✨ The craving: make it attractive. Pair it with something you love, like your favourite tea, only with the book. Researchers call it temptation bundling: in one study, people who could only hear their favourite audiobooks at the gym went more often.
🪶 The response: make it easy. Start with one page. Book open at your page, lamp already on.
🏆 The reward: make it satisfying. A tick on the calendar, every night. What feels good right away gets repeated.
🔒 The summit: cue, craving, response, reward, on repeat.

Why it works: this is the habit loop (Charles Duhigg's The Power of Habit), turned into 4 levers by James Clear in Atomic Habits. To break a bad habit, flip them: make it invisible, unattractive, hard and unsatisfying.

Do this: tonight, pick one habit and set its cue. Put the thing where your hand already goes.

Send this to the friend who scrolls till 1 am.

#atomichabits #habits #readingathome #selfimprovement #focus

10 hours to actually get AI. Hold the dots and slide 👀

Wharton professor Ethan Mollick (Co-Intelligence) has a loose rule of thumb: you need about 10 hours of real use before AI "clicks". That's 20 minutes a day for 30 days:

📅 Day 1: bring it one real task from your day. His rule 1: always invite AI to the table.
⭐ Week 1: talk to it like a new colleague. Give it a role and context, then push back on its answer.
🔎 Week 2: find its edges. Ask about something you know cold. Where it's wrong, it's confidently wrong, and now you know where to check.
🧑 Week 3: stay the human in the loop (rule 2). It drafts, you decide.
🧠 Day 30: you get it. And rule 4: assume this is the worst AI you will ever use.

Why it works: AI is uneven. It's brilliant at some tasks and weak at others that look similar. Only hands-on use shows you where the line is for your work.

Do this: tomorrow, block 20 minutes and bring AI one real task. Repeat for 30 days.

Send this to the friend who keeps saying "I should learn AI".

That was Samsung in 2023. After staff uploaded sensitive internal code to ChatGPT, the company banned generative AI tools on its work devices.

The rule to keep: think postcard, not diary.

Missed a day? Don't start over. The research is on your side.

THE STUDY: 96 people picked one daily habit and tracked it for 12 weeks. Missing a single day didn't materially set them back. The habit kept building. (It took 66 days on average to feel automatic, anywhere from 18 to 254.)

WHY PEOPLE QUIT ANYWAY: it's not the miss. It's the story that comes after it: "I blew it, I'll restart Monday." Then Monday becomes next month. Atomic Habits puts it simply: never miss twice. Here's how to make that real.

THE METHOD:
1. Decide your 2-minute version now, before the bad day: one page instead of a chapter, one line of the budget, one push-up.
2. On a bad day, do only that. It counts. It keeps the trigger and the time connected.
3. Missed it completely? Tomorrow, same time, same anchor. No doubling up to "catch up". Double days feel like punishment, and punishment is what makes people quit.
4. Mark the miss on your calendar and move on. One mark is a blip, not a verdict.

WHAT CHANGES: Week 1, a miss stops feeling like failure. Month 1, you have a plan for bad days instead of a guilt spiral. Year 1, you're still going, misses and all, because you never let one turn into two.

The rule that stays: one miss is a blip. Two is a new habit.

Do this: tonight, write your habit's 2-minute version on the same note as your anchor.

Send this to the friend who restarts every Monday.

#habits #consistency #selfimprovement #motivation #productivity

posts.caption:
Can't make yourself go to the gym? Make the gym the only place you get your favourite thing.

THE STUDY: researchers at Wharton gave people gripping audiobooks they could only listen to at the gym. At first, they went 51% more often than people with no deal. Afterwards, most said they'd even pay to keep their audiobooks locked at the gym.

WHY IT WORKS: you stop relying on willpower for the chore. The chore becomes the only door to something you already want. It's called temptation bundling (Atomic Habits gives it a whole chapter).

HOW TO SET IT UP:
1. List 2 wants (a show, a podcast, a fancy coffee) and 2 shoulds (the treadmill, laundry, the expense report).
2. Pair one want with one should: true crime podcast + walking; the new season + folding laundry; the good coffee + the budget.
3. LOCK it. The want happens only during the should. If you binge the show on the couch, the deal is dead.
4. Make it easy: download the episodes to the gym headphones, leave the laundry basket by the TV.

THE HONEST PART: in the study, the boost faded after a holiday break. So when life interrupts, restart the deal on purpose, with a fresh show.

WHAT CHANGES: Day 1, you go because you want to know what happens next. Week 1, you catch yourself looking forward to it. Month 1, the chore is the good part of your day.

The rule that stays: only here, only then.

Do this: pick one show or podcast you love, and only play it during the chore you avoid.

Send this to the friend who keeps skipping the gym.

#habits #motivation #gymmotivation #productivity #behaviorchange

RRSP refund just landed? It isn't a bonus. Here's where it comes from, and how one refund can become about $29,000.

Earn $80,000 in Ontario and put $5,000 in an RRSP, and your tax for the year drops by about $1,480. Your job already took tax off every paycheque, so the CRA sends the extra back as a refund.

The part nobody tells you: it's your own tax, coming back. You pay tax on that money later, when you take it out.

So why bother? You skip tax at 29.65% today and, if your income is lower in retirement, pay it later at a lower rate. You keep the difference.

The trap: spend the refund on a trip, and your RRSP only did half its job.

Now watch it grow. Invest the $1,480 at 30, at 10% a year, and leave it alone:
At 40: about $4,006
At 50: about $10,846
At 60: about $29,359
One refund.

Refund day, 3 steps:
1. Open your TFSA (or next year's RRSP contribution).
2. Move the whole refund in, the same day it lands.
3. Invest it in your usual long-term fund, don't leave it sitting as cash.

The mindset: The Richest Man in Babylon's oldest rule is to keep part of everything you earn. A refund is the easiest money to keep, because you were already living without it.

Do this: before March 1, 2027 (the deadline for your 2026 taxes), check your RRSP limit in CRA My Account. Then decide your refund's job before it arrives.

The rule to remember: the refund goes back to work.

“I'm fine on 6 hours.” Your brain disagrees, and you won't feel it.

THE STUDY: in a sleep lab, people slept 6 hours a night for two weeks, and their focus was tested every day. It got worse every single day. By day 14, it was as bad as going 1 to 2 nights with no sleep at all.

WHY THIS IS THE SURPRISE: they only felt a little sleepier. The damage kept growing; the feeling didn't. So "I feel fine" tells you nothing. Canada's guidelines say adults need 7 to 9 hours, at regular times.

THE 8-HOUR SETUP:
1. Pick one wake time and keep it all 7 days, weekends too.
2. Set a second alarm, the bedtime alarm, 8 hours before it. Up at 6:30? Alarm at 10:30.
3. Phone charges outside the bedroom. Buy a $10 alarm clock if you need one.
4. When the bedtime alarm rings: lights low, screens off, teeth, book, bed. Same order every night, so the routine becomes the cue.
5. Can't fall asleep after about 20 minutes? Don't lie there fighting it. Get up, read something dull in dim light, and go back when you're sleepy. That's standard advice from sleep doctors.

WHAT CHANGES: Night 1, an alarm tells you to stop instead of a show ending. Week 1, going from 6 to 7 hours is about 7 more hours of sleep. Week 2, you get to find out what rested you is actually like.

The rule that stays: obey the bedtime alarm like the morning one.

Do this: tonight, set a bedtime alarm 8 hours before your wake-up alarm.

Send this to the friend who "runs on 6 hours."

#sleep #focus #productivity #sleepdeprivation #healthyhabits

General information only, not medical advice.

Tried AI once and it was meh? That's backwards. 4 rules for working with AI, from the book Co-Intelligence.

Most of us try AI once, get a so-so answer, and decide it's overhyped. Ethan Mollick, a Wharton professor who co-led the Harvard and BCG study of 758 consultants, argues that's exactly backwards. His book's ideas, in our words:

Rule 1 (week 1): bring AI to everything. It's the only way to find where it really helps in your work, because its skills are jagged.
Rule 2 (always): stay the human in the loop. You check it, you decide, your name goes on it.
Rule 3 (month 1): tell it who to be. "You're a tough editor. Find the three weakest points." A clear role gets sharper answers.
Rule 4 (year 1): assume today's AI is the worst you'll ever use. Learn it now, while it's new.

Why it works: you're not learning one app. You're learning to work with a coworker that keeps improving.

The catch: it still makes things up. Rule 2 never takes a day off.

Do this: this week, bring AI into one real task a day. Note where it helped and where it slipped.

Send this to your work bestie.

#ai #futureofwork #careers #cointelligence #productivity #hourback

“Where did all my money go?” 30 days of writing down every dollar answers it. Hold the dots and slide 👀

📅 Day 1: write down every purchase, even the $2 one. No judging yet. Just look.
⭐ Week 1: sort it into 3 buckets: needs, wants, savings. A classic target from Elizabeth Warren's All Your Worth: 50% needs, 30% wants, 20% savings.
🔍 Week 2: find the leaks. Forgotten subscriptions, fees, delivery charges. Cancel one.
🏠 Week 3: then the big 3. Shelter, transportation and food were about 64% of what Canadian households spent in 2023. A better phone plan or insurance rate there beats skipping a latte.
🔑 Day 30: you know your number: what a normal month really costs you.

Why it works: The Millionaire Next Door found that the people who quietly built wealth tended to know exactly where their money went. Awareness comes first; the budget comes after.

Do this: starting tomorrow, write down every purchase for 30 days. One line each.

Baby finally fell asleep. Now where? Find your spot and follow the line 👉

🛋️ Asleep on you, on the couch: gently move baby to their crib, on their back. Never sleep with a baby on a couch, sofa or armchair.
🚗 Asleep in the car seat or swing: fine for the ride, but these aren't for long, unsupervised sleep. At home, move them to their crib.
🛏️ Asleep in your bed: room-share, not bed-share. Their own crib, cradle or bassinet beside your bed, for the first 6 months.

The basics, every sleep, naps too: on their back, on a firm, flat mattress, in their own space. In the crib: a fitted sheet, nothing else. No pillows, bumpers, toys or loose blankets. Chilly? A sleep sack or onesie instead of a blanket, and don't let them overheat. Keep your home smoke-free.

Why it matters: these are the steps Canada's health agencies recommend to lower the risk of sudden infant death. Simple, and they work best when every sleep follows them.

Do this: tonight, take everything out of the crib except the fitted sheet, and move it beside your bed.

Send this to someone expecting.

General information only, not medical advice.

#safesleep #newborn #newparents #canadianparents #babysleep

Can't focus at your desk? Rebuild it for focus in 5 swipes 👉

1. Phone in another room. In one study, people did worse on focus tests with their phone on the desk, even face down and silent.
2. One window, full screen. When you switch tasks, part of your attention stays behind. Researcher Sophie Leroy called it attention residue.
3. Do Not Disturb for the hour, and check messages at set times. In one experiment, people told to check email only 3 times a day felt less stressed.
4. The desk holds only this task's stuff. What you see is what you're cued to do. Atomic Habits calls it environment design.
5. Before you stop, write tomorrow's first step. Making a plan for an unfinished task quiets it in your head, so it stops nagging you.

Why it works: willpower is a bad tool against a phone that buzzes all day. Change the room once and every session gets easier. Cal Newport's Deep Work makes the same bet.

Do this: before your next work block, phone out, one window, Do Not Disturb on, one task on the desk.

Send this to your study buddy.

#deepwork #focus #studytips #productivity #desksetup

“Write an email to my landlord.” Sound like your last prompt? Fix it in 5 swipes 👉

1. Add who, what and why. "Write an email to my landlord" becomes "Polite email to my landlord about the leaky tap. Second time asking. I want it fixed by Friday." Both OpenAI's and Anthropic's own guides start here: clear, specific instructions with context.
2. Paste a message written in the tone you want. Showing it steers the style better than adjectives like "professional".
3. Ask it to think it through step by step before answering, for anything with trade-offs. Newer reasoning models do this on their own.
4. Ask it to say when it's unsure and where each fact comes from. Models can guess and still sound confident.
5. Push back. "Shorter. Warmer. Drop the last line." The second draft is almost always better.

Why it works: the model predicts its answer from what you give it. Better input, better prediction.

Do this: take your last prompt, rewrite it with all 5 fixes, and compare the two answers side by side.

Send this to the friend who says AI gives bad answers.

Spend the refund, or turn it into $29,000?

Put $5,000 in an RRSP while earning $80,000 in Ontario, and your tax drops by about $1,480. It feels like a little bonus.

Here's the part nobody tells you: invest that $1,480 at 30, let it grow 10% a year, and leave it alone. Watch it grow:
At 40: about $4,000
At 50: about $10,800
At 60: about $29,000
One refund. Like a snowball, it just needs time. Do it every year and each refund starts its own snowball.

Do this on refund day (5 minutes):
1. When the deposit notice arrives, open your bank app.
2. Move the whole refund into your TFSA the same day, before it melts into everyday spending.
3. Invest it in your usual long-term fund. Cash sitting in a TFSA doesn't snowball.

The rule to remember: the refund goes back to work.

Can't crack it at your desk? Stand up. But know which kind of stuck you are.

THE STUDY: Stanford researchers tested people's ideas while they sat and while they walked. Walking raised creative output by about 60% on average. It worked on a treadmill facing a blank wall, so it's the walking, not the view. And the boost carried on when people sat back down after the walk.

THE PART MOST PEOPLE MISS: walking did NOT help the kind of thinking where there's one right answer. Brainstorming? Walk. Checking the numbers? Sit.

HOW TO DO IT:
1. Write the question on one line: "3 ways to fix the onboarding email."
2. Walk for 10 minutes: around the block, the hallway, the parking lot. No podcast, no scrolling.
3. Capture ideas as they come: a voice note or a pocket notebook. Don't judge them yet.
4. Sit back down while the boost lasts, and now pick the best one.

WHAT CHANGES: Day 1, you come back with more ideas than you left with. Week 1, "I'm stuck" turns into "I'll walk on it". Month 1, the walk becomes the first step of every hard problem.

The rule that stays: walk for ideas, sit for answers.

Do this: next time you're stuck, write the question down and walk 10 minutes with it. Then sit and pick.

Send this to the friend glued to their desk all day.

Follow for one small focus fix a day, each one backed by research.

#creativity #focus #productivity #walking #worklife

Bedtime turned into a battle again? Turn it into the best 20 minutes of the day.

STEP 0, THE HOUR BEFORE: the Canadian Paediatric Society says no screens for at least 1 hour before bedtime. Tablet and TV off, lights a little lower.

THEN THE SAME 3 STEPS, EVERY NIGHT (the American Academy of Pediatrics calls it Brush, Book, Bed):
1. Brush. You help, because little hands miss spots. Spit out the extra toothpaste, don't rinse: the fluoride left behind keeps working. (A rice-grain smear under 3, a pea-size blob from 3 to 6.)
2. Book. About 15 minutes, snuggled close. Let them pick, even if it's the same one for the 40th night.
3. Bed. Lights low, same time every night. Our favourite last line: "What was the best part of today?" Then tell them yours.

WHY IT WORKS: when the steps never change, your child knows exactly what comes next, and there's less to fight about. The book and the chat are pure connection time, every single day.

NIGHT 1 → WEEK 1 → YEAR 1: night 1, they test it. By week 1, the steps start to run themselves. Picture year 1: 365 bedtime stories, and a child who saves the best part of their day to tell you.

Do this: tonight, tablet off 1 hour before bed. Then brush, book, bed, and ask the best-part question.

The rule that stays: same steps, same words, every night.

Send this to someone in bedtime battles.

Follow for one calm thing a night, from bump to toddler.

General information only, not medical advice.

#bedtimeroutine #toddlerlife #screentime #canadianparents #bonding

No RESP yet? It's not too late. Here's the catch-up plan.

SOUND FAMILIAR? "We'll start next year." Then the baby is five.

THE PART NOBODY TELLS YOU: your child's grant room builds up every year from birth, even if you never opened an RESP. The government matches 20% of what you save through the Canada Education Savings Grant.

YOU PUT IN, THEY ADD (per year):
• $1,000 in → $200 added
• $2,500 in → $500 added (the normal yearly max)
• $5,000 in → $1,000 added (*only if you have unused room from past years)

Catching up, the grant can be up to $1,000 a year, until the full $7,200 per child is used.

CAN'T DO $5,000? $2,500 a year still gets the full $500, and any amount gets 20% added.

THE DEADLINE: grants stop at the end of the year your child turns 17. At 16 and 17 they only qualify if at least $2,000 went in before the end of the year they turned 15, or $100 a year in any 4 earlier years. So for an older child, start now.

Do this: this week, ask your bank to open an RESP and use your catch-up room. Bring your child's SIN.

The rule that stays: the room waits for you, but not forever.

Send this to a parent who never opened one.

Counting on CPP to pay your rent? Here's the real number.

The average new CPP pension at 65 is about $858 a month (canada.ca, 2026). The most anyone can get at 65 is about $1,508.
Old Age Security adds up to about $763 a month from 65 to 74 (October to December 2026).
Average CPP plus full OAS: about $1,620.0 a month. Now picture your rent or mortgage next to it.

Why so low? CPP was built to replace about a quarter of your work earnings, rising to a third as the CPP enhancement phases in. Never the whole thing.

Think of a house: CPP and OAS are the floor. Your own savings (TFSA, RRSP, a work pension) build the rest.

Now watch it grow. Just $50 a month from age 30, at 10% a year:
At 40: about $10,242
At 50: about $37,968
At 60: about $113,024
At 65: about $189,832
That's what one small automatic transfer can add on top of the floor.

Find your gap in 10 minutes:
1. Log in to My Service Canada Account and check your CPP estimate.
2. Add up your monthly bills today (housing, food, transport, phone, insurance).
3. Subtract CPP and OAS. The difference is your gap: what your savings need to cover.

The mindset: The Wealthy Barber's simplest lesson is to pay yourself first, automatically, before the bills. Retirement is just the day the bills keep coming and the paycheques stop.

Do this: this payday, set up $50 a month into your TFSA. Raise it with every raise.

The rule to remember: CPP is the floor, not the house.

Rereading the same line again? A 40-second break that actually works, and you don't even need to go outside.

THE STUDY: at the University of Melbourne, 150 students did a long, boring focus task. Halfway through, they took a 40-second break looking at a city rooftop. Half saw a roof covered in flowering plants. Half saw bare concrete. The green-roof group made fewer mistakes and held their concentration better afterwards.

THE TWIST: it wasn't a real roof. It was a photo on a computer screen. 40 seconds of looking at green was enough to give tired attention a short rest.

WHEN TO TAKE IT: you're rereading the same line, typos are piling up, you've opened the same tab twice. That's the signal.

WHERE TO LOOK:
1. A window with trees or grass. Best.
2. No window? A real plant on your desk, at eye level.
3. Neither? Set a green landscape photo as your laptop wallpaper and look at it between tasks.

NOT YOUR PHONE: a scroll is more things to read and react to. That's more load, not a rest. Eyes on green for 40 seconds, then straight back to the task.

WHAT CHANGES: Day 1, three 40-second breaks, under 2 minutes in total. Week 1, fewer "wait, what did I just read?" moments in the afternoon. It's the cheapest focus upgrade there is.

The rule that stays: rest your eyes on green.

Do this: today, put a plant or a green photo where you look between tasks.

Send this to the friend who scrolls on every break.

#focus #productivity #breaks #nature #worklife

How does ChatGPT actually know stuff? It learned patterns, not facts. 5 steps, zero jargon.

1. It read a library. Models like ChatGPT are trained on huge amounts of text: books, websites, code.
2. It learned patterns, not facts. It doesn't store a filing cabinet of answers. It learns which word tends to come next, like a friend who's read everything but can't quote the page.
3. It took a mountain of chips. Training runs on thousands of specialised chips, mostly made by Nvidia. That demand is why Nvidia became one of the world's most valuable companies.
4. People taught it manners. Humans ranked its answers, and it learned to give the kind people preferred.
5. You hit send. It builds the reply one word-piece at a time, picking a likely next piece each time.

Why this helps you: it explains why AI is brilliant at writing and still wrong about facts.

The rule to keep: it's a pattern machine, not a fact machine. Use it to draft, then verify.

Do this: next time AI answers, ask yourself: is this writing (trust it more) or a fact (check it)?

Send this to the friend who calls it magic.

#ai #chatgpt #howitworks #nvidia #learnai #hourback

When will baby say “mama”? Baby's first year of talking, one step at a time 👉

🍼 By 2 months: sounds that aren't crying. Answer every one. Copy the sound back.
🎵 By 4 months: cooing ("oooo", "aahh"), and sounds back when you talk. Say something, then pause. That pause is their turn.
😛 By 6 months: taking turns making sounds, raspberries, squeals. Blow one back.
🗣️ By 9 months: "mamamama", "babababa". Name what you touch: "Cup. Your cup." Short words, said often, in your home language.
💛 By 12 months: "mama", "dada" or another special name, and a bye-bye wave.

Why your part matters: a study at MIT found that the number of back-and-forth conversational turns, more than the number of words a child simply heard, was linked to activity in the brain's language areas. Talk with them, not at them.

These are the CDC's milestones: what most babies (75% or more) do by each age. Every baby has their own pace. If you're worried, ask your doctor; early help works best.

Do this: today, talk through one routine out loud (a diaper change, a bath). Name it, then pause for their turn.

Send this to someone with a baby under 1.

General information only, not medical advice.

#babytalk #babymilestones #bonding #newparents #canadianparents

posts.caption:
Sunday scaries? Plan your week in 20 minutes. Follow the Sunday route 👉

🧠 Stop 1: brain dump. Every open loop on paper. Unfinished tasks keep nagging at you; making a plan for them quiets them.
🔙 Stop 2: look back. What moved last week? In a study of about 12,000 work diary entries, making progress, even small wins, was the biggest boost to people's motivation.
🎯 Stop 3: pick 3 things that matter most. Not 12. Everything else is a maybe.
📅 Stop 4: block them. Give each a time and a place. Plans with a when and a where get followed far more often.
🌅 Stop 5: pick Monday's highlight, one thing that would make the day a win, and do it first.

Why it works: you decide once, calmly, on Sunday, instead of 40 times under pressure during the week. Cal Newport's time-blocking and Make Time's daily highlight are both built on that idea.

Do this: this Sunday, set a 20-minute timer and drive the route.

Send this to the friend whose Mondays are chaos.

#weeklyplanning #productivity #timeblocking #focus #habits
