posts.caption:
Consultants using AI were 25% faster. On some tasks, they did worse. Is AI good at your task? Pick it and follow the line 👉

In 2023, researchers from Harvard, Wharton and MIT ran an experiment with 758 consultants at Boston Consulting Group. Some got GPT-4, some didn't, same tasks.

✍️ Inside what they called the "jagged frontier" (drafting, rewriting, brainstorming, product ideas): consultants using AI finished 12.2% more tasks, 25.1% faster, with over 40% higher quality.
🔢 Facts and numbers: verify. AI can sound sure and be wrong. Ask for sources, then check them.
🧩 Outside the frontier (a task built to trip AI up, mixing numbers and interviews): consultants using AI were 19 percentage points less likely to get the right answer than those working without it. They trusted it where they shouldn't have.

Why it matters: AI isn't good or bad at "work". It's brilliant at some tasks and quietly weak at others that look similar. Ethan Mollick, one of the authors, calls learning that line the key skill.

Do this: this week, sort your tasks into 3 piles: AI drafts it; AI helps and I check; mine alone.

Send this to your team's AI skeptic, and its biggest fan.

#ai #futureofwork #chatgpt #productivity #hourback

posts.caption:
Your parents taking CPP early? Here's what 60, 65 and 70 pay.

Every month you start before 65, your CPP drops 0.6%. Every month you wait after 65, it grows 0.7%. And it's for life.
That's up to 36% less at 60, or up to 42% more at 70.

Watch it grow, at the 2026 maximum, per month:
Start at 60: about $965
Start at 65: about $1,508
Start at 70: about $2,140
(Most people get less than the maximum; your own estimate is in My Service Canada Account.)

The rule to remember: each year you wait after 65 adds about 8.4% (0.7% × 12), for life, and it's indexed to inflation.

The honest part: waiting isn't right for everyone. Your health, your savings and when you stop working all matter. Die With Zero makes the other side of the case well: money is for living, and some years are worth more than others. Many people use savings to bridge the gap so they can start CPP later.

Do this tonight (5 minutes):
1. Log in to My Service Canada Account.
2. Open Canada Pension Plan and find your estimate at 60, 65 and 70.
3. Write the three numbers down and talk them through with your partner (or your parents).

Send this to your parents. Seriously.

Follow for one money move a day, in plain words.

#CPP #retirementcanada #retirementplanning #personalfinancecanada #moneyfoundations

Skimming just the AI summary? Apple's AI wrote a headline. It was false.

In December 2024, Apple Intelligence's notification summaries condensed a BBC News alert and claimed that Luigi Mangione, the suspect in a high-profile shooting, had shot himself. He hadn't. After complaints from the BBC, Apple paused AI summaries for news apps in January 2025 and started showing other summaries in italics so you know they're AI-written.

Why: a summary squeezes the facts. When AI squeezes, it can drop a word like "not" or merge two stories, and the result still sounds completely confident.

The rule to keep: a summary is a pointer, not the story.

Do this: when AI sums up news, an email or a letter, open the original before you act on it.

posts.caption:
First cold morning? Coat off, then buckle. The warm layer goes on top of the straps.

Why: puffy coats and snowsuits squash flat in a crash. That leaves the harness loose, with room for a child to slip out of the straps.

THE PINCH TEST: buckle up and tighten. Then try to pinch the strap flat at their chest. If you can pinch a fold of strap, it's too loose. Tighten until you can't.

TO STAY WARM:
1. Thin, close-fitting layers underneath (a thin fleece is fine).
2. Buckle, tighten, pinch test.
3. Coat on backwards over the buckled straps, or a blanket on top.
4. Hat, mittens and socks.
Babies usually need one more layer than you. Take the blanket off once the car warms up so they don't overheat.

Do this: coat off, buckle, blanket on. Every cold morning.

Send this to whoever does daycare drop-off.

Follow for one calm thing a night, from bump to toddler.

General information only, not medical advice.

#carseatsafety #winterbaby #newparents #canadianparents #toddlermom

posts.caption:
Coffee at 4 pm? Your sleep noticed, even if you didn't.

THE STUDY: in a sleep study, people had 400 mg of caffeine, about 2 to 3 cups of coffee, 6 hours before bed. Measured in the lab, they slept more than an hour less. And here's the loud part: they didn't notice. Their own reports said they slept fine. (It was a small study of 12 adults, but it's why sleep doctors say 6 hours is the minimum.)

YOUR CUTOFF, DONE FOR YOU: bedtime minus 6 hours.
Bed at 10 pm: last cup by 4 pm.
Bed at 11 pm: last cup by 5 pm.
Bed at midnight: last cup by 6 pm.
Earlier is better if you can.

COUNT THE SNEAKY ONES: black and green tea, cola, energy drinks, pre-workout powder and some pain relievers all contain caffeine. Decaf has a little, but far less.

3 PM SLUMP INSTEAD: a 10-minute walk, or 40 seconds looking at something green, then back to work.

WHAT CHANGES: Night 1, nothing you can feel, and that's the point: you're getting back sleep you never knew you lost. Week 1, that's up to an hour a night back, if you were drinking late.

The rule that stays: bedtime minus 6.

Do this: set a phone reminder at your cutoff time that just says "last coffee".

Send this to the friend on their 4th coffee.

Follow for one small focus fix a day, each one backed by research.

#sleep #caffeine #coffee #focus #healthyhabits

General information only, not medical advice.

posts.caption:
Sore gums tonight? A cold cloth and a gentle rub. Two simple things that help.

THE RUB: wash your hands, then gently massage the sore spot with a fingertip or knuckle.

THE CLOTH: wet a clean washcloth, twist it, and chill it in the freezer for a bit. Let them chew it. Nothing frozen rock-hard: hard objects can hurt tender gums.

SKIP: teething necklaces and beads (amber, wood, marble or silicone): choking and strangulation risk. And numbing gels with benzocaine: they can be dangerous for children, and drool washes gels away anyway.

THE CATCH: a fever isn't a teething sign. Fever, diarrhea or a lot of crying? Call your baby's doctor.

Do this: tonight, twist a wet cloth and put it in the freezer, ready for the next sore night.

Send this to someone in the teething months.

Follow for one calm thing a night, from bump to toddler.

General information only, not medical advice.

posts.caption:
Too sick to work for months? Here's what EI pays.

EI sickness benefits pay 55% of your average weekly earnings, up to $729 a week in 2026, for up to 26 weeks.

Earn $80,000 a year? Your usual week is about $1,538. EI pays $729. That's a gap of about $809 every week, while rent, groceries and the car payment keep coming. And after 26 weeks, EI sickness stops.

The part nobody tells you: some illnesses and injuries keep people off work much longer. Long-term disability (LTD) insurance replaces part of your pay while you can't work. Many people have some through work, but don't know how much.

Do this this week (10 minutes):
1. Open your benefits booklet or portal and search "long-term disability".
2. Write down three things: what % of pay it covers, the waiting period before it starts, and how long it pays.
3. If you're self-employed or have none, get a quote from a licensed advisor, and ask: "Is this own-occupation or any-occupation coverage?"

The mindset: your ability to earn is worth more than anything you own. I Will Teach You to Be Rich and The Psychology of Money both come back to it: protect the downside first, then grow.

The rule to remember: your paycheque is your biggest asset. Insure it.

Send this to the friend who says "I'm healthy."

Follow for one money move a day, in plain words.

#disabilityinsurance #EI #personalfinancecanada #insurance #moneyfoundations

posts.caption:
New habit keeps not sticking? Floss before or after brushing shows why, and the fix works for any habit.

THE STUDY: researchers asked 50 people to floss every day, either just before or just after brushing. The "after" group built the stronger habit, and it was still there 8 months later.

WHY: brushing is something you already do without thinking. Floss right after it, and brushing becomes the trigger. The new habit rides on the old one. Atomic Habits calls this habit stacking; Tiny Habits calls the old habit your anchor.

THE METHOD:
1. Anchor: pick something you already do every day, in the same place (brushing, the first coffee, sitting down at your desk).
2. Tiny: make the new habit so small it's silly. BJ Fogg's famous version: floss one tooth. You'll often do more; one still counts.
3. Visible: put the floss on top of the toothbrush, so you can't brush without seeing it.
4. Right after: not "sometime tonight". The second the anchor ends.

THE RECIPE TO KEEP: "After I [old habit], I will [tiny new habit]." After I pour my coffee, I'll open my budget sheet. After I sit on the train, I'll read one page.

WHAT CHANGES: Day 1, one tooth. Week 1, you feel odd brushing without it. Around 2 months on average, it's automatic (in a study of 96 people, 66 days on average; anywhere from 18 to 254). Year 1: 365 nights of flossing, from one sentence.

The rule that stays: hang the new habit on an old one.

Do this: tonight, brush, then floss right after. Same sink, every night.

Send this to the friend who never flosses.

Follow for one small focus fix a day, each one backed by research.

#habits #habitstacking #selfimprovement #productivity #behaviorchange

“Just a little honey on the soother?” Not before their first birthday. Not even a tiny bit.

Health Canada says: no honey of any kind for babies under 1. Not in food, water or formula, and never on a soother. Cooked or pasteurized honey isn't safe either.

Here's why: honey can carry botulism spores. Heat doesn't kill them, and a baby's gut can't fight them yet. After age 1, healthy kids have the gut bacteria to handle them.

Call your doctor right away if a baby is constipated, floppy, too weak to cry or suck as usual, or has trouble breathing or swallowing.

THE GRANDPARENT SCRIPT: "No honey before her first birthday. Not even a little on the soother. The doctor's rule, not mine."

Do this: today, check baby's snacks and cereals for honey on the label. Then tell the grandparents.

The rule that stays: no honey before 1. Not a drop.

Send this to the grandparents.

General information only, not medical advice.

Payday. Where should the money go first? Follow this order.

1. A safety net: one month of bills in savings, then build toward 3 to 6 months.
2. If your employer matches retirement savings, put in enough to get the full match. Skip it and you leave part of your pay on the table.
3. Then invest in your TFSA, in a low-fee index fund, and leave it alone.

Why this order: the safety net keeps a surprise bill off your credit card. The match only pays if you put money in. Then time does the rest.

The catch: carrying card debt at 20% or more? Paying it down usually comes before step 3.

Do this: this payday, set up one automatic transfer to stop 1. Add the others as you go.

Not guaranteed. Returns vary. Education, not advice.

How long do you stay on one screen before switching? In 2004 it was about 2.5 minutes. Guess first 👀

Researcher Gloria Mark has timed how long people stay on one screen before switching. In 2004: about two and a half minutes. In her studies from 2016 to 2020: 47 seconds, on average.

Why it matters: every switch costs a little focus, and 47-second hops add up to a day that felt busy but didn't get far.

Your bank texts “Was this you?” That's AI predicting. AI made prediction cheap. Here's what gets valuable.

Your bank texts "Was this you?" Your map says "12 minutes faster this way." Both are AI predictions.

The big idea, from three University of Toronto economists (Ajay Agrawal, Joshua Gans and Avi Goldfarb, in Prediction Machines and Power and Prediction): AI's core skill is prediction, filling in what you don't know from what you do.

When light got cheap, we lit everything. Now prediction is getting cheap, and it's showing up everywhere.

So what gets valuable? Judgment: knowing what matters and what to do about the prediction. AI drafts three options; your value is picking the right one and knowing why.

The electricity lesson: factories first just swapped steam engines for electric motors. The big gains came decades later, when they redesigned the whole factory around electricity. The authors argue AI is in that in-between stage now.

The rule to keep: AI predicts. You judge.

Do this: this week, spot one prediction AI makes for you. Ask: which decision is still mine?

Can't make yourself start? It's the feeling, not the task. Pick your reason and follow the line 👉

🥱 It's boring: make it a game. Set a 25-minute timer (the Pomodoro Technique) and a small treat when it rings.
🏔️ It's too big: write the next physical step, like "Open the doc. Type the title." Do only that. (Getting Things Done calls it the next action.)
😰 You're scared it'll be bad: allow a bad first draft. Anne Lamott's Bird by Bird made this famous. Fixing beats starting from nothing.

Chatbot, reasoner, agent… what comes next? OpenAI's 5 levels on the way to AGI. Climb them 👉

In July 2024, Bloomberg reported that OpenAI uses five levels to track progress toward AGI (OpenAI hasn't published it as an official framework). What each one looks like in the real world:

💬 Level 1, chatbots: AI with natural conversation. ChatGPT, November 2022.
🧠 Level 2, reasoners: human-level problem solving. OpenAI's o1 (September 2024) was built to think step by step before answering.
🤖 Level 3, agents: AI that takes actions for you. Anthropic's computer use (October 2024) and ChatGPT agent (July 2025) click, type and complete tasks in a browser, asking before anything important.
🔬 Level 4, innovators: AI that helps invent and discover. Early signs are in science: Google DeepMind's AlphaFold, which predicts protein structures, earned Demis Hassabis and John Jumper a share of the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
🏢 Level 5, organizations: AI that can do all the work of an organization. Not here.

Why it matters: "AGI is here" and "AI is just autocomplete" are both lazy. The levels let you place any announcement on the map.

Do this: next time a headline says AGI, ask which level, then check what actually shipped.

Your TFSA, after you die? If nobody is named on it, it goes through your estate.

When you open a TFSA or RRSP, it asks who gets the money if you die. That person is your beneficiary (for a spouse on a TFSA, it can be a "successor holder").

Why it matters: with a name there, the money can go straight to that person, outside your estate. In Ontario, the estate administration tax is $15 for every $1,000 over $50,000, so $100,000 going through the estate costs about $750. Money paid to a named beneficiary isn't counted. It's also usually faster.

Do this tonight (10 minutes):
1. Log in to your bank or broker and open each TFSA, RRSP and FHSA.
2. Find "Beneficiary" or "Successor holder" (often under account details or documents). Blank, or an ex? Fix it.
3. Check your work life insurance and pension in your benefits portal too.
Moved in with someone, had a baby, or split up since you opened them? Update every one.

The rule to remember: life changed? Change the name.

Rules differ by province (in Quebec, most designations go in your will). Send this to your partner.

Follow for one money move a day, in plain words.

New dad, feeling left out? You don't need to feed the baby to bond with them.

Bonding is built in small, daily care: the same jobs, done by the same person, every day. Here's how to own a few.

Do this: tonight, take bath time. Same time, same song, your job, from now on.

Studying with your playlist on? Check the words.

THE STUDY: students read passages and answered questions in quiet, with instrumental music, or with songs with lyrics. Songs with words lowered their scores, even songs they liked. Music without words did about as well as quiet.

WHY: your brain has one channel for language. Lyrics and the page are both words, so they fight for it. Instrumental music doesn't.

THE PLAYLIST METHOD:
1. Build one focus playlist with no words: classical, film scores, video game soundtracks, lo-fi beats.
2. Keep it low, just loud enough to cover the room.
3. Play the same playlist every focus hour. Over time, the first track becomes your start signal.
4. Save the songs you love for chores and workouts. That's a reward, not a distraction.

THE HONEST PART: it was a small study (30 students), about reading. For tasks without words, like sorting files, lyrics may matter less.

WHAT CHANGES: Day 1, the page gets your full channel. Week 1, the first track means "we're working now". Month 1, you sit down, press play, and you're in.

The rule that stays: words or music, not both.

Do this: make one no-lyrics playlist tonight and use it for your next focus hour.

Send this to your study buddy.

Follow for one small focus fix a day, each one backed by research.

#studytips #focus #studymusic #productivity #deepwork

posts.caption:
Everything takes longer than you think? It's not just you. You're not bad at planning. Everyone is.

THE STUDY: students guessed their thesis would take 34 days on average. It took 56. Even their worst-case guess, 49 days, was too short. Only about 3 in 10 finished in the time they predicted. It's called the planning fallacy.

WHY IT HAPPENS: when we plan, we picture the day where everything goes right: no sick kid, no slow reply, no file that won't open. And we quietly ignore how long the last one actually took.

THE FIRST FIX:
1. Before you guess, ask "how long did this take LAST time?", not "how long should it take?"
2. Look it up if you can: your calendar, old emails, the last report's date.
3. Then add half again. Think 2 hours? Plan 3. Think a week? Plan a week and a half.

WHAT CHANGES: Day 1, your plan looks worse on paper. Week 1, you finish when you said you would, maybe for the first time in a while. Month 1, people start trusting your "by Friday".

The rule that stays: plan from your past, not your hopes.

Do this: today, add half again to your next time guess.

Send this to the friend who says "it'll be quick." Part 2 tonight at 7: break it into steps, the fix that's backed by research.

Why that helps: a hard week isn't proof you're doing it wrong. It's a stage, and for most babies it eases.

What helps, in order (Canadian Paediatric Society):
1. Check first: hungry, wet diaper, too hot or cold, fever.
2. Hold them. You can't spoil a baby by picking them up.
3. Dim the lights, shush, sway, or walk them close to you.

The catch: under 3 months with a fever? Get care right away. And if it's too much, put baby in their crib, step out and take a moment. It's OK to ask for help.

Do this: next cry, check first, then hold close and sway.

Send this to someone in week 3.

Follow for one calm thing a night, from bump to toddler.

Your TFSA room could be $109,000.

If you were 18 or older in 2009 and have lived in Canada since, every year's limit has added up: $109,000 by 2026.
Watch it build: $5,000 in 2009, $41,000 by 2015, $69,500 by 2020, $109,000 by 2026. Unused room never expires. It just waits for you.

Why it matters: every dollar of growth inside a TFSA is tax-free, forever, even when you take it out.

Now watch it grow. Fill it with $7,000 a year from age 30, growing 10% a year:
At 40: about $111,562
At 50: about $400,925
At 60: about $1,151,458
All of it tax-free. Can't do $7,000? Any amount grows the same way, just smaller.

The part nobody tells you: put in more than your room, and the CRA charges 1% a month on the extra, every month it stays in.

Your room in 5 minutes:

2. Find "TFSA room". It's your room as of January 1.
3. Subtract anything you've already put in this year. That's what you can still add.

Felt like you did nothing this week? You probably did more than you think. You just can't see it.

THE STUDY: Harvard researchers had 238 people at 7 companies write a short diary every workday, about 12,000 entries in all. On people's best days, one thing showed up far more than anything else: making progress on work that mattered, even a small win. On their worst days: setbacks.

WHY YOU FEEL BEHIND: a to-do list only shows what's left, and it never ends. Four Thousand Weeks makes the point bluntly: you will never get to the bottom of it. So if the list is your scoreboard, you lose every day. A done list shows how far you came.

THE DONE LIST:
1. Every evening, 2 minutes. Same notebook, same spot (next to the laptop, by the kettle).
2. Write 3 things you moved forward. Finished or not.
3. Small counts: "sent the quote", "fixed one bug", "called Mom back", "10 minutes on the budget".
4. Friday: read the week's page before you plan next week.

BAD-DAY RESCUE: when you feel behind, read last week's list before you open this week's to-do list. Proof beats feelings.

WHAT CHANGES: Day 1, three lines. Week 1, 15 wins you would have forgotten by Saturday. Year 1, a notebook full of proof that you're moving.

The rule that stays: count what moved, not what's left.

Do this: tonight, write down 3 things you moved forward this week. Small ones count. Then do it every evening.

Send this to the friend who feels behind.

Put TFSA money back too soon? The room you took out only comes back next January 1.

Say you take out $5,000 in March and put it back in June. Feels harmless. But the contribution room from a withdrawal only comes back on January 1 of the next year. If your TFSA was already full (no other room left), that $5,000 is an over-contribution, and the CRA charges 1% a month on the extra for as long as it stays in: $50 a month, about $350 from June to December.

Do this: Wait until January 1 to put it back. Not sure if you have room left? Check your TFSA room in CRA My Account. It shows your room as of January 1, so subtract what you've already put in this year.

Moving money between banks? Ask for a direct transfer. It doesn't count as a withdrawal.

Already did it? Take the extra out as soon as you can, and look up form RC243 (the TFSA return) on canada.ca.

Send this to your TFSA friend.

Follow for one money move a day, in plain words.

It's OK to step away. Still crying, and you're at your limit? That happens to loving parents too.

Why it's OK: the Canadian Paediatric Society says that if you're feeling frustrated, take a deep breath, put your baby in a safe place like their crib, and take a moment to calm yourself. Taking a break can help, and it's OK to ask for help.

The plan:
1. Crib first: baby on their back.
2. Step out. Breathe. Take a moment.
3. Text your person: “Can you come?”
4. Go back when you're calmer.

Never shake a baby. Shaking can cause lifelong injury or even death.

If baby seems unwell, or is under 3 months with a fever, get care right away.

Do this: tonight, pick who you'll text, and tell them they're it.

Send this to every new parent. Part 2 of 2.

"It'll take an hour." It won't. Here's the fix that's backed by research.

THE RESEARCH: in a study, people who listed every step of a task before guessing how long it would take made longer, more realistic guesses. Hidden steps are where the time goes. It works best for tasks with lots of parts.

HOW TO DO IT ("update the website", unpacked):
1. Find the old photos (15 min)
2. Wait for the new ones from Sam (1 day of waiting, 5 min of asking)
3. Write the new text (45 min)
4. Send it for a check, then fix the comments (30 min + a day)
5. Upload and test on your phone (20 min)
"An hour" was really about 2 hours of work and 2 days of waiting. (The website task is made up for this post.)

THE HIDDEN STEPS TO ALWAYS ADD: waiting for someone, setup (logins, finding files), the back-and-forth, travel, and the check at the end.

WITH THIS MORNING'S FIX: compare your total with how long it took last time, and if they disagree, trust last time.

WHAT CHANGES: Day 1, Monday's plan fits inside Monday. Week 1, fewer 9 pm "how is this not done?" moments. Month 1, your estimates become the ones people plan around.

The rule that stays: guess the steps, not the task.

Do this: tonight, take Monday's biggest task, write down its steps, then guess the time.

Gulping, then fussing, every feed? Pause and burp partway through the feed, not just at the end.

Why: babies swallow air while they feed, and swallowed air makes them fussy. Fussing makes them gulp even more air. A pause and a change of position slows the gulping.

WHEN:
Bottle: burp after every 2 to 3 ounces (60–90 ml).
Breastfeeding: burp when you switch sides.

HOW (pick one):
1. Over your shoulder: baby upright, head on your shoulder, your hand supporting their head and back.
2. Sitting on your lap: support their chest and head with one hand, gently pat their back with the other.
3. Tummy-down across your lap: back up, head a little higher than their chest.
Pat gently, or rub slow circles on their back.

After the feed, keep them upright for 10 to 15 minutes to help with spit-up.

Do this: next feed, pause partway, burp, then finish.

Send this to whoever does the night feeds.

Follow for one calm thing a night, from bump to toddler.

General information only, not medical advice.

#newbornbaby #babyfeeding #newparents #canadianparents #babytips

posts.caption:
How long until $10K is $20K? Divide 72 by the yearly return. At 8% a year: about 9 years.

It's called the rule of 72. It's a shortcut for compounding: growth earning growth.

THE MATHS: $10,000 growing 8% a year is $19,990 after 9 years (1.08 to the power of 9 = 1.999). At 6%: 72 ÷ 6 = about 12 years. At 10%: about 7 years.

WHY IT MATTERS: every doubling builds on the last one. $10K becomes $20K, then $40K, then $80K, about every 9 years at 8%. Fees and starting late cut doublings off the end.

THE CATCH: real returns jump around year to year. The rule shows the shape, not a promise. Fees come off the return first: 8% minus a 2% fee is 6%, and that's 12 years, not 9.

Do this: open your investing app, find the yearly return after fees, and divide 72 by it.

Send this to your "I'll start later" friend.

Follow for one money move a day, in plain words.

Education only, not financial advice. Not guaranteed. Returns vary.

#ruleof72 #compoundinterest #investing #personalfinance #moneytips

Monday plans gone by noon? Write down when and where you'll do the one that matters.

Why it works: "I'll do the report today" is a wish. "At 9, at my desk, I'll start the report" is a plan your brain can catch. When 9 o'clock and the desk show up, the next step is already decided.

THE RESEARCH: in a UK study of 248 people (Milne, Orbell & Sheeran, 2002), 91% of those who wrote down when and where they'd exercise did it in the next week. In the other groups, fewer than 4 in 10 did.

HOW:
1. Pick one task for today.
2. Write: "At [time], at [place], I'll [first step]."
3. Put it where you'll see it: a sticky note on your screen, or a calendar event with the sentence as the title.

THE CATCH: one or two of these a day. Ten of them is just a new to-do list.

Do this: write one now on a sticky note: "At 9, at my desk, I'll open the report."

Send this to your Monday-chaos friend.

Follow for one small focus fix a day, each one backed by research.

Paid Friday. Broke by Wednesday? The habit: pay yourself first.

Rich Habits, Decoded No. 1. Each episode takes one money habit and shows you how to do it on a normal paycheque.

WHAT IT MEANS: savings come out the day your pay lands, automatically, before you can spend it. You live on what's left, instead of saving what's left.

WHY IT WORKS: you don't rely on willpower. Save more with every raise: in the 'Save More Tomorrow' study, workers who saved more at each pay raise went from saving 3.5% of their pay to 13.6% over 40 months (about 3 years).

HOW TO DO IT (10 minutes in your banking app):
1. Open a separate savings account (ideally one that pays interest and that you don't see every day).
2. Set an automatic transfer for payday. Start at 10%; if that's too much, start at 1% or 2%.
3. Every raise: add 1 percentage point.
4. Leave it. The point is not having to decide again.

THE CATCH: if you carry card debt at 20%+, point the automatic payment at that first. Keep a small buffer so the transfer never bounces.

Do this: set one automatic transfer for your next payday, even if it's $10.

Rich Habits, Decoded No. 2 is Wednesday at 5 pm.

Education only, not financial advice.

Follow for one money move a day, in plain words.

posts.caption:
It's 3 am. You're feeding. Your eyes keep closing.

3 am Club No. 1: where you feed matters most on the nights you're running on empty.

THE RULE: falling asleep with your baby on a sofa or armchair is one of the riskiest places to doze off together. The Lullaby Trust says the risk of SIDS is 50 times higher when a baby sleeps on a sofa or armchair with an adult. If there's any chance you'll nod off, move before you sit down.

SET UP YOUR 3 AM SPOT BEFORE BED (5 minutes):
1. Pick the spot now, while you're awake: never the sofa or armchair. Safest is baby back in their own crib beside you.
2. If you feed in bed and might doze, keep pillows and duvets away from baby.
3. Baby's own sleep space (crib or bassinet, flat, firm, empty) within arm's reach.
4. Water, a dim light and your phone charger by the spot, so you don't end up on the sofa.
5. After the feed, baby goes back in their own space, on their back.

THE CATCH: no spot is risk-free if you've been drinking, smoke, or take medicine that makes you drowsy, or if your baby was premature or low birth weight. Then baby sleeps in their own space only.

Do this: tonight, set up your 3 am spot before you go to bed.

3 am Club No. 2 is Wednesday at 5 pm: what to do when the baby is wide awake at 3 am.

Follow for one calm thing a night, from bump to toddler.

General information only, not medical advice.

posts.caption:
Inbox open all day again? Today's word: Batch.

One Word No. 2 (No. 1 was "Later"). Each episode is one word that guards your focus.

THE RESEARCH: in a 2-week study, people who checked email only 3 times a day felt less stressed than when they could check as often as they liked.

HOW TO BATCH:
1. Pick 3 times: say 9:30, 1:00 and 4:30.
2. Close the email tab (and turn off email notifications) between them.
3. At each check: reply, file or schedule. Nothing stays "unread to deal with later".
4. Worried about missing something urgent? Tell people to call or text for urgent things.

THE CATCH: if your job is answering email (support, dispatch), batch something else, like chat or news.

Do this: tomorrow, write your 3 check times on a sticky note and close the tab.

One Word No. 3 is Wednesday at 5 pm.

Follow for one small focus fix a day, each one backed by research.

#focus #productivity #email #deepwork #oneword

AI, for real · Day 8. One real test of what AI can do, with the output shown.

WHY IT WORKS: a chatbot fills every gap in your request with the most average guess. Asking it to question you first makes it name the gaps, and you fill them with your real details.

Request (made up): "Plan a birthday dinner for 6 people, $150 budget. Before you answer, ask me 3 questions."

posts.caption:
Stranger in your best photo? Your phone's AI can erase them in seconds.

Why it works: the AI looks at what's around the person (sand, wall, sky) and paints that in where they stood.

iPhone (15 Pro or newer, iOS 18.1 or later): open the photo in Photos, tap Edit, then Clean Up, then tap, brush or circle what you want gone.
Any iPhone or Android: open the photo in the free Google Photos app, tap Edit, find Magic Eraser (Actions), circle the person, tap Erase, then Done.

The catch: zoom in before you post. Busy backgrounds (fences, text, crowds) can come out smudged. Google Photos needs 3 GB of RAM or more, and some tools download first.

Privacy tip: don't erase people to pass a photo off as the real moment, and ask before posting anyone who's still in it.

Do this: Photos, Edit, Clean Up, circle them.

posts.caption:
Scratches on their face again? Keep those tiny nails short and smooth, so they can't scratch themselves.

THE GENTLE WAY: a soft emery board. File each nail smooth. Baby nail clippers or small round-ended safety scissors work too. Go slowly: a nick to the fingertip hurts and bleeds.

THE EASY TIME: while they're asleep. Or right after a bath, if they'll lie quietly.

HOW OFTEN: in the early weeks, fingernails can need a trim about twice a week. Toenails grow slower: once or twice a month.

SKIP: biting them short. Biting can pass an infection to their finger.

Do this: tonight, file their nails while they sleep.

Send this to someone with a brand-new baby.

Follow for one calm thing a night, from bump to toddler.

General information only, not medical advice.

#newborn #babycare #newparents #canadianparents #babytips

posts.caption:
Bath water too hot? Dip your elbow in before your baby goes in.

The water should feel warm, not hot. The NHS says it should feel about the same as your body temperature on your elbow. The AAP says warm, not hot, on the inside of your wrist or elbow.

How to run it:
1. Run the cold water first, then add the hot.
2. Mix it well so there are no hot patches.
3. Elbow in. Warm, not hot? Then baby in.
For a newborn basin, the AAP suggests about 2 inches (5 cm) of water.

The one rule with no exceptions: never leave your baby alone in the bath, not even for a second. If the phone or the door goes, take your baby with you.

Do this: Elbow in. Then baby in.

Send this to whoever does bath time.

Follow for one calm thing a night, from bump to toddler.

General information only, not medical advice.

posts.caption:
Paid on time, but still charged interest? Here's why.

Pay only the minimum and you pay interest on everything you didn't pay. On a $3,000 balance at 20% a year, paying the $90 minimum still costs about $48.50 in interest that month. The maths: ($3,000 − $90) × 20% ÷ 12 = $48.50.

Pay the whole statement balance by the due date and new purchases cost $0 in interest. You get at least 21 days to pay, with no interest (Canada; most US cards have a grace period too). Carry a balance and you usually lose it: interest starts on new purchases from the day you buy.

Do this: set autopay to full balance. In your card's app or online banking, find Autopay and pick the full statement balance.

The catch: only do this if your chequing account can cover the whole bill. If it can't, set a fixed amount above the minimum. Cash advances and balance transfers have no interest-free period.

Send this to whoever just got their first credit card.

Follow for one money move a day, in plain words.

#creditcards #personalfinance #moneytips #debtfree #moneyfoundations

posts.caption:
Breastfeeding? 5 signs it's going well. Check the diapers, not the clock.

What to look for (NHS):
• From day 5 after birth: at least 6 heavy, wet diapers every 24 hours.
• From day 4 after birth: at least 2 soft, yellow poops a day for the first few weeks.
• Feeds start with a few quick sucks, then long, rhythmic sucks and swallows.
• Baby seems calm during feeds and lets go of the breast on their own.
• Steady weight gain after the first few days (some early loss is normal).

THE CATCH: these signs are for breastfed babies. Worried about how much milk your baby is getting? Ask your midwife, nurse or a breastfeeding specialist early.

Do this: count wet diapers for 24 hours. A tick in your phone notes for each one is enough.

Send this to someone in their first weeks.

Kid's fractions and you forgot how? Ask AI for hints, not the answer.

Why it works: "Don't give the answer" changes what AI does. Instead of solving it, it breaks the problem into questions you can ask out loud, so your kid does the thinking.

How: open ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini. Type your kid's grade and the question, then add: "Give me 3 short hints I can say out loud, one at a time. Don't give the answer."

ChatGPT also has Study mode, free on all plans: tap +, then Study. It's built to ask questions instead of answering, though OpenAI says it can still give a direct answer sometimes.

The catch: work out the answer yourself before the last hint, and check your school's rules on AI for homework.

Privacy tip: type or crop to just the question. Leave out your kid's name, school, teacher and any photo of them.

posts.caption:
Swaddling? Leave room for the hips, so the legs can bend up and out.

Why: the AAP says straightening and tightly wrapping a baby's legs can lead to hip dislocation or hip dysplasia. Hip-healthy swaddling lets the legs bend up and out.

How to wrap (AAP):
1. Use only a thin blanket. Spread it flat with one corner folded down.
2. Lay baby face-up, head above the fold.
3. Wrap one side corner over, then the other.
4. Fold or twist the bottom loosely and tuck it under one side.
5. Check the chest: you should fit at least two or three fingers between the wrap and their chest.

When to stop: as soon as your baby shows any signs of trying to roll over. Some babies start as early as 2 months. Always put baby to sleep on their back. Swaddling can make babies overheat, so watch for sweating, damp hair or flushed cheeks.

Do this: Tonight, leave room at the hips.

Send this to whoever does the night feeds.

Follow for one calm thing a night, from bump to toddler.

General information only, not medical advice.

posts.caption:
Exam next week? Stop rereading. Testing yourself works better.

Why it works: pulling an idea back out of your memory makes it easier to find next time. Rereading just makes the page look familiar.

The study: students learned a short passage. One group read it 4 times. Another read it once, then wrote down everything they remembered, 3 times. A week later, the write-from-memory group recalled 61% of it and the read-it-4-times group 40%. The readers also felt more sure they'd remember it.

The catch: 5 minutes after studying, reading looked better (83% vs 71%). The gain shows up days later, which is when your exam is.

Do this: Shut the book. Write what you remember. Then open it and check what you missed.

Send this to whoever's cramming this week.

Follow for one small focus fix a day, each one backed by research.

#studytips #studyhacks #focus #learning #lockedhour

posts.caption:
$15 lunch, every workday? The habit: pack lunch 3 days a week.

Rich Habits, Decoded No. 2. Each episode takes one money habit and shows you how to do it on a normal paycheque.

THE MATHS (prices made up for this post: $15 to buy lunch, $4 to pack one, 48 work weeks a year):
• Buy lunch all 5 days: $15 × 5 × 48 = $3,600 a year.
• Pack 3 days, buy 2: ($30 + $12) × 48 = $2,016 a year.
• You keep $1,584 a year, and you still buy lunch twice a week.

WHY IT WORKS: daily spending is small enough that you never decide on it. Picking 3 set days turns it into one decision a week, and the 2 bought lunches stop feeling like a slip.

HOW (one Sunday, 30 minutes):
1. Pick your 3 packed days. Same days every week.
2. Cook one big batch on Sunday and split it into 3 containers.
3. Check your own numbers: what you really pay for lunch, minus what a packed one costs you.
4. Move the difference to savings on payday, so it doesn't just get spent somewhere else.

THE CATCH: the saving only counts if it goes somewhere. Your prices will be different, so use your own.

Do this: this Sunday, cook once and pack 3 lunches for the week.

Rich Habits, Decoded No. 3 is Friday at 5 pm.

Education only, not financial advice.

Follow for one money move a day, in plain words.

WHY IT WORKS: newborns don't know night from day yet. The NHS says you can teach the difference from the start: keep nights dull and days bright, and your baby gradually learns that night-time is for sleeping. It takes weeks, not one night.

AT 3 AM:
1. Keep the lights down low. A small lamp, not the big light.
2. Don't talk much, and keep your voice quiet.
3. Don't play, even if they're smiling at you.
4. Change the diaper only if it needs it.
5. Fed and changed? Put baby straight back down, on their back, in their own crib.

IN THE DAY: open the curtains, play, and don't tiptoe around everyday noise when they nap.

THE CATCH: waking at night to feed is normal, and young babies need it. Worried about how your baby sleeps or feeds? Talk to your doctor, nurse or health visitor.

Do this: tonight, at the first wake-up, leave the big light off and keep your voice to a whisper.

posts.caption:
Your $10,000 earning 0% interest? If prices rise, money that earns no interest buys less every year.

WHY: prices rise over time. The Bank of Canada and the US Federal Reserve both aim for about 2% inflation a year. Money earning 0% doesn't keep up, so the same dollars buy a little less each year.

THE MATHS (2% a year, the central-bank target, not a forecast): $10,000 earning 0% for 10 years buys what $8,203 buys today. $10,000 ÷ 1.02^10 = $8,203. Real inflation is higher in some years and lower in others.

HOW TO CHECK (2 minutes):
1. Open your bank app and tap your savings account.
2. Find the interest rate (often under 'Account details').
3. Look up your country's latest inflation rate from its official statistics agency.
4. If your interest rate is under 2%, ask your bank what its high-interest savings rate is, and compare a few other deposit-insured accounts.

THE CATCH: a high rate can be a short promo that drops after a few months, so check the rate after it ends. Keep your emergency money easy to reach; this is about money that's just sitting. Interest is usually taxed unless it's in a tax-free account.

Do this: check your savings interest rate. Earning under 2% interest? Move it to a high-interest savings account.

Send this to whoever keeps all their savings in chequing.

Follow for one money move a day, in plain words.

Education only, not financial advice.

#inflation #savings #personalfinance #moneytips #savingmoney

posts.caption:
For whoever studies on their phone: you understand more on paper.

WHY: researchers think screens nudge us to skim, and we feel more sure we got it than we really did. On paper, people tend to read more slowly and carefully.

THE RESEARCH: a review of 54 studies with 171,055 readers found people understood texts better on paper than on screens. The gap was biggest when people were reading against the clock and reading to learn (textbooks, articles, work documents). For stories and novels there was no real difference. And the paper advantage got bigger in newer studies, not smaller.

HOW:
1. Pick the pages you'll be tested on, or the document you must really understand.
2. Print them (a library or campus printer works).
3. Read with a pen in hand. Mark the 2 or 3 lines that matter.
4. Keep the screen for quick lookups and reading for fun.

THE CATCH: the paper advantage is small on average, and it's about understanding, not speed. If printing isn't possible, slow down on screen and avoid scrolling while you read.

Do this: print the pages you must understand.

Send this to whoever studies on their phone.

Follow for one small focus fix a day, each one backed by research.

posts.caption:
For the friend buying a car: the lower monthly payment can cost thousands more.

WHY: a longer loan spreads the same debt over more months. Each payment is smaller, but interest keeps running for longer.

THE MATHS (loan made up for this post: $30,000 at 8% a year, fixed payments):
• 5 years (60 payments): about $608 a month, $6,498 in total interest.
• 7 years (84 payments): about $468 a month, $9,277 in total interest.
• The 7-year loan costs about $2,780 more, for a payment about $141 a month lower.

HOW TO COMPARE OFFERS:
1. Ask each lender for the total interest in dollars over the whole loan, not only the monthly payment.
2. Compare offers at the same loan length.
3. Pick the shortest length whose payment you can comfortably afford.

THE CATCH: your rate depends on your credit, the lender and where you live, so use your own numbers. If money is tight, a lower payment can matter more; just know what it costs.

Do this: before you sign, ask the lender: 'What's the total interest, in dollars?'

posts.caption:
For whoever keeps adding blankets: feel the back of baby's neck, not their hands.

WHY: overheating can increase the risk of SIDS, says the NHS. Babies' hands and feet usually feel cool, and that's normal. So cold little hands are not a sign to add another layer.

THE CHECK (5 seconds):
1. Put two fingers on the back of their neck, or on their chest.
2. Hot or sweaty? Take off a layer of clothing or bedding.
3. Warm and dry? They're fine as they are.

THE ROOM: the NHS and The Lullaby Trust suggest about 16 to 20°C where baby sleeps. A room thermometer takes the guessing out.

THE CATCH: no hats indoors. Take hats and extra layers off as soon as you come inside or get in the car, even if it means waking them. For sleep, use lightweight blankets or a baby sleeping bag, never a duvet. A baby who seems unwell or has a fever needs a call to your doctor or nurse, not a layer change.

Do this: check baby's neck, not the hands.

Send this to whoever keeps adding blankets.

Follow for one calm thing a night, from bump to toddler.

posts.caption:
Turn your phone grey tonight. A boring phone is easier to put down.

WHY: bright app icons and red badges are built to catch your eye. With colour off, the same apps just look less tempting.

THE STUDY: 84 young adults (average age 22) let an app log their phone use for 2 weeks. Week 1 normal, week 2 in grayscale. In the grey week they spent about 20 minutes less a day on their phones, and said they felt more in control of their phone use and less stressed.

HOW:
1. iPhone: Settings > Accessibility > Display & Text Size > Color Filters. Turn it on and pick Grayscale.
2. Android: open Settings and search "grayscale" (on many phones it's under Accessibility > Color correction).
3. Optional: add it to your Accessibility Shortcut so you can switch colour back for photos and maps.
4. Keep it on for one full week before you judge it.

THE CATCH: they picked up their phones just as often (about 80 times a day both weeks). The visits got shorter, not fewer. It was one week and 84 people, and it didn't change their sleep or how productive they felt.

Do this: turn on Grayscale tonight.

Send this to the friend who says "one quick scroll" and loses an hour.

Follow for one small focus fix a day, each one backed by research.

#focus #screentime #digitalwellbeing #productivity #phonehabits

Song stuck in your head and no idea what it's called? Hum it. Google names it.

WHY IT WORKS: Google says a song's melody is like its fingerprint. Its machine-learning models turn your hum into a number pattern of the tune and compare it with thousands of songs, so you don't need the words or perfect pitch.

HOW (about 20 seconds):
1. Open the free Google app (Android or iPhone).
2. Tap the mic in the search bar.
3. Tap "Search a song".

THE CATCH: you get possible matches, not a sure answer. Hum the catchiest part, usually the chorus. On iPhone it works in English; on Android it works in more than 20 languages.

PRIVACY TIP: what the mic hears is sent to Google to find the match. Hum somewhere quiet, away from conversations you'd rather keep private.

posts.caption:
Back to sleep. Tummy to play. Asleep, babies go on their back. Awake and watched, they spend some time on their tummy.

WHY: tummy time helps babies build the strong muscles they need for milestones like pushing up, rolling and crawling (AAP). It also helps prevent a flat spot on the back of the head, because babies sleep on their backs (Canadian Paediatric Society).

HOW (AAP):
1. Start the day your baby comes home.
2. 3 to 5 minutes, 2 to 3 times a day, while they're awake. After a diaper change or a nap is a good time.
3. Add time as they enjoy it. Work up to 15 to 30 minutes a day in total by about 7 weeks.
4. Easiest start: recline, wide awake, and put baby tummy-down on your chest. They'll lift their head to look at your face.

THE CATCH: tummy time is only for when baby is awake and you're right there watching. For sleep, always on their back, in their own crib.

Do this: recline. Baby on your chest.

Send this to someone bringing a baby home soon.

Follow for one calm thing a night, from bump to toddler.

General information only, not medical advice.

It's 3 am. They'll only sleep on you. Those cuddles are lovely while you're wide awake.

3 am Club No. 3: the moment to watch for is the one where YOU start to drift off.

WHY: The Lullaby Trust says: any time you feel you might fall asleep with your baby, put them on their back in a clear, flat, separate sleep space. Dozing off with a baby on a sofa or armchair is especially dangerous.

AT 3 AM:
1. Keep their crib or bassinet next to your bed, so putting them down takes seconds.
2. Feeling sleepy yourself? Move baby to their own crib now, on their back. Don't wait for the perfect moment.
3. Never settle in on the sofa or an armchair with a sleeping baby.

THE CATCH: if you've had alcohol, smoke, or take medicine that makes you drowsy, or your baby was premature or small, it's even more important that baby sleeps in their own space. Worried about how your baby sleeps? Talk to your doctor, nurse or health visitor.

Do this: tonight, the moment you feel sleepy yourself, move baby to their own crib, on their back.

Send this to whoever's on the night shift with you.

3 am Club No. 4 is Monday at 5 pm: the next night tip.

Follow for one calm thing a night, from bump to toddler.

A head start makes you finish. Even a fake one.

WHY: a goal that already looks started feels closer, and closer goals pull harder. Starting from zero feels like a long way to go.

THE RESEARCH: a car wash handed out 300 loyalty cards. Card A needed 8 stamps. Card B needed 10, but came with 2 already stamped. Same 8 washes to go. 34% of Card B people finished it, against 19% of Card A people, and they came back sooner.

HOW:
1. Open today's to-do list (paper or your notes app).
2. At the top, write 2 things you've already done today: made coffee, replied to a message.
3. Tick them both.
4. Start the first real task straight after.

THE CATCH: the study was about car washes, not to-do lists. The idea that carries over is that seeing progress already made helps you keep going. Write real things you did, not invented ones.

Do this: Start your list with 2 done things.

Send this to the friend whose list never gets started.

Follow for one small focus fix a day, each one backed by research.

posts.caption:
Trying to break a habit? A new place does more than wanting it more.

WHY: strong habits run on cues around you: the same room, the same people, the same time. Change the setting and the cues are gone, so you're choosing again instead of running on autopilot.

THE RESEARCH: 115 students who switched universities were followed through the move. Their strong habits (exercising, watching TV, reading the news) carried on only where the setting stayed similar. In another study of 521 people, a push to change everyday habits worked better for people who had just moved house.

HOW:
1. Spot your next change: a new job, a new home, a new term, even a new desk.
2. Pick one habit you want and one you want gone.
3. In the first weeks, set the new setting up for the habit you want (shoes by the new door, no TV in the new bedroom).

THE CATCH: in that second study the boost showed up only in the first 3 months after a move, and the effect was small. A move doesn't change anything by itself; it gives you an opening.

Do this: New job, home or term? Set up the habit you want in the first weeks.

Send this to the friend who's moving next month.

Follow for one small focus fix a day, each one backed by research.

#habits #focus #productivity #behaviorchange #lockedhour

posts.caption:
Daydreaming the goal? You may do less. Picture what's in the way too.

WHY: a vivid daydream of success feels a bit like you're already there, so your body relaxes instead of gearing up. Naming the obstacle reminds you there's still work to do, and a plan tells you what to do when it shows up.

THE RESEARCH: in 4 small experiments, people who pictured an ideal outcome had less energy afterwards. In one, people who daydreamed an ideal week said a week later they'd got less done than people who didn't. A review of 21 studies (15,907 people) found the 3-step version (wish, obstacle, if-then plan) helped people reach their goals; the effect was small to medium.

HOW:
1. Wish: write the one thing you want done ("finish the report").
2. Obstacle: write what usually gets in the way ("I keep checking email").
3. Plan: "If [obstacle], then I'll [action]" ("If I open email, I close it and keep going").
4. Keep it where you work.

THE CATCH: the energy studies were small and mostly measured how people felt. Dreaming isn't banned; just don't stop at the dream.

Do this: Write the wish, the obstacle, then your plan.

Send this to the friend with the vision board.

Follow for one small focus fix a day, each one backed by research.

#goals #focus #productivity #mindset #lockedhour

posts.caption:
Cramming the night before again? Today's word: Space.

One Word No. 4. Each episode is one word that guards your focus.

WHY: when you come back to something after a gap, you have to dig it back out of memory, and that digging makes it stick. Cramming feels productive because it all feels familiar in the moment, then it fades.

THE RESEARCH: a review of 317 experiments found that spreading the same study time over separate sessions beat cramming it into one, for remembering it later. The longer you need to remember it, the bigger the gaps can be.

HOW:
1. Take the hour you'd spend cramming.
2. Split it into 3 sessions of 20 minutes.
3. Put them on 3 different days (say Mon, Wed, Fri) in your calendar.
4. Start each session by writing what you remember before you look.

THE CATCH: it needs a few days' notice. The night before, it's too late to space it out, so plan as soon as you know the date.

Do this: Split your next study hour into 3 sessions on 3 different days. Put them in your calendar.

Send this to whoever has an exam in two weeks.

One Word No. 5 is Monday at 5 pm.

Follow for one small focus fix a day, each one backed by research.

No FHSA open? No room yet. In Canada, your FHSA (First Home Savings Account) room, meaning how much you're allowed to put in, only starts the year you open your first one.

WHY IT MATTERS: open an FHSA by December 31, 2026 and you get 2026's $8,000 of room, even if you put nothing in yet. Unused room carries forward (up to $8,000), so in 2027 you could put in up to $16,000. Open it in January instead and 2027 starts at $8,000. 2026's room never existed for you.

HOW (about 15 minutes):
1. Check you qualify (below).
2. Open an FHSA at your bank, credit union or brokerage, online or in a branch.
3. You don't have to deposit anything to start the room. Put money in when you're ready.
4. Keep track of your room: CRA My Account shows it.

THE CATCH: the room is per person and the lifetime limit is $40,000. Put in more than your room and CRA charges 1% a month on the extra. Opening an account doesn't mean you have to buy a home.

WHO QUALIFIES: adults living in Canada who are first-time home buyers. CRA's test: you haven't lived in a home you owned (or your spouse or common-law partner owned) in the past four years.

Do this: open an FHSA at your bank or investing app before December 31.

Send this to a friend saving for a first home.

Education only, not financial advice.

Follow for one money move a day, in plain words.

posts.caption:
Your FSA money can expire. In the US, health FSA money you don't use by your plan's end date can be lost.

WHY: a health flexible spending account (through your employer) is 'use it or lose it'. You put pre-tax pay in, and you normally have to use it on eligible costs by the end of the plan year. For plans that run January to December, that's December 31.

HOW (10 minutes tonight):
1. Log in to your FSA app or benefits site.
2. Check two things: your balance and your plan's end date.
3. Check whether your plan has extra time (a grace period of up to 2½ months) or lets some money carry over. An employer can offer one or the other, not both.
4. If money is left, book what you already need before the deadline, like a dental cleaning, new glasses or a prescription refill. Your plan lists what counts.

THE CATCH: don't buy things you don't need just to spend it. Plans that don't run January to December have a different end date. A dependent care FSA has its own rules.

WHO THIS IS FOR: people in the US with a health FSA through work.

Do this: log in to your FSA or benefits account today and check your balance and deadline.

Send this to a friend in the US with an FSA.

Education only, not financial advice.

posts.caption:
Insurance due. Surprised again? The habit: divide each yearly bill by 12 and save that much every month.

Rich Habits, Decoded No. 3. Each episode takes one money habit and shows you how to do it on a normal paycheque.

THE MATHS (bills made up for this post: $1,200 a year for insurance, $600 a year for gifts):
• $1,200 ÷ 12 = $100 a month.
• $600 ÷ 12 = $50 a month.
• Save $150 a month and both bills are covered when they land.

WHY IT WORKS: yearly bills aren't surprises, they're just far apart. Saving a twelfth each month turns one big hit into a small, boring line in your budget, so the bill never has to go on a card.

HOW (20 minutes):
1. List every bill that comes once or twice a year: insurance, car registration, memberships, gifts, the holidays.
2. Divide each yearly total by 12 and add them up.
3. Open a separate savings account and name it 'Bills'.
4. Set an automatic transfer of that amount for payday. Paid every two weeks? Divide the yearly total by 26 instead.
5. When a bill comes, pay it from that account.

THE CATCH: if a bill is due soon, the first year needs a catch-up (divide what's left by the months left). Your bills will be different, so use your own.

Do this: list your yearly bills tonight and divide the total by 12.

Rich Habits, Decoded No. 4 is Monday at 5 pm.

Education only, not financial advice.

Returning something? Paste the store's return policy into AI and ask for your last day.

WHY IT WORKS: the AI answers from the policy you paste, not from a guess. Add the day you bought it and the day it arrived, and it does the date maths and points out the catches, like sale items.

THE REAL TEST (policy and dates made up for this post):
We pasted a 3-line return policy (30 days from delivery, sale items store credit only, $7.99 return fee) and asked: "I bought a jacket on sale on Oct 12 and it arrived Oct 20. What's my last day to return it, and what will I get back?"
Claude's reply, word for word: "Your last day to return the jacket is November 19 (30 days from the Oct 20 delivery), as long as it's unworn with tags attached. Because it was a sale item, you'll get store credit only, likely the sale price you paid minus the $7.99 return shipping fee."
We checked the maths: Oct 20 plus 30 days is Nov 19.

THE CATCH: the answer is only as good as what you paste. Copy the whole returns section from the store's site or receipt, and check the date against the policy before you count on it.

PRIVACY TIP: you don't need your order number, name or address. The policy and two dates are enough.

Do this: paste the return policy into ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini and ask, "What's my last day to return it?"

posts.caption:
Before you say yes to the mechanic, ask AI for the questions to ask.

WHY IT WORKS: you can't push back on a quote you don't understand. AI turns "it makes a noise" into the questions a mechanic should be able to answer: what's wrong, how urgent it is, and where the money goes.

THE PROMPT (swap the parts in brackets for yours):
"My [car] makes [a squeal when I brake]. Give me 5 short questions to ask the [mechanic] so I understand the quote before I say yes."

THE REAL TEST (the car and the squeal are made up for this post). Claude's 5 questions, word for word (it also explained each one; that part is left out for length):
1. "What exactly is causing the squeal?"
2. "How much pad life is left, and is this urgent or can it wait?"
3. "Do the rotors really need replacing, or can they be resurfaced or reused?"
4. "Can you break the quote into parts and labour, and what grade of parts is that?"
5. "What warranty comes with the parts and the work, and what if it still squeals afterward?"

THE CATCH: AI doesn't know your car or your shop. Use the questions to understand the quote, not to diagnose the problem yourself.

PRIVACY TIP: no plate number, VIN or address needed. "My car" is enough.

Do this: before you call the shop, paste the prompt into ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini with your car and the noise.

Diaper rubbing the cord stump? Fold the top of the diaper down, below the stump.

WHY: the stump heals best when it stays clean and dry. With the diaper folded below it, pee can't soak it and the waistband can't rub it (AAP).

HOW (AAP):
1. At every change, fold the front of the diaper down so its top edge sits below the stump.
2. Keep the stump clean and dry, open to the air. There's no need to put alcohol on it.
3. Leave it be. It dries, shrinks and falls off on its own, usually by the time your baby is 3 weeks old.
4. A few drops of blood on the diaper around the time it falls off is normal.

THE CATCH: call your baby's doctor if you see red skin around the base, a yellowish discharge that smells bad, or your baby cries when you touch it. If the cord is actively bleeding, call right away. If it's still there after 3 weeks, book a visit.

Do this: next diaper, fold it below the stump.

Send this to someone with a brand-new baby.

Follow for one calm thing a night, from bump to toddler.

Under 3? Toothpaste is just a smear the size of a grain of rice.

WHY: fluoride toothpaste protects new teeth from decay. A tiny amount gives that protection to a child who can't spit well yet (NHS, AAP).

HOW (NHS, AAP):
1. Start brushing as soon as the first tooth comes through.

posts.caption:
Close your eyes to remember more. Mind goes blank when someone asks what you saw? Shut your eyes, then answer.

WHY: your eyes keep pulling in new things to look at, like a phone lighting up or someone walking past. Shutting them takes that load off, so more of your attention goes into remembering, and it's easier to picture the scene again.

HOW:
1. When someone asks about something you saw or heard, close your eyes before you answer.
2. Keep them shut while you talk it through. Picture where you were standing.
3. Open them when you're done.

THE RESEARCH: in 5 experiments, people watched a short video or a staged live event, then answered questions about it with their eyes open or shut. In 4 of the 5, the eyes-shut group recalled more correct details, without more wrong ones.

THE CATCH: it helps you get back what you saw and heard. It can't add anything you never noticed, and it was tested on recent events, not on things you studied weeks ago.

Do this: Close your eyes, then answer.

Send this to the friend who always says "I don't remember."
Follow for one small focus trick a day.

posts.caption:
Fewer temptations beat more willpower. Move one temptation out of the room.

WHY: every time a temptation is in front of you, you have to say no to it again, and that wears you down. Take it away and there's nothing left to say no to.

HOW:
1. Before you start, look around: what keeps pulling you away? Snacks, the game controller, the TV remote.
2. Pick one.
3. Put it in another room, or a closed drawer, until you're done.

THE RESEARCH: researchers followed 159 first-year university students through a semester. Five times a day for a week, students said what they wanted in that moment and whether they resisted it. At the end of term they rated progress on their goals. Students who ran into more temptations made less progress and felt more drained. How hard they resisted didn't predict their progress at all.

THE CATCH: it's one study and it shows a link, not proof that removing things causes success. Resisting was measured with a single question.

Do this: Move one temptation out of the room.

Send this to the friend who says they just need more willpower.
Follow for one small focus trick a day.

posts.caption:
Miss the "no interest" end date, and the interest can go back to the day you bought it.

WHY: many store-card deals in the US and Canada say "no interest if paid in full in 12 months". That is often deferred interest. If any of the price is still unpaid when the promotion ends, interest can be charged on the whole purchase, back to day one, not just on what's left.

THE CFPB'S NUMBERS: a $400 TV on a 12-month deal. You pay $25 a month, so $300. $100 is left at the end. At a 25% rate, $65 of interest from the past year lands on top: you owe $165, not $100.

HOW (5 minutes, when you sign up):
1. Find the exact end date on the agreement or your statement. Write it in your phone calendar.
2. Divide the price by the number of months. $400 / 12 is about $34 a month (math). Pay at least that every month. The minimum payment is usually not enough.
3. Have other balances on the card? Ask the card company to put your extra payments on the promotional balance.

THE CATCH: terms differ. Some plans charge interest only on what's left, some on the full amount from the purchase date, and some lose the 0% after one missed payment. Read your plan's terms. Your plan's real rate may be higher or lower than 25%.

WHO THIS IS FOR: anyone in the US or Canada using a store card or "buy now, pay later" plan with a no-interest period.

Do this: divide the price by the months and pay at least that, every month.

Send this to a friend who just bought something on a store card.

Education only, not financial advice.

Follow for one money rule a day, in plain words.

#deferredinterest #creditcards #moneytips #personalfinance #buynowpaylater

posts.caption:
Card bill 30 days late? It can stay on your credit report for up to 6 years in Canada and 7 in the US.

WHY: lenders look at your payment history when you apply for a loan, a car, a rental or a mortgage. In Canada, a late or unpaid credit card or loan can stay on your report for up to 6 years. In the US, most negative information can be reported for 7 years. A payment that hits 30 days late this month can stay until 2032 in Canada and 2033 in the US.

Paying it later doesn't erase it: the late mark stays even after you pay the past-due amount.

HOW (5 minutes tonight):
1. Open your card's app or online banking.
2. Find autopay (it may be called automatic or pre-authorized payments).
3. Set it to at least the minimum payment, on or before the due date. If you can, set it to the full balance so you pay no interest.

THE CATCH: a payment a few days late usually costs a late fee, but it generally isn't reported to the credit bureaus until it's 30 or more days past due. So if you just missed one, pay it today. Autopay only works if the money is in your account; a failed payment can cost a fee from your card company and your bank.

WHO THIS IS FOR: anyone with a credit card or loan in Canada or the US.

Do this: turn on autopay for at least the minimum payment.

Send this to a friend who pays their bills by hand.

Education only, not financial advice.

Follow for one money rule a day, in plain words.

posts.caption:
Holding baby with a hot drink? Put the mug down first, well out of reach.

WHY: babies grab at bright things, and mugs are bright. Their skin burns more easily than an adult's. And the NHS says a hot drink can still scald 15 minutes after it was made.

HOW:
1. Before you pick baby up, put your tea or coffee down somewhere high or far back, well out of reach.
2. Not on the edge of a table, and not on a low coffee table.
3. Holding baby? Hold the baby, not the drink. Your tea can wait.

THE CATCH: "it's cooled down by now" is easy to believe. 15 minutes later it can still scald. Keep hot drinks away from toddlers too.

Do this: mug down, out of reach, then pick baby up.

Send this to the grandparent who always has a cup of tea.

Follow for one calm thing a night, from bump to toddler.

General information only, not medical advice.

#newborn #babysafety #newparents #grandparents #babytips

posts.caption:
Reaching for the wipes mid-change? Keep one hand on baby, every time.

WHY: babies wriggle, and they can roll off a changing table, a bed or a sofa in a second (NHS). Health Canada says to keep one hand on your baby the whole time, even with the safety strap done up.

HOW:
1. Before baby goes up: diaper, wipes and clean clothes, all within reach.
2. One hand stays on baby's tummy for the whole change.
3. Doorbell, phone, something on the stove? Take baby with you. Never leave them up there, even for a second.
4. Or skip the height: the NHS suggests changing on a changing mat on the floor.

THE CATCH: the strap helps, but it can't replace your hand.

Do this: one hand on baby, every change.

Send this to whoever does the diaper changes with you.

Follow for one calm thing a night, from bump to toddler.

General information only, not medical advice.

#diaperchange #babysafety #newborn #newparents #babytips

posts.caption:
It's 3 am and your baby feels hot. If they're under 3 months, don't wait for the morning.

3 am Club No. 4: the night fever rule.

WHY: for babies under 3 months, a temperature of 38°C (100.4°F) or higher needs a call right away, even if they seem fine otherwise (AAP). The NHS counts 38°C or more as a high temperature.

AT 3 AM:
1. Check with a digital thermometer. Just out of a bath or wrapped in a blanket? Wait a few minutes and check again.
2. Under 3 months and 38°C (100.4°F) or more: call your doctor or your health line now (in the UK, NHS 111). 3 to 6 months: call at 39°C (102.2°F) or more.
3. While you call: keep feeding. Don't undress them or sponge them down.

THE CATCH: no paracetamol (acetaminophen) for babies under 2 months, says the NHS. Ask your doctor or pharmacist before giving any medicine.

Do this: tonight, find your digital thermometer and save your doctor's number in your phone.

Send this to whoever's on the night shift with you.

3 am Club No. 5 is Wednesday at 5 pm.

Follow for one calm thing a night, from bump to toddler.

General information only, not medical advice.

#newborn #nightfeeds #babyfever #newparents #3amclub

posts.caption:
Switching tasks? Your mind stays behind. Before you switch, write one line: where you stopped and what's next.

WHY: when you leave a task in the middle, part of your mind stays on it. That leftover thinking takes attention away from whatever you switched to. A quick note tells your brain the task is parked, so it can let go for now.

HOW:
1. Someone interrupts, or you have to jump to something else.
2. Take about a minute. On a sticky note or the top of the doc, write where you stopped and your very next step ("stopped: slide 4. next: fix the chart").
3. Leave the note where you'll see it when you come back. Then switch.

THE RESEARCH: in a lab study, people pulled off an unfinished task under time pressure kept thinking about it during the next task, and did worse on it. In two lab studies, people who wrote a quick plan for coming back first did better on the task they switched to: they recalled more and made better choices.

THE CATCH: it was tested on the task you switch TO, not on how well you finish the first one later. And it takes the minute before you switch, which is the minute you'll feel like skipping.

Do this: Before you switch, write your next step.

Send this to the coworker who's always "just got a quick question."
Follow for one small focus trick a day.

#focus #deepwork #productivity #worksmarter #attention

posts.caption:
A to-do list helps you sleep. Lying awake running through tomorrow? Write it down before bed.

WHY: unfinished tasks keep circling at bedtime because your brain is trying not to forget them. Once they're on paper, there's less to hold on to, so it's easier to switch off.

HOW:
1. Keep a notepad and pen by the bed.
2. Before lights out, take 5 minutes and write every task you need to do tomorrow and the next few days.
3. Be specific: not "work stuff" but "email Sam the budget by 10".
4. Close the notepad. Lights out.

THE RESEARCH: 57 healthy young adults spent a night in a sleep lab, with their sleep measured by brain-wave recording. Before bed, half wrote a to-do list for the next few days and half wrote about tasks they'd already finished. The to-do group fell asleep faster: about 15 minutes on average, against about 25. The more specific the to-do list, the faster they fell asleep.

THE CATCH: it's one small lab study of young people without sleep problems, and it compared two kinds of writing (there was no group that wrote nothing). It isn't a treatment for insomnia.

Do this: Write tomorrow's list. Be specific.

Send this to whoever plans tomorrow at 1 am.
Follow for one small focus trick a day.

#sleep #focus #habits #todolist #productivity

posts.caption:
Blank page? Stand up. Today's word: Walk.

One Word No. 5. Each episode is one word that guards your focus.

WHY: walking seems to loosen up the flow of ideas. You don't need a nice view: in the study, a treadmill facing a blank wall worked.

THE RESEARCH: in four experiments with 176 people, mostly students, people came up with more new uses for everyday objects while walking than while sitting. In one experiment, 81% of people had more ideas walking. The boost carried over a bit when they sat back down after a walk.

HOW:
1. When you need ideas (a gift, a title, a way round a problem), stand up.
2. Walk: a hallway, around the room, around the block.
3. Say every idea out loud into a voice memo. Don't judge them yet.
4. Sit down and pick the best ones.

THE CATCH: it helps brainstorming, where you want many ideas. On problems with one right answer, walkers did slightly worse than sitters, so do that part sitting down.

Do this: Stuck for ideas? Get up and walk, even around the room. Say every idea into a voice memo.

Send this to whoever has been staring at a blank page all afternoon.

One Word No. 6 is Wednesday at 5 pm.

Follow for one small focus trick a day.

#creativity #focus #brainstorming #deepwork #oneword

posts.caption:
Never filed your 2023 taxes? In the US, if tax came out of your pay, you usually have until April 15, 2027 to claim that refund. After that, the government keeps it.

WHY: the IRS gives most people 3 years to file a return and claim a refund. A 2023 return was due April 15, 2024, so the window closes April 15, 2027. In March 2026, a few weeks before the 2022 deadline (April 15, 2026), the IRS said over 1.3 million people still hadn't claimed their 2022 refunds, and half of those refunds were bigger than $686. The 2023 deadline is a year later, so there's still time.

HOW (one evening):
1. Get your 2023 W-2s and 1099s. Lost them? Ask your employer, or use Get Transcript Online on IRS.gov for a free wage and income transcript.
2. Get the 2023 forms from IRS.gov (Forms & Instructions, prior years).
3. File your 2023 return before April 15, 2027.

THE CATCH: the IRS may hold the refund if you have other years you haven't filed, and it can use it to pay taxes you owe, past-due child support or federal debts like student loans. Some disaster areas get extra time.

WHO THIS IS FOR: people in the US who had federal tax taken from their 2023 pay (or may qualify for the Earned Income Tax Credit) and never filed for 2023.

Do this: file your 2023 return before April 15, 2027.

Send this to a friend in the US who skipped filing in 2023.

Education only, not tax advice.

Follow for one money rule a day, in plain words.

#taxrefund #IRS #taxes #moneytips #personalfinance

posts.caption:
Co-sign, and you can owe all of it. In Canada and the US, if the borrower stops paying, the lender can ask you for the unpaid balance.

WHY: co-signing isn't a reference. You sign the loan too, so the lender can ask you for the unpaid balance. In the US, the FTC says you may have to pay up to the full amount, plus late fees or collection costs, and the lender can come to you without first trying to collect from the borrower. Their missed payments can also show up on your credit report.

HOW (before you sign):
1. Ask the full amount, the monthly payment and how long the loan runs.
2. Check your own budget: could you make that payment alone, for the whole loan?
3. If not, say no, or offer a smaller amount you can afford to give.
4. If you do sign, ask the lender to tell you if a payment is missed, and keep copies of everything.

THE CATCH: you usually can't take your name off later just by asking. Saying no can feel unkind; paying someone else's loan for years is harder.

WHO THIS IS FOR: anyone in Canada or the US asked to co-sign a car loan, a student line of credit, a credit card or a lease.

Do this: only co-sign what you could pay alone.

Send this to whoever was asked to co-sign.

Education only, not legal or financial advice.

Follow for one money rule a day, in plain words.

#cosigning #credit #moneytips #personalfinance #personalfinancecanada

posts.caption:
Rent due before payday? The habit: live one month ahead. Keep one month of bills in the bank, so you pay this month's bills with last month's pay.

Rich Habits, Decoded No. 4. Each episode takes one money habit and shows you how to do it on a normal paycheque.

THE MATHS (made up for this post: bills of $2,000 a month):
• Set aside $200 a month.
• $2,000 ÷ $200 = 10 months to get there.

WHY IT WORKS: when the rent is due on the 1st and payday is the 5th, every month starts with a scramble or a card balance. With one month already saved, the bills come out of money you already have, and a late paycheque or a short month stops being an emergency.

HOW (15 minutes):
1. Add up one month of bills: rent, phone, insurance, groceries, loan payments.
2. Open a separate account and name it 'Next month'.
3. Set an automatic transfer for payday. Start with whatever you can, even $50.
4. When it reaches one month of bills, pay next month's bills from it, and refill it from each paycheque.

THE CATCH: it takes time, and it isn't an emergency fund (that's extra). If you carry card debt with interest, paying that down usually comes first. Your bills will be different, so use your own.

Do this: add up one month of your bills tonight and open a 'Next month' account.

Send this to a friend whose rent is due before payday.

Rich Habits, Decoded No. 5 is Wednesday at 5 pm.

Education only, not financial advice.

Follow for one money rule a day, in plain words.

#personalfinance #budgeting #moneytips #paycheck #richhabits
