posts.caption:
Office card coming? AI writes your line. Ask it for 3 short, warm lines, then pick the one that sounds like you.

WHY IT WORKS: a blank card is hard because you have to invent something from nothing. Give AI two facts (a first name and what they do) and it hands you options to react to. Choosing is much easier than starting cold.

THE REAL TEST: we made up a coworker, Dana from accounting, and asked Claude (Anthropic) on Oct 28, 2026: "I have to sign a birthday card for a coworker I barely know. Her name is Dana and she works in accounting. Give me 3 short, warm lines I could write. Nothing cheesy."
Its 3 lines, word for word:
1. "Happy birthday, Dana! Hope your year ahead is a good one, and that it balances out in your favour."
2. "Wishing you a relaxing birthday and a great year ahead. Thanks for everything you do to keep us all on track!"
3. "Happy birthday, Dana! I hope today brings you some well-earned time off from the spreadsheets."
It added: "If you want to keep it simplest, #2 works for anyone, even if you've never really talked."

HOW (about 30 seconds):
1. Open ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini.
2. Type: "I have to sign a birthday card for a coworker I barely know. Her name is [first name] and she works in [team]. Give me 3 short, warm lines I could write. Nothing cheesy."
3. Pick one, change a word so it sounds like you, and write it in by hand.

THE CATCH: AI doesn't know the person, so the lines are friendly but general. If you know one real thing about them (a new dog, a big trip), add it to the prompt.

PRIVACY TIP: a first name and a team is all it needs. Leave out their last name, age, birthday date and anything personal.

Do this: Ask AI for 3 lines. Pick one.

Send this to whoever's signing the card next.

posts.caption:
Toddler eating grapes? Cut each grape into 4 small pieces.

WHY: small round foods are the easiest for little ones to choke on. A whole grape is round and firm. Cut into quarters, it isn't round any more (NHS). The AAP says round, firm foods like grapes are fine once they're chopped small.

HOW:
1. Cut the grape in half, the long way.
2. Cut each half the long way again. That's 4 small pieces.
3. Same for cherry tomatoes, strawberries and other berries: quarters. Cherries: take the stone out first, then quarter.
4. Apple and melon: slices, not small chunks.

THE CATCH: a halved grape is still a round shape. Go all the way to 4. The AAP says to keep this up until at least age 4.

Do this: tonight, cut the grapes into 4.

Send this to whoever packs the snack box.

Follow for one calm thing a night, from bump to toddler.

posts.caption:
Babies can drown in 5 cm (2 inches) of water. That's why someone stays for the whole bath.

WHY: the NHS says baths are one of the most common places for babies and young children to drown, and it's often silent. You won't necessarily hear a thing.

HOW:
1. Get the towel, clean clothes and diaper ready before the water goes in.
2. Stay with them the whole time. Phone or doorbell? Take baby out, wrapped in the towel, or let it ring.
3. A big brother or sister in the bath too doesn't count as someone watching.
4. Bath done? Pull the plug straight away.

THE CATCH: a bath seat isn't a safety device. You still need to stay right there. Same for paddling pools: empty them straight after use.

Do this: tonight, empty the bath as soon as baby is out.

Send this to whoever does bath time at your place.

Follow for one calm thing a night, from bump to toddler.

General information only, not medical advice.

posts.caption:
Can't fall asleep? Shower 90 minutes before bed. A warm shower, timed right, helps you fall asleep sooner.

WHY: warm water sends blood out to your hands and feet. Afterwards your body lets that heat go and your core temperature drops, and that drop is one of the signals your body uses to start sleep.

HOW:
1. Pick your bedtime (say 11 pm).
2. Count back about 90 minutes (9:30 pm). Anywhere from 1 to 2 hours before bed works.
3. Warm, not hot: about 40 to 42.5 °C (104 to 108.5 °F). A bath works too.
4. 10 minutes in the water is enough.

THE RESEARCH: a review of 17 studies (13 with data to combine) found that warm showers or baths 1 to 2 hours before bed shortened the time it took to fall asleep, even with as little as 10 minutes in the water. People also rated their sleep as better.

THE CATCH: the studies were small, and the timing matters. A hot shower right before bed hasn't had time to cool you down. It helps you drift off; it is not a treatment for insomnia.

Do this tonight: Bed at 11? Shower warm at 9:30. 10 minutes in the water is enough.

Send this to whoever is still scrolling at midnight because they can't drop off.

Part 2 is tomorrow (Monday) at 7 pm: the lamp. Why ordinary room light in the evening tells your body it's still daytime, and the one switch to flip after dinner.

Follow for one small focus trick a day.

#sleep #bedtimeroutine #focus #habits #sleepbetter

posts.caption:
Your ceiling light says it's daytime. After dinner, switch to one small lamp.

Fall asleep sooner, Part 2. (Part 1, yesterday: a warm shower about 90 minutes before bed.)

WHY: melatonin is the hormone your body releases when it decides it's night. It starts to rise in the evening, a couple of hours before you usually fall asleep. Ordinary indoor light, the kind from a ceiling light, holds it back, so your body's night starts later.

HOW:
1. After dinner, turn off the big overhead light.
2. Use one small lamp, low and warm, for the rest of the evening.
3. Keep it that way until bed. (Your phone screen is light too: turn it down.)

THE RESEARCH: in a lab study, young adults spent the 8 hours before bed either in ordinary room light or in dim light. In room light, the body's "it's night" signal (melatonin) lasted about 90 minutes less, and started later in 99% of them.

THE CATCH: the study measured melatonin, not how fast people fell asleep, and it was a lab study with healthy 18 to 30 year olds over 8 hours of light. Dimming for your evening is a sensible way to use it, not something the study tested exactly.

Do this tonight: Big light off. One small lamp on.

Send this to whoever keeps every light in the house on until midnight.

posts.caption:
Studying tonight? 24 minutes on, 6 off: set a timer for your breaks. Planned breaks keep you fresher than breaking whenever you feel like it.

WHY: when you wait until you feel tired, you tend to push past the point where focus is already slipping, and then take a long break to recover. A timer decides for you, so you stop before you're drained.

HOW:
1. Pick one task (one chapter, one problem set).
2. Set a timer for 24 minutes. Work until it rings.
3. When it rings, really stop: 6 minutes. Stand up, stretch, get water. No phone.
4. Reset the timer for the next round.

THE RESEARCH: 87 university students did a self-study session. Some took breaks whenever they wanted; others had timed breaks (24 minutes on, 6 off, or 12 on, 3 off). The students on timed breaks reported less fatigue, better concentration and more motivation, and, in the authors' words, reached 'similar task completion in shorter time'. The ones who chose their own breaks took longer breaks.

THE CATCH: one study, one session, with feelings measured by self-report. Timed breaks didn't make students finish more tasks; they finished the same work feeling fresher.

Do this tonight: Timer: 24 minutes on, 6 off. That's the timing from the study (not a typo for 25). Then the next round.

Send this to whoever is about to pull a 'no breaks' study night.

Follow for one small focus trick a day.

#studytips #focus #pomodoro #studywithme #deepwork

posts.caption:
Boring call? Grab a pen. Today's word: Doodle.

One Word No. 6. Each episode is one word that guards your focus.

WHY: on a dull call your mind drifts off. Simple doodling gives it just enough to do to stay in the room, without pulling your attention away from what's being said.

THE RESEARCH: 40 people listened to a dull 2.5-minute phone message and wrote down the names of people coming to a party. Half also filled in printed squares and circles while they listened. The doodlers caught more names, and in a surprise memory test they remembered 29% more: 7.5 details on average against 5.8.

HOW:
1. Before a long call, meeting or lecture, put a pen and a scrap of paper in front of you.
2. While you listen, fill in simple shapes: boxes, circles, lines.
3. Keep it simple. A detailed drawing becomes its own task.

THE CATCH: it's one small study with a boring message, and the doodling was filling in simple shapes. Drawing something you have to think about, or doodling on your phone, isn't the same thing.

Do this: Long call or lecture? Keep a pen and paper. Fill in simple shapes while you listen.

Send this to whoever has a 90-minute meeting tomorrow.

One Word No. 7 is Friday at 5 pm.

Follow for one small focus trick a day.

#focus #memory #doodle #productivity #oneword

posts.caption:
Living with your partner 12 months? You're common-law. In Canada, after 12 months of living together, the CRA counts you as common-law, even if you never married.

WHY: the CRA treats someone as your common-law partner when you live together in a conjugal relationship for at least 12 continuous months (or sooner if you have a child together). After that, your benefits and credits are worked out from your family net income: your net income plus your partner's. That's the number the CRA uses for things like the Canada child benefit, so your benefits may drop.

HOW (10 minutes):
1. Sign in to CRA My Account.
2. Go to Profile, then Marital status, then Edit.
3. Pick common-law and the date your status changed.

THE CATCH: the CRA wants to hear by the end of the month after your status changed (moved in last October? the 12 months ended this October, so tell them by the end of November). If they later find they paid you too much, they send a notice and you pay it back. A short split of under 90 days doesn't restart the 12 months.

WHO THIS IS FOR: couples in Canada living together, not married, especially if either of you gets the Canada child benefit or the GST/HST credit.

Do this: update your marital status in CRA My Account.

Send this to the person you moved in with.

Part 2 is tomorrow (Mon) at 7 pm: why your partner has to file taxes every year, even with no income, to keep the Canada child benefit coming.

Education only, not financial advice.

Follow for one money rule a day, in plain words.

#personalfinancecanada #commonlaw #CRA #canadianmoney #couplesandmoney

posts.caption:
Partner didn't file a tax return? In Canada, to keep getting the Canada child benefit, you and your spouse or common-law partner each have to file a tax return every year, even with no income.

Part 2 of yesterday's post (living together 12 months makes you common-law for the CRA).

WHY: the Canada child benefit is worked out from your family net income: your net income plus your partner's. If one return is missing, the CRA can't work it out, and the CRA says payments will stop if you don't do your taxes. File late and payments may stop for a while.

HOW:
1. Each of you files your own return for 2026 by April 30, 2027.
2. Earned $0, or only tax-free income? Still file.
3. Check that your marital status is right in CRA My Account (Part 1).

THE CATCH: it's every year, not once. One missed return can pause the payments for the whole family.

WHO THIS IS FOR: parents in Canada who get the Canada child benefit, especially when one partner stays home, studies or earns nothing.

Do this: both of you: file by April 30, 2027.

Send this to the partner who "didn't need to file".

There's no joint return in Canada: two returns, every year.

Education only, not tax advice.

Follow for one money rule a day, in plain words.

posts.caption:
Too sick to make decisions? Who handles your bills? In Ontario, if illness or an accident leaves you unable to make decisions and you have no continuing power of attorney for property, your family, including your spouse, can't automatically manage your money.

WHY: a continuing power of attorney for property is a document where you name the person who can handle your bank accounts, bills and home, and 'continuing' means it can still be used after you're no longer able to make those decisions yourself. Without one, your family may need a court or the government to approve them first. Ontario's kit explains that the Public Guardian and Trustee can become your guardian of property automatically by law, and a family member or friend can apply to replace it, or someone may apply to a court to be appointed guardian.

HOW (one evening):
1. Search 'Ontario power of attorney kit' and download the free kit (Ministry of the Attorney General).
2. Fill in the Continuing Power of Attorney for Property. Name someone you trust: your spouse, a family member or a long-time friend. They don't have to be a lawyer.
3. Sign it in front of two witnesses. These people can't be witnesses: your attorney or their spouse or partner; your own spouse, partner or child (or someone you treat as your child); a person whose property is under guardianship or who has a guardian of the person; anyone under 18.
4. Tell your person where it is.

THE CATCH: it only works if you sign it while you can still decide. If your money is complicated, Ontario suggests a lawyer. This is Ontario's rule; other provinces have their own.

WHO THIS IS FOR: adults in Ontario, married or not, with a bank account, bills or a home someone may need to manage.

Do this: sign a continuing power of attorney for property.

Send this to your partner, so you both do it.

Education only, not legal or financial advice.

Follow for one money rule a day, in plain words.

posts.caption:
Money talk only in a fight? The habit: book a 20-minute money date, same day every month, alone or with your partner.

Rich Habits, Decoded No. 5. Each episode takes one money habit and shows you how to do it on a normal paycheque.

WHY IT WORKS: when money only comes up after a surprise bill, every talk starts stressed. A short, booked check-in turns it into a routine: you see the month before it surprises you, and you only decide one thing at a time.

HOW (20 minutes, once a month):
1. Pick a fixed day, like the 7th, and put it in both calendars.
2. Open your bank and card apps side by side.
3. Ask three questions: What came in this month? What went out? What's the next big bill?
4. Pick one thing to change next month, then stop when the timer ends.

THE CATCH: keep it short and kind. It's a check-in, not a trial. If one of you carries debt the other didn't know about, start with that.

Do this: put a 20-minute money date in your calendar, same day every month.

Send this to the person you share bills with.

posts.caption:
Best friend's wedding and no toast yet? Give AI 3 true stories about your friend and ask for a toast you can say in 1 minute.

WHY IT WORKS: the hard part of a toast is shape, not memories. You already have the stories. AI is good at putting them in order (hello, a story, why they fit, raise your glass) and finding the joke that ties them together.

THE REAL TEST: we made up a couple, Maya and Theo, and asked Claude (Anthropic) on Nov 1, 2026: "I'm giving a toast at my best friend's wedding tonight and I haven't written anything. Her name is Maya, his name is Theo. Three things: we met in a college dorm when she set off the fire alarm making toast, she drove six hours to help me move, and Theo is the only person who can beat her at Scrabble. Write me a toast I can say in about one minute. Warm, a little funny."
It turned the fire alarm into the opening joke, word for word: "…Maya had set off the fire alarm. Making toast. So it feels right that I'm the one up here making one tonight."
And it added a delivery tip, word for word: "Pause after "Making toast." The laugh lands there."

HOW (5 minutes):
1. Open ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini.
2. Type who it's for and 3 true things: how you met, one time they showed up for you, one thing about their partner.
3. Ask: "Write me a toast I can say in about one minute. Warm, a little funny."
4. Read it out loud once with a timer, and change any line that doesn't sound like you.

THE CATCH: AI only knows the 3 stories you give it, so it can add small details that aren't true (ours added "2 a.m." and "pajamas"). Cut anything that didn't happen before you say it.

PRIVACY TIP: first names and the stories are enough. Leave out last names, the venue and anything the couple wouldn't want typed into an app.

posts.caption:
Toast tonight and you can't memorize it? Paste the whole toast into AI and ask for a 5-line cue card you can glance at.

Part 2 of our toast series. (Part 1, yesterday: AI writes the toast from 3 true stories.)

WHY IT WORKS: you don't forget a toast because it's long. You forget what comes next. A cue card gives you one short prompt per part, so one look tells you where you are, and you say the rest in your own words.

THE REAL TEST: we pasted yesterday's made-up toast (Maya and Theo) into a new Claude (Anthropic) chat on Nov 1, 2026 and asked: "I have to give this toast tonight and I can't memorize it. Turn it into a cue card: 5 short prompts, a few words each, that I can glance at to remember each part."
Its cue card, word for word:
1. Intro: best friend since college, week one
2. Fire alarm, 2 a.m. → "Making toast." (pause)
3. She shows up: six-hour drive, boxes (complained a little)
4. Theo beat her at Scrabble → genius and the one
5. Raise glasses: showing up, Scrabble, quiet smoke detector
And a reminder, word for word: "If you lose it, skip straight to the glasses. Nobody will notice."

HOW (2 minutes):
1. Open ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini.
2. Paste your toast or speech.
3. Ask: "Turn it into a cue card: 5 short prompts, a few words each, that I can glance at to remember each part."
4. Copy the 5 lines onto an index card or your phone's lock screen, and practise once with only the card.

THE CATCH: the cue card only works if you've said the toast out loud at least once. It reminds you; it can't speak for you.

PRIVACY TIP: a toast is full of other people's stories. Use first names only and leave out anything they'd want kept private.

posts.caption:
Potluck tomorrow and 3 different diets? Tell AI who can't eat what, your time and your budget, and ask for 3 dishes that work for all of them.

AI, for real · Day 12. One real test of what AI can do, with the output shown.

WHY IT WORKS: one rule at a time is easy; three at once is where you get stuck. AI checks every idea against all of them at the same time (no animal products, no nuts, no gluten) and against your 30 minutes and $20.

THE REAL TEST (guests made up for this post):
Prompt: "I'm bringing a dish to a potluck tomorrow. One guest is vegan, one can't eat nuts, and one is gluten-free. I have about 30 minutes to cook and $20. Give me 3 dishes that work for all of them, one line each."
Claude's 3 dishes (names word for word, with its own time and cost):
1. Black bean & corn salad: about 15 minutes and roughly $10
2. Coconut chickpea curry over rice: about 30 minutes and roughly $12
3. Roasted potatoes and veggies: about 30 minutes and roughly $10
It added, word for word: "Check the labels on canned goods and spice blends for hidden gluten, nut or dairy ingredients."

THE CATCH: AI can't read your labels and prices are its estimates. Some people with nut allergies also avoid coconut, so ask the guest before you make the curry (or bring the salad). posts.caption:
A swallowed coin battery can burn a child's throat in 2 hours. Swallowed, or think so? Go to the ER now (or call 911). Don't wait for Part 2.

WHY: the 20 mm lithium coin batteries (about the size of a nickel) are the most dangerous small batteries. Swallowed, they set off a chemical reaction that can burn through the throat (the esophagus) within 2 hours (AAP). Health Canada says the same: as little as two hours.

WHERE THEY HIDE (AAP + Health Canada lists):
- remote controls and key fobs
- toys, singing books and musical greeting cards
- flameless candles and holiday ornaments
- thermometers, bathroom scales, calculators
- watches, flashing shoes and jewellery, hearing aids

HOW:
1. Check every battery lid is shut tight. The AAP says to consider taping it shut for an extra layer.
2. Keep new and used batteries out of sight and reach, never near food or medicine.
3. Used ones: tape over both sides, then recycle them right away (check your city's battery drop-off).

THE CATCH: used batteries are still a risk. Kids find them loose on the floor, in the garbage and on counters (Health Canada).

Do this: Tonight: tape the remote's battery lid.

Send this to whoever has the TV remote at your place.

Follow for one calm thing a night, from bump to toddler.

Part 2 is tomorrow (Thursday) at 7 pm: what to do if a battery is swallowed, the 2-teaspoon honey step and what to tell the ER.

posts.caption:
Lying awake? After about 20 minutes, get out of bed. Lying there longer teaches your brain that bed is a place for being awake.

WHY: your brain learns from where things happen. If bed keeps meaning tossing, worrying and checking the time, getting into bed starts to switch you on instead of off. Getting up when sleep isn't coming, and only going back when you feel sleepy, re-teaches it: bed means sleep.

HOW:
1. Turn the clock to the wall (or put the phone face down, out of reach). Guess the 20 minutes; don't check.
2. Not asleep after about 20 minutes? Get up and go to another seat or room.
3. Dim lamp, something calm and a bit dull: a paper book, folding laundry, quiet music. No bright screens.
4. Back to bed only when you feel sleepy. Still awake? Repeat. Same wake-up time in the morning.

THE RESEARCH: this is called stimulus control. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine's insomnia guideline lists it as a standard treatment, with the instruction: if you can't fall asleep (or back to sleep) within about 20 minutes, get out of bed, do something relaxing until drowsy, then go back. The academy's 2021 guideline still suggests it for chronic insomnia.

THE CATCH: it can feel worse for the first few nights, and it works over nights, not in one. The 20 minutes is a guess, not a stopwatch. If you've been sleeping badly for weeks, talk to a doctor: insomnia has good treatments.

Do this tonight: Hide the clock. Up after 20 minutes. Dim lamp, a dull book, another seat. Back to bed only when you're sleepy.

Send this to whoever was still awake at 2 am last night.

Follow for one small sleep or focus trick a day.

#sleep #insomnia #cantsleep #sleepbetter #focus

Part 2 is tomorrow (Thursday) at 7 pm: working out at night. How late a hard workout can finish before it costs you sleep.

posts.caption:
Save $100 for your baby. Canada adds $20. In Canada, the RESP grant adds 20% to what you save for a child, but it needs your baby's Social Insurance Number (SIN).

WHY: the Canada Education Savings Grant (CESG) adds 20% on the first $2,500 you put into an RESP each year. That's $20 for every $100, up to $500 a year, with a $7,200 lifetime max. An RESP (Registered Education Savings Plan) is a savings plan for school after high school. To open an RESP, you and the child both need a SIN.

HOW:
1. When you register the birth, tick the box to apply for your baby's SIN (every province offers this; in the territories, apply through Service Canada).
2. Book a meeting with a bank or other RESP provider.
3. Bring your SIN and your baby's SIN, open the RESP, and ask them to apply for the grant.

THE CATCH: no SIN, no RESP, so no grant yet. Missed years aren't all lost: unused grant room carries forward, but you can only catch up a little at a time (at most $1,000 of grant in one year). Grants stop after the year your child turns 17.

WHO THIS IS FOR: kids living in Canada; grants are paid until the end of the year the child turns 17. Parents and grandparents can open the RESP. Lower-income families may also get extra grant money and the Canada Learning Bond.

Do this: get baby's SIN with the birth registration.

Send this to someone who just had a baby.

Education only, not financial advice.

posts.caption:
Interview at 9 am and you haven't prepared? Paste the job posting into AI and ask for the 5 questions they're most likely to ask.

WHY IT WORKS: a job posting is a list of what they're worried about. AI reads every line of it and turns each duty into the question an interviewer would ask about it. It answers from what you paste, so the more of the posting you give it, the closer the questions get.

THE REAL TEST: we made up a job posting and asked Claude (Anthropic) on Nov 2, 2026: "My job interview is tomorrow at 9 am and I haven't prepared at all. Here's the job posting: [Shift Supervisor, neighbourhood bakery café. Open the store at 6 am two days a week, lead a team of 4, handle customer complaints, count the cash drawer at close, and train new staff. 1+ year in food service. Weekend availability.] Based on this posting, what are the 5 questions they're most likely to ask me? Keep each one short, and add one line on what they're really checking."
Its question 4, word for word: "Your cash drawer is $20 short at close. What do you do?"
And what that question is really checking, word for word: "honesty and process. Recount, document, report, and don't cover it up or guess."

HOW (10 minutes tonight):
1. Open ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini.
2. Paste the whole job posting.
3. Ask: "What are the 5 questions they're most likely to ask me? Keep each one short, and add one line on what they're really checking."
4. Answer each one out loud once, with a real 30-second story from your own work.

THE CATCH: these are likely questions, not their real list. The interviewer can ask anything, and AI doesn't know your experience, so the answers have to come from you. Never let it invent a story for you to tell.

PRIVACY TIP: the posting is public, so paste it freely. Leave out your full name, address and anything private from your résumé; you don't need them to get the questions.

posts.caption:
Giving kids liquid medicine? 0.5 mL is not 5 mL. Mix them up and it's 10 times the dose.

WHY: the AAP says mixing up 0.5 mL and 5 mL can mean giving 10 times more medicine than your child needs, or 10 times less. And kitchen spoons come in lots of different sizes, so they can't measure a dose.

HOW:
1. Use the syringe, dropper, cup or dosing spoon that came with the medicine. An oral syringe is usually the most accurate (AAP).
2. Measure in mL, not teaspoons.
3. Look at the lines and numbers. Don't just fill it to the top.
4. Medicine cup? Set it on the table to check the level.
5. Lost the syringe? Ask your pharmacist for one (NHS).

THE CATCH: a dosing tool that's too big makes it easy to give too much. Match the tool to the dose.

Do this: Measure in mL, with its own syringe.

Send this to whoever does the night-time doses.

Follow for one calm thing a night, from bump to toddler.

posts.caption:
Stressed already? Sigh slowly for 5 minutes: one deep breath in through your nose, a short sip more, then a long breath out through your mouth.

WHY: a long, slow breath out is the part that calms you. In the study, people who did this every day ended up with a slower breathing rate, and their mood lifted more than people who meditated for the same time.

HOW:
1. Breathe in through your nose.
2. When your lungs feel full, take one more short sip of air on top.
3. Breathe out slowly through your mouth, all the way.
4. Repeat for 5 minutes. Nose-only is fine too.

THE RESEARCH: 108 adults did 5 minutes a day for a month of one of three breathing exercises or mindfulness meditation. The 'cyclic sighing' group (the one above) gained the most positive mood, more than the meditation group, and the effect grew over the days they practised.

THE CATCH: both groups felt less anxious by about the same amount; the difference was in good mood. It was a small, remote study over one month, and it didn't change sleep. It's a stress tool, not a treatment. Stop if you feel dizzy.

Do this now: Set a 5-minute timer. In, in, long out. Keep going until it rings.

Send this to whoever has a big meeting this morning.

Follow for one small sleep or focus trick a day.

#stressrelief #breathwork #focus #morningroutine #calm

posts.caption:
Coin battery swallowed? Go to the ER now. On the way, if they're over 1: 2 teaspoons of honey.

Part 2 of coin batteries (Part 1, yesterday: a nickel-sized battery can burn a throat in 2 hours, and where they hide).

WHY: a swallowed coin battery can start burning through the throat within 2 hours, so every minute counts (AAP, Health Canada). The AAP says honey can be given on the way to help while you get to the ER.

HOW (AAP HealthyChildren.org):
1. Go to the ER right away, or call 911.
2. Over 12 months, can swallow liquids, and the battery was swallowed within the last 12 hours? While you wait for or travel to emergency care, give 2 teaspoons of honey.
3. Repeat about every 10 minutes, up to 6 doses.
4. Tell the doctors and nurses: "It might be a coin battery."
5. Don't make them throw up. If they vomit, no more honey.

THE CATCH: never delay the ER to find honey. No honey at all for babies under 1. Health Canada's own advice is simply: get to the nearest emergency department immediately; some poison centres suggest honey on the way, for healthy children over one year only.

Do this: Save the poison centre number tonight.

Quebec: 1-800-463-5060 (Centre antipoison du Québec)
US: Poison Control, 1-800-222-1222

posts.caption:
Bed at 11? Hard workout done by 10. Finish hard workouts 1 hour before bed. Evening exercise is fine for sleep; it's the hard session that ends right before bed that can keep you up.

Sleep tonight, Part 2. (Part 1, yesterday: lying awake? After about 20 minutes, get out of bed.)

WHY: a hard session leaves your heart rate and body temperature up for a while. Moderate exercise doesn't seem to do that enough to matter, and in the studies evening exercise slightly increased deep sleep.

HOW:
1. Pick your bedtime (say 11 pm).
2. Hard stuff (intervals, heavy lifting, a race-pace run) done by 10 pm.
3. The last hour: easy only. A walk, a stretch, a shower.

THE RESEARCH: a review of 23 studies (Stutz, Eiholzer & Spengler, ETH Zurich) found the studies 'do not support the hypothesis that evening exercise negatively affects sleep'. The authors' one caution: falling asleep, total sleep and sleep efficiency 'might be impaired after vigorous exercise ending ≤ 1 h before bedtime'.

THE CATCH: that caution rests on very little data (ETH's own summary says it was based on just one study), and the studies were in healthy adults. So it's a sensible buffer, not a hard law. If evening training clearly wrecks your sleep, move it earlier.

Do this tonight: Finish hard workouts 1 hour before bed. A walk or easy stretch later is fine.

Send this to whoever trains at 10:30 pm and then can't sleep.

Follow for one small sleep or focus trick a day.

#sleep #eveningworkout #fitness #sleepbetter #focus

posts.caption:
One pension? Split it. Pay less tax? In Canada, a retired couple (married or common-law) can split eligible pension income on their tax returns: up to half can be reported by the other spouse.

WHY: Canada's income tax rates rise as income rises. When one person has all the pension income, more of it can land in a higher bracket. Moving up to 50% to the partner with less income can lower the couple's total tax. It's a paper move on the returns; no money changes accounts.

HOW:
1. At tax time, fill in form T1032, Joint Election to Split Pension Income.
2. Both of you sign it, with the same numbers on both copies.
3. Each of you files the same election with your own return by the filing deadline. You can pick a different share each year.

THE CATCH: CPP and OAS don't count. Income from a RRIF counts only once the person with the pension is 65 or older at the end of the year (or after a spouse's death). Workplace pension payments (a life annuity from a pension plan) generally count at any age. You both need to be residents of Canada on December 31 and not separated for 90 days or more because the relationship broke down.

WHO THIS IS FOR: married or common-law couples in Canada, not separated, where one partner gets much more pension income than the other.

Do this: both sign form T1032 at tax time.

Send this to your parents.

Education only, not financial advice.

Follow for one money rule a day, in plain words.

#personalfinancecanada #retirementcanada #CRA #canadianmoney #pensionsplitting

posts.caption:
Flight at 6 am and you haven't packed? Tell AI about the trip and ask for a packing list sorted by room, so you walk through your place once.

WHY IT WORKS: a normal list makes you run back and forth. Sorting it by where things live (bedroom, bathroom, kitchen, front door) turns it into one walk. And because AI works from what you tell it (carry-on only, a wedding, a hike, rain), the list fits this trip instead of every trip.

THE REAL TEST: we made up a trip and asked Claude (Anthropic) on Nov 2, 2026: "My flight is at 6 am tomorrow and I haven't packed. 3 nights in Vancouver, carry-on only. There's a wedding on Saturday (I'm wearing a suit), one day hike, and it'll probably rain. Make me a packing list sorted by room in my apartment (bedroom, bathroom, kitchen, front door) so I only walk through once. Keep it short."
It came back with 4 rooms. A few lines, word for word: "Rain jacket (wear it on the plane)" · "Liquids in a clear bag, 100 ml max each" · "Reusable water bottle (empty for security)" · "ID or passport, wallet, keys".
And the carry-on trick, word for word: "Hiking shoes (wear them on the plane, since they're the bulkiest pair)".

HOW (2 minutes, then one walk):
1. Open ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini.
2. Type the trip: how many nights, the bag you're allowed, the plans and the weather.
3. Ask: "Make me a packing list sorted by room in my apartment so I only walk through once. Keep it short."
4. Walk the rooms in its order and tick each line as it goes in the bag.

THE CATCH: AI doesn't know your airline's rules or what's already in your bag. Check your airline's carry-on size and liquids rules before you go, and add anything personal it couldn't guess (glasses, contacts, chargers you always forget).

PRIVACY TIP: "Vancouver, 3 nights" is enough. Leave out your flight number, hotel and home address.

Trip made up for this post.

Do this: Ask for a packing list sorted by room.

Send this to whoever always packs at midnight.

Follow to learn one real AI trick a day.

posts.caption:
High chair? Buckle all 5 straps, every time: 2 shoulders, 2 hips and 1 between the legs.

WHY: the NHS says to use a 5-point harness every time you put your baby in a highchair, and to keep using it for toddlers. The AAP says to use the safety straps whenever your child sits in the chair, including the crotch strap (the one between the legs).

HOW:
1. Both shoulder straps on.
2. Both hip straps on.
3. The strap between the legs, every time, even for a quick snack.
4. Keep the chair away from tables and counters. The AAP says a child can push off them hard enough to tip the chair.
5. Never leave a young child alone in the high chair, and never let them stand in it (AAP).

THE CATCH: a high chair that hooks onto a table is not a good substitute for a freestanding one (AAP). Chair with fewer straps? The AAP rule still applies: use the safety straps, including the one between the legs.

Do this: next meal, buckle all 5 before the food goes on the tray.

Send this to whoever feeds them lunch: grandparents, daycare, the sitter.

Follow for one calm thing a night, from bump to toddler.

General information only, not medical advice.

#babyproofing #highchair #toddlermom #newparents #childsafety

3 am bottle? Use water boiled in the last 30 minutes, so it's still at least 70°C: hot enough to kill germs in the powder.

3 am Club No. 6: the night bottle.

WHY: the NHS says sealed tins and packets of powdered formula can sometimes contain bacteria, and water at 70°C or more will kill harmful bacteria. Boiled water left to cool no more than 30 minutes stays at least 70°C.

AT 3 AM (NHS):
1. Boil fresh tap water. Don't use water that's been boiled before.
2. Use it within 30 minutes, so it's still 70°C or hotter.
3. Make the formula, then cool the bottle, lid on, under cold running water.
4. Test a drop on the inside of your wrist. It should feel like body temperature.

THE CATCH: never warm formula in the microwave. It heats unevenly and can burn your baby's mouth. Formula left in the bottle after a feed: throw it away. Make feeds 1 at a time, as your baby needs them.

Do this: tonight, set the kettle, a clean bottle and the formula out before bed.

Send this to whoever's on the night shift with you.

posts.caption:
Kids' skin burns 4 times faster than yours. So keep hot tap water at 49°C (120°F) or less.

WHY: the Public Health Agency of Canada says hot tap water can burn a young child in seconds, and a child's skin burns in a quarter of the time an adult's does. That's 4 times faster.

HOW (Public Health Agency of Canada):
1. Keep the water heater itself at 60°C (140°F). PHAC says this helps prevent harmful bacteria such as Legionella from growing.
2. Fit anti-scald mixing valves on taps, showers and tubs (or one on the water heater), set so hot water comes out at about 49°C (120°F).
3. Bath time: run the cold water first, and finish with cold.
4. Always test the water before your child gets in, and stay with them the whole bath.

THE CATCH: don't just turn the heater down. The 60°C is there to stop bacteria; the valve is what brings the tap down to 49°C.

RENTING? Ask your landlord about anti-scald valves (a plumber fits them). Until then: cold first, then hot, and always test the water before they get in.

Do this: bath tonight? Run the cold first, then add hot (the NHS says the same: cold water in first, then some hot).

Send this to anyone who gives your little one a bath at their place.

Follow for one calm thing a night, from bump to toddler.

General information only, not medical advice.

#babyproofing #childsafety #bathtime #newparents #toddlermom

posts.caption:
Hit snooze again? 30 minutes is okay. Today's word: Snooze.

One Word No. 7. Each episode is one word that guards your focus.

WHY: if you're someone who snoozes anyway and falls back asleep easily, a short snooze barely costs you sleep, and waking in stages may mean you're less likely to be pulled out of deep sleep.

THE RESEARCH: 31 regular snoozers slept in a sleep lab. One morning they snoozed for 30 minutes; another morning the first alarm got them up. Snoozing cost about 6 minutes of sleep, and on tests right after waking they did as well or a bit better. Mood, sleepiness and the morning stress hormone showed no clear change.

HOW:
1. Set the first alarm no more than 30 minutes before you have to be up.
2. Snooze if you like.
3. The last alarm means feet on the floor.

THE CATCH: it's one small lab study of people who already snooze, and only 30 minutes was tested. If you find it hard to fall back asleep, or you feel groggy all morning, one alarm at your real wake-up time is the simpler choice.

Do this: Snoozing anyway? Stop at 30 minutes, then get up.

Send this to whoever sets 5 alarms every morning.

Follow for one small sleep or focus trick a day.

#sleep #morningroutine #snooze #focus #oneword

posts.caption:
Maths test coming up? Mix 3 kinds of problems in every practice set. It feels harder while you practise, and you remember more on the test.

WHY: when every problem on the page is the same kind, you know the method before you even read the question. On the real test the kinds are mixed, so the hard part is spotting which method each problem needs. Mixed practice trains exactly that.

HOW:
1. Pick 3 kinds of problems the test will cover (say, one from each of your last 3 chapters).
2. Take a few problems of each kind.
3. Put them in order 1 of each kind, then repeat: A, B, C, A, B, C.

THE RESEARCH: in a study by Rohrer and Taylor (University of South Florida), students learned to find the volume of 4 unusual shapes. While practising, the students who did one shape at a time scored 89% and the mixers 60%. A week later, on the test, it flipped: mixers 63%, one-at-a-time 20%. A 2019 review of 59 studies (Brunmair & Richter) found mixing helps on average, maths included.

THE CATCH: that experiment was small (18 students), and mixing feels worse while you do it, so expect more mistakes in practice. It helps when you have to tell kinds of problems apart (maths, science, question types). For learning lists of words, the same review found mixing did worse.

Do this tonight: 1 of each kind, then repeat. Take problems from your last 3 chapters and shuffle them into one set.

Send this to a friend with a maths test this week.

Follow for one small sleep or focus trick a day.

#studytips #studying #maths #exam #focus

posts.caption:
Can't switch off? 45 minutes of calm music at bedtime, every night. In a 3-week study, calm music improved students' sleep. An audiobook didn't.

WHY: slow, quiet music gives a busy mind something easy to follow, without the story or words that keep you listening. Done every night, it also becomes a cue that it's time to sleep.

HOW:
1. Pick a calm playlist: slow, quiet, no lyrics you'll sing along to.
2. Volume low, phone face down out of reach.
3. Set a sleep timer for 45 minutes. On Spotify: tap ••• on the song, then Sleep timer, then 45 minutes.
4. Repeat every night for a few weeks.

THE RESEARCH: 94 students with poor sleep were split into 3 groups. One listened to calm classical music for 45 minutes at bedtime, one to an audiobook, one did nothing, every night for 3 weeks. Sleep quality improved only in the music group (Harmat, Takács & Bódizs 2008). A 2022 Cochrane review of 13 trials (1,007 adults with insomnia) found music probably improves how well people feel they sleep (moderate-certainty evidence).

THE CATCH: the improvement is in how people rated their sleep, and it builds over nights, not in one. Evidence that music makes you fall asleep faster is weaker (low certainty). If you've slept badly for weeks, talk to a doctor: insomnia has good treatments.

Do this tonight: Calm playlist on. Sleep timer: 45 minutes.

Send this to whoever is still scrolling at 1 am.

Follow for one small sleep or focus trick a day.

#sleep #insomnia #cantsleep #sleepbetter #focus

posts.caption:
Buying together? Up to $60,000 each. In Canada, the Home Buyers' Plan (HBP) lets each first-time buyer take up to $60,000 out of their own RRSP to buy a home, without paying tax on it, as long as they pay it back a bit each year.

WHY: the limit is per person, not per home. So a couple who both qualify and both have the money in their RRSPs can use up to $120,000 between them for the same home. The CRA's own first-home guide walks through a couple doing exactly this.

HOW:
1. Sign a written agreement to buy (or build) the home first.
2. Each of you fills in form T1036 (Home Buyers' Plan request) and gives it to the bank or provider that holds your RRSP. One form for each withdrawal.
3. Buy or build the home before October 1 of the year after your first withdrawal, and plan to live in it.
4. Pay it back a bit each year, over 15 years: at least 1/15 of the total a year once repayments start (after the grace period, per CRA). The CRA shows your minimum each year on your HBP statement of account, with your notice of assessment. You can always pay back more.

THE CATCH: it's a loan to yourself, not free money. You can only take what's already in your RRSP. Money you put into an RRSP in the 89 days before you take it out may not be deductible. A missed or short yearly payment is added to your income that year and taxed. And it all comes out of your retirement savings until you pay it back.

WHO THIS IS FOR: residents of Canada who count as first-time buyers: in the year you withdraw or the 4 years before it, you didn't live in a home that you owned. A home your current spouse or common-law partner owned counts too: if you lived in their home in that time, you don't qualify (CRA). Right now, for a first withdrawal from 2022 to 2028, repayments start the fifth year after it (CRA).

Do this: sign the deal to buy, then each ask your RRSP bank for form T1036.

Send this to the person you're house-hunting with.

Education only, not financial advice.

Follow for one money rule a day, in plain words.

posts.caption:
Saving $0? Canada still adds $500. In Canada, the Canada Learning Bond puts $500 into a child's RESP for families with lower incomes, and you don't have to put in any money of your own.

WHY: the bond pays $500 for the first year your child qualifies, then $100 for each more year your family's income qualifies (based on the primary caregiver's adjusted family income), up to age 15. That's up to $2,000 in total. The bond is retroactive: amounts build up for each year of eligibility (to the end of the year the child turns 15), so years you missed aren't lost. An RESP (Registered Education Savings Plan) is a savings plan for school after high school. Personal contributions aren't required to get the bond. Canada also adds $25 to help cover the cost of opening the plan.

HOW:
1. Get a Social Insurance Number (SIN) for your child. It's free (Service Canada, or with the birth registration).
2. Pick a bank or other RESP provider that offers the Canada Learning Bond.
3. Open an RESP and ask them to apply for the bond. Bring your SIN and your child's.
4. Keep filing your taxes every year, so the CRA can see that your family still qualifies.

THE CATCH: you only get it if someone opens an RESP and asks. Each year is checked against family income, so some years may qualify and others not. The bond goes into one RESP per child. Kids born in 2024 or later: Canada plans to start opening one automatically from April 2028, but you can open one now.

WHO QUALIFIES: kids born in 2004 or later with a valid SIN, living in Canada, in a lower-income family. For July 2026 to June 2027, the family's adjusted income must be $58,523 or less with 1 to 3 children (under $66,036 with 4, under $73,577 with 5). Missed it as a kid? A young adult can still ask for it themselves until the day before they turn 21.

Do this: open an RESP and ask for the Canada Learning Bond.

Send this to a new parent.

Education only, not financial advice.

Follow for one money rule a day, in plain words.

#personalfinancecanada #RESP #canadalearningbond #newparents #canadianmoney

posts.caption:
Only 2 left? Sleep on it 24 hours. The habit: wait a day before you buy anything you didn't plan to.

Rich Habits, Decoded No. 6. Each episode takes one money habit and shows you how to do it on a normal paycheque.

WHY IT WORKS: countdown timers and 'only 2 left' messages are built to rush you. Canada's Competition Bureau warns about fake urgency like this, where 'the timer runs out or resets but the offer is still available.' A one-day pause takes the rush away, so you decide with a clear head instead of a ticking clock.

HOW:
1. Leave it in the cart (or take a screenshot of it). Don't pay yet.
2. Set a phone reminder for the same time tomorrow: 'Still want it?'
3. When it goes off, buy it only if you still want it and it fits this month's budget.

THE CATCH: this is for wants, not needs. Groceries, rent and medicine don't wait a day. And sometimes a real sale does end; if it's gone tomorrow and you'd still pay full price, you didn't lose much.

Do this: next time a page says 'only 2 left', set a 24-hour reminder instead.

Send this to the friend with 12 open shopping tabs.

posts.caption:
Baby shower's over and 20 thank-you notes left to write? Paste who gave what into AI and ask for a short note for each one.

WHY IT WORKS: the hard part of 20 notes isn't the writing, it's starting each one. Once AI knows the gift, it can say how you'll use it, and that's the line that makes a note feel personal. Asking for them to sound different stops 20 copies of the same sentence.

THE REAL TEST: we made up a baby shower with 20 guests and gifts and asked Claude (Anthropic) on Nov 3, 2026: "My baby shower was on Saturday and I have 20 thank-you notes to write today. Here's who gave what: [1. Aunt Rosa: a handmade quilt … 20. My book club: a basket of snacks for late nights] Write a 2-sentence note for each one. Name the gift and say one specific way we'll use it. Don't make them all sound the same."
It wrote all 20. Note 3 (Grandpa Joe, a rocking chair he fixed up), word for word: "I can't believe how beautiful the rocking chair turned out after all your work on it. It's going right next to the crib, and every 3 a.m. feeding will happen in it."

HOW (about 15 minutes):
1. Open ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini.
2. Type each person and their gift, one per line.
3. Ask: "Write a 2-sentence note for each one. Name the gift and say one specific way we'll use it. Don't make them all sound the same."
4. Read each note, change anything that isn't true for you, then copy it into the card by hand.

THE CATCH: AI guesses details it can't know: read every note and fix anything that isn't true before you send. It wrote about a nursery chair, morning walks and the spot next to the crib, and for the $50 gift card it wrote "We're going to use it to stock up on diapers and wipes". None of that came from us. Add one real detail of your own where you can.

PRIVACY TIP: first names and the gift are enough. Leave out addresses, last names and anything about anyone's health.

posts.caption:
Store closes at 9 and no plan for the week? Ask AI for 5 dinners that share ingredients, with one shopping list.

WHY IT WORKS: food goes to waste when each recipe needs its own half-bag of something. Asking for dinners that share ingredients makes AI plan the week as one shop: the same chicken, peppers and beans turn up on different nights, so the list gets shorter and less is left over.

THE REAL TEST: we made up the ask and gave it to Claude (Anthropic) on Nov 3, 2026: "The grocery store closes at 9 and I need to shop for the week. Plan 5 weeknight dinners for 2 adults, each under 30 minutes, that share ingredients so nothing goes to waste. Budget about $80. Give me the 5 dinners (one line each), then one shopping list, then tell me which ingredients get used more than once. Keep it short."
Its 5 dinners, word for word: "Mon: Chicken fajitas." · "Tue: Chicken fried rice." · "Wed: Black bean quesadillas." · "Thu: Garlic chicken and broccoli pasta." · "Fri: Rice and bean burrito bowls."
It priced the list at "about $70 to $80" (its estimate), and listed what gets reused, word for word: "Chicken: Mon, Tue, Thu" · "Bell peppers: Mon, Wed, Fri" · "Black beans: Wed, Fri".

HOW (5 minutes before you leave):
1. Open ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini.
2. Say how many dinners, for how many people, how much time and your budget.
3. Ask for dinners "that share ingredients so nothing goes to waste", one shopping list, and which ingredients get used more than once.
4. Cross off what you already have, then shop the list.

THE CATCH: read the plan before you trust it. One of its tips said "Rice: Tue, Fri. Cook a double batch Tuesday, since day-old rice is better for fried rice anyway." But the fried rice is on Tuesday, so to have day-old rice, cook it Monday night. Prices are its guesses, not your store's.

PRIVACY TIP: "2 adults, about $80" is all it needs. No names, address or health details.

posts.caption:
16°C inside and the landlord still hasn't fixed the heat? Tell AI what's wrong, since when, what you've done and what you need, and ask for a short, polite but firm email.

AI, for real · Day 13. One real test of what AI can do, with the output shown.

WHY IT WORKS: when you're cold and annoyed, the email comes out either too soft or too angry. Giving AI the four facts (what's wrong, since when, what you've already done, what you need by when) gets you a message that's calm, dated and hard to ignore, and a written record if you need one later.

THE REAL TEST (names, unit and dates made up for this post), Claude (Anthropic):
Prompt: "Today is Friday, November 6. The heat in my apartment has been off since Wednesday, November 4, and it's 16°C inside. I texted my landlord, Dan, on Wednesday and he said he'd look at it, but nothing has happened. Write me a short email to send him before 5 pm today. Polite but firm: what's wrong, since when, what I've already done, and that I need the heat repaired by Saturday, November 7. Sign it from Alex in unit 4B. Under 120 words."
Slide 2 is its email, word for word. Notice it turned our ask into one clear request with a time: "Please let me know today when someone will come, and I'll make sure they can get in."

THE CATCH: AI doesn't know the rules where you live. Heat and repair rules for rentals depend on your province or city, so check your local tenant rules before you quote any of them. Keep a copy of the email and of your first text, and check every date in the draft before you send it.

PRIVACY TIP: you don't need to paste your lease, your landlord's details or your phone number. A first name and unit number are enough to draft it.

Do this: in ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini, type what's wrong, since when, what you've already done, and what you need by when. Then ask: "Write me a short email. Polite but firm. Under 120 words."

Toddler at home? Windows should open 10 cm (4 inches), no more.

WHY: the Canadian Paediatric Society says to fit window guards, or make sure windows are latched so they can't open more than 10 cm. A screen is not a stop: CPS says window screens do not prevent falls and cannot hold the weight of a toddler.

HOW (Canadian Paediatric Society):
1. Fit window stops or window guards so each window opens 10 cm (4 inches) at most.
2. No stops yet? Keep the windows latched.
3. Keep furniture, including the crib, away from windows that open.
4. Don't count on the screen to hold anyone.

THE CATCH: a screen keeps bugs out, not toddlers in. And a stop only helps when it's in place, so check it after you open a window wide.

RENTING? Ask your landlord about window stops or guards.

Do this: this weekend, fit window stops so every window opens 10 cm at most.

Send this to anyone whose home your toddler visits.

Newborn breathing pauses at 3 am? Pauses under 10 seconds are normal, if your baby is comfortable.

3 am Club No. 7: the breathing pause.

WHY: the AAP's HealthyChildren.org says newborns often take short breathing pauses of less than 10 seconds, called periodic breathing. A few faster 'catch-up' breaths often follow. It usually settles by 1 month of age.

AT 3 AM (AAP HealthyChildren.org, NHS):
1. Watch for a few breaths. A short pause, then a few quick breaths, is the usual pattern.
2. Check they look comfortable: settled, normal colour.
3. Breathing stopped for more than 10 seconds, even if it's normal now? Call your doctor or get care now.
4. Not breathing? Call 911 (NHS: call for an ambulance if your child stops breathing). Bluish or grey lips, tongue or face, struggling for each breath, or new grunting with each breath? Call 911 too (AAP).

THE CATCH: 'normal' only applies to short pauses in a baby who is comfortable. If you're worried, call your doctor. Trust your gut.

Do this: tonight, watch one pause and count. Under 10 seconds, then normal breathing? You can breathe too.

Send this to whoever's on the night shift with you.

posts.caption:
Heating on? Keep the room your baby sleeps in at 16 to 20°C (about 61 to 68°F).

WHY: the NHS says overheating can increase the risk of SIDS (sudden infant death syndrome). The Lullaby Trust recommends 16 to 20°C so babies don't get too hot.

HOW (Lullaby Trust, NHS):
1. Put a room thermometer in the room where your baby sleeps. It's hard to guess the temperature.
2. Use a well-fitting baby sleeping bag, or lightweight bedding firmly tucked in no higher than their shoulders. No loose blankets, duvets or pillows in the cot.
3. Baby's skin hot or sweaty? Take off one or more layers.
4. Take hats and extra clothing off as soon as you come indoors. Babies don't need hats indoors.

THE CATCH: hands and feet usually feel cooler, and that's normal. Feel their chest or the back of their neck instead.

Do this: tonight, put a room thermometer in the room where your baby sleeps.

Send this to whoever puts your baby down at their place.

Follow for one calm thing a night, from bump to toddler.

General information only, not medical advice.

#safesleep #newborn #newparents #babysleep #sids

posts.caption:
Bed at 11? Last coffee by 2 pm. That's 9 hours before bed. Caffeine keeps working long after you stop feeling it.

WHY: caffeine blocks the signal that makes you sleepy as the day goes on, and it stays in your body for hours. So an afternoon coffee can still be working at bedtime. You may fall asleep fine and still get less sleep, and less deep sleep.

HOW:
1. Pick your usual bedtime.
2. Count back 9 hours. Bed at 11 pm means your last coffee by 2 pm.
3. After that: decaf or herbal tea.
4. Count tea, cola and energy drinks too. Stronger drinks need even longer.

THE RESEARCH: a 2023 review pooled 24 studies (Gardiner et al., Sleep Medicine Reviews). On average, caffeine cut total sleep by 45 minutes and sleep efficiency by 7%. To avoid losing sleep, the authors estimated a regular coffee (107 mg) should come at least 8.8 hours before bed, and a pre-workout drink (217.5 mg) at least 13.2 hours. In an earlier study (Drake et al. 2013), a large dose (400 mg) taken 6 hours before bed still cut measured sleep by more than an hour, and people didn't notice.

THE CATCH: these are averages from mostly small studies, and people handle caffeine very differently. 9 hours is a guide for a regular cup, not an exact line. If you sleep well after an afternoon coffee, you may not need it.

Do this tomorrow: Pick your bedtime. Count back 9 hours. Bed at 11? Last coffee by 2 pm. After that, decaf or herbal tea.

Send this to whoever grabs a coffee at 4 pm.

Follow for one small sleep or focus trick a day.

#sleep #caffeine #coffee #cantsleep #sleepbetter

posts.caption:
Slept in Sunday? Same alarm, all 7 days. Today's word: Same.

One Word No. 8. Each episode is one word that guards your focus.

WHY: your body clock runs on routine. Waking at very different times on different days keeps shifting it, a bit like flying across time zones every weekend. A steady wake-up time gives it one fixed point to set itself by.

THE RESEARCH: 60,977 adults in the UK Biobank wore wrist trackers for about a week. Researchers scored how regular their sleep times were and followed them for about 6 years (mean 6.3, up to 7.8). Regularity predicted the risk of dying early (from any cause) better than how long people slept. The least regular sleepers did worst.

HOW:
1. Pick a wake-up time you can keep on a Saturday too.
2. Set one alarm for it, 7 days a week.
3. Tired on the weekend? Go to bed earlier rather than sleeping in.

THE CATCH: this study shows a link, not proof that changing your schedule changes your health. Most people in it were older (average age 63), and the study adjusted for many other factors but can't rule out all of them. Shift workers and new parents can't always keep one time, and that's okay.

Do this: Pick one wake-up time. Keep it all 7 days.

Send this to whoever sleeps till noon on Sundays.

Follow for one small sleep or focus trick a day.

#sleep #sleepschedule #morningroutine #focus #oneword

posts.caption:
Got it right once? Don't drop the flashcard yet. Keep it in until you get it right 3 times, then review it again in a few days.

WHY: pulling an answer out of memory is what makes it stick, and each extra right answer strengthens it. A card you get right once and set aside often slips away before the test. Coming back to the pile on later days locks it in.

HOW:
1. Go through the pile. Each time you get a card right, make a tally mark on its corner.
2. Wrong? It goes to the back of the pile.
3. 3 tallies: set that card aside for tonight.
4. Go through the whole pile again on 3 later days, until you get each card right once.

THE RESEARCH: in 3 experiments with 533 students (Rawson & Dunlosky 2011), the authors' recommended schedule was 3 right answers in the first session, then 3 relearning sessions spread out over time; the later sessions mattered most on tests 1 to 4 months later. In 4 experiments, Kornell & Bjork (2008) found that letting people drop flashcards had small but consistently negative effects on learning, and forcing a drop after one right answer hurt the most.

THE CATCH: more right answers take more time, and after the first few the extra gain gets smaller. It works best for facts and definitions you can put on a card, not for practising problems.

Do this tonight: Right 3 times? Set it aside. Tally mark on the corner each time. Then review the pile again in a few days.

Send this to whoever is making flashcards tonight.

Follow for one small sleep or focus trick a day.

#studytips #flashcards #studying #exam #focus

posts.caption:
Dentist, glasses, pills: $2,000 this year? Claim them on one return, usually the lower earner's.

In Canada, one of you can claim the medical bills for both partners and your kids under 18, all together, on one tax return (line 33099).

WHY: only the part of the bills above a floor counts. The floor is 3% of the claimer's net income, or a fixed amount if that is less ($2,891 for 2026; $2,834 for 2025). A lower income means a lower floor, so more of the same bills count.

The maths (made up for this post): $2,000 of bills.
• You earn $90,000: 3% is $2,700, more than the bills, so $0 counts.
• Your partner earns $40,000: 3% is $1,200, so $800 counts for the credit.
That $800 is not money back. It's the amount the credit is worked out on: $800 x 14% = $112 off your federal tax for 2026, plus your province's own credit.

HOW:
1. Gather every receipt: dentist, prescription glasses, prescription drugs, and the rest of the CRA's list.
2. Pick any 12-month period that ends in the tax year.
3. In your tax app, enter the bills on the lower earner's return first, then check the other return too, and keep the one that cuts more tax.

THE CATCH: it's a non-refundable credit, so it only lowers tax the claimer owes. If the lower earner owes little or no tax, the other return may work better. Purely cosmetic work and over-the-counter medicine don't count. Keep the receipts.

WHO THIS IS FOR: you, your spouse or common-law partner, and your or their kids under 18. Bills for other relatives who depend on you (an adult child, a parent) go on line 33199, with their own rules.

Do this: Claim them on line 33099, usually on the lower earner's return. Check both in your tax app.

Send this to whoever does the taxes in your home.

Education only, not financial advice.

Follow for one money rule a day, in plain words.

Free 30-day trial? Set a day-28 reminder. The habit: the minute you start a free trial, set a phone reminder for 2 days before it ends.

Rich Habits, Decoded No. 7. Each episode takes one money habit and shows you how to do it on a normal paycheque.

WHY IT WORKS: many trials take your card and roll into a monthly charge on their own. Canada's Competition Bureau warns that some 'free trials' are subscription traps. A reminder turns an automatic charge into a choice you make on purpose.

HOW:
1. Before you sign up, find the end date and how to cancel in the terms.
2. In your phone's calendar or reminders app, set an alert 2 days before the end date: 'Still using it?'
3. When it goes off: still using it? Keep it. If not, cancel, and save the cancellation email.
4. Next month, check your card bill for the charge, to be sure it stopped (or that you meant to keep it).

THE CATCH: some services end your access the moment you cancel, and some charge the minute the trial ends. Read the terms first. If you can't cancel, call your credit card provider.

Do this: Set a day-28 reminder the day you start a 30-day trial.

Send this to the friend who just signed up for a free trial.

posts.caption:
Earn twice what your partner does? Save in their RRSP, and you still get the tax break.

In Canada, a spousal (or common-law partner) RRSP is an RRSP in your partner's name that you pay into. You claim the deduction on your own return. When the money comes out later, it's normally taxed as your partner's income, not yours.

WHY: the higher earner gets the deduction now, and later the money is taxed in the hands of the partner with less income, often at a lower rate.

THE 3-YEAR RULE: if you paid into any spousal RRSP in the year your partner takes money out, or in the 2 years before, that withdrawal is taxed as your income instead (form T2205). Last deposit in 2026? A withdrawal in 2029 or later is clear, as long as you add nothing in 2027 or 2028. Every new deposit restarts the 3-year clock.

HOW:
1. Ask your bank or brokerage to open a spousal RRSP: your partner owns it, you pay in.
2. Pay in from your own RRSP room. It counts against your limit, not theirs.
3. Claim the deduction on your return.
4. Count 3 calendar years from your LAST deposit (not from opening the account) before your partner takes any out.

THE CATCH: it uses your own RRSP room, and the money legally belongs to your partner. Take it out too soon and it's taxed as yours.

WHO THIS IS FOR: married or common-law couples. You can keep paying in until the December your partner turns 71.

Do this: Ask your bank for a spousal RRSP.

Send this to your partner.

Education only, not financial advice.

Follow for one money rule a day, in plain words.

posts.caption:
Nonna turns 90 tomorrow and you want to write her card in Italian? Ask AI for the message in her language, with the English under each line.

WHY IT WORKS: you know what you want to say; AI handles the grammar. Asking for the English under each line lets you check that every sentence says what you meant before you copy it into the card. Giving it one true memory (gnocchi on Sundays) turns a translation into a message that sounds like you.

THE REAL TEST: we made up a grandmother and a memory and asked Claude (Anthropic) on Nov 4, 2026: "My grandmother turns 90 tomorrow. She grew up in Italy and still reads Italian best, but my Italian is very basic. Write a short birthday message for her card in Italian: 3 sentences, warm and simple, and mention that she taught me to make gnocchi on Sundays. Put the English meaning under each Italian sentence. Sign it from Marco."
Its card, word for word: "Tanti auguri per i tuoi 90 anni, cara Nonna! Non dimenticherò mai le domeniche passate con te in cucina, quando mi hai insegnato a fare gli gnocchi. Ti voglio tanto bene e ti auguro una giornata piena di gioia. Con tanto affetto, Marco"
It added a note: "This uses the informal "tu" form, which is natural for a grandmother."

HOW (5 minutes):
1. Open ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini.
2. Say who it's for, which language she reads best, and one true memory.
3. Ask for 3 short sentences in her language, with the English meaning under each one.
4. Read the English, change anything that isn't true, then copy her language into the card by hand, accents and all.

THE CATCH: AI can be correct and still miss how your family talks: a dialect word, a nickname, the way she signs off. If you can, ask someone who speaks the language to read it before it goes in the card.

PRIVACY TIP: a first name and one memory are enough. Leave out her full name, address and anything about her health.

31 years at the same desk, and you get 2 minutes to say goodbye? Give AI 3 true things about the person and ask for a 2-minute speech you can read out loud.

WHY IT WORKS: speeches land on small true details. AI only knows what you give it, so 3 real things (a habit, a long-time job, a small kindness) become its stories. Short sentences are easy to read out loud.

THE REAL TEST: we made up a coworker and asked Claude (Anthropic) on Nov 4, 2026: "My coworker Linda is retiring after 31 years at the front desk of our town library, and I'm giving a 2-minute speech at her send-off tomorrow at 3 pm. Three true things about her: she knew every regular's name, she ran Saturday story time for 20 years, and she kept a jar of lemon candies at the desk for anyone having a rough day. Write a warm 2-minute speech (about 250 words) with one light joke, and end with a line everyone can raise a glass to. Use short sentences I can read out loud."
It turned the candy jar into this, word for word: "And then there's the jar. The lemon candies on the desk, for anyone having a rough day. Linda never asked what was wrong. She just slid the jar a little closer."
And it ended: "To Linda, who knew all our names and made every one of us feel known."

HOW (10 minutes):
1. Open ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini.
2. Say who it's for, how long they've been there, and 3 true things about them.
3. Ask for a 2-minute speech (about 250 words) in short sentences, with one light joke and a line everyone can raise a glass to.
4. Read it out loud once with a timer and cut anything that isn't true.

THE CATCH: AI fills gaps with things that sound true. It wrote that Linda knew regulars' "kids' names" and that kids from story time "now bring their own kids". We never said either. Cut or fix every line like that before you stand up.

PRIVACY TIP: a first name and the 3 stories are enough. Leave out last names, health news and anything they told you in confidence.

posts.caption:
Stairs need 2 gates: one at the top and one at the bottom. Keep them up until your child is at least 2.

WHY: the NHS says to keep using safety gates at the top and bottom of stairs until your little one is at least 2 years old. The Canadian Paediatric Society says pressure-mounted gates are not safe at the top of stairs.

HOW (NHS, Canadian Paediatric Society):
1. Fit a gate at the bottom of the stairs and another at the top.
2. At the top, use a gate that screws into the wall. Fix it securely into the studs.
3. Choose a gate with vertical bars, made of metal or wood.
4. Check the gaps between banisters. More than 6.5 cm (2.5 inches)? Cover them with boards or safety netting.
5. Carrying your baby on the stairs? Hold the handrail, in case you trip.

THE CATCH: a pressure-mounted gate wedges in place without screws. The Canadian Paediatric Society says it isn't safe at the top of the stairs, so the top gate gets screwed into the wall.

Do this: fit gates at the top and bottom.

Send this to whoever's babyproofing this weekend.

Follow for one calm thing a night, from bump to toddler.

General information only, not medical advice.

3 am feed? Newborns need 8 to 12 feeds a day. For breastfed newborns in the first few weeks, that's 8 to 12 feeds in 24 hours, and night feeds are part of it.

3 am Club No. 8: the 3 am feed.

WHY: the CDC and the Canadian Paediatric Society both say newborns breastfeed about 8 to 12 times in 24 hours in the first few weeks. At first, babies need to eat every 2 to 4 hours to get enough nutrition and to grow. Tiny tummies, so the feeds come round the clock.

AT 3 AM (CDC, Canadian Paediatric Society):
1. Follow their hunger cues and feed when you see them.
2. Let your baby set the pace.
3. In the first few days, it's common to need to wake a baby for a feed.
4. Still needing to wake them for feeds in the second week? Talk to your doctor.

THE CATCH: 8 to 12 is the usual range for breastfed newborns in the first weeks, not a target to hit exactly. Bottle-feeding? Ask your doctor or nurse how much and how often for your baby.

posts.caption:
Guess 5 answers, then read. Before you read a chapter tonight, guess the answers to 5 of its end-of-chapter questions. Even wrong guesses help.

WHY: a question you've already tried to answer stays in your head while you read, so you notice its answer when it comes up. And a wrong guess that you then fix tends to stick better than an answer you simply read.

HOW:
1. Turn to the questions at the end of the chapter.
2. Write a quick guess for 5 of them. Wrong is fine.
3. Read the chapter.
4. When you reach each answer, check your guess and fix it.

THE RESEARCH: a preregistered 2024 review pooled the studies on guessing before you learn (St. Hilaire, Chan & Ahn, Psychonomic Bulletin & Review). Guessing first improved memory for the questioned material by a moderate amount (g = 0.54, 97 effects). In one of the first studies (Richland, Kornell & Kao 2009), people who tried questions before reading an essay did better on the later test, even on the questions they had got wrong at first.

THE CATCH: it helps with what the questions ask, not the rest of the chapter. The same review found almost no boost for material the questions didn't cover, so pick questions on what matters. You also have to read the real answers afterwards. 5 is our pick to keep it quick; the studies used different numbers of questions.

Do this tonight: Turn to the end. Guess 5 answers. Use the end-of-chapter questions. Then read, and check each one.

Send this to someone with a chapter to read tonight.

Follow for one small sleep or focus trick a day.

#studytips #studying #exam #focus #studyhacks

posts.caption:
2 drinks before bed? Less dream sleep. Today's word: Skip.

One Word No. 9. Each episode is one word that guards your focus.

WHY: a drink can make you drowsy, but it changes how the night goes. It pushes back and shortens REM, the sleep stage where most vivid dreams happen.

THE RESEARCH: a 2025 review pooled 27 lab studies of healthy adults (Gardiner et al., Sleep Medicine Reviews). On average, alcohol cut REM sleep by about 11 minutes, and bigger doses cut more. The authors put the point where REM loss showed up at about 2 standard drinks. Falling asleep faster took a high dose, about 5 drinks, and by then REM loss was bigger still. Their verdict: using alcohol as a sleep aid "is not an appropriate strategy".

HOW:
1. On nights when sleep matters (a test, an early start), skip the drink before bed.
2. Wind down another way: a book, a warm shower, the lights down.

THE CATCH: their standard drink was 10 g of alcohol, a bit less than a can of beer, so 2 of theirs is less than 2 cans. The paper says 3 drinks in one place; we use the authors' own summary (2). Most drinks were given within 3 hours of bed, so the review couldn't say how early is early enough. Total sleep time didn't change clearly on average, and these were small lab studies.

Do this: Skip it. Wind down without a drink.

Send this to whoever swears by a nightcap.

Follow for one small sleep or focus trick a day.

#sleep #sleepbetter #alcohol #focus #oneword

posts.caption:
You both gave $200 to charity? Put both receipts on one return, and you can get more back.

In Canada, if you're married or common-law, you can claim your spouse's or common-law partner's donations on your own return. The federal tax credit is 14% of the first $200 you claim (2026) and 29% of every dollar after that.

The maths (made up for this post): you each give $200.
• Two returns: $200 x 14% = $28 credit, twice. $56 back.
• One return with both receipts ($400): $28 + ($200 x 29% = $58). $86 back.
Same gifts, $30 more back. "Back" here means less federal tax to pay: the credit can't go below $0 tax.

HOW:
1. Collect both official donation receipts (from registered charities).
2. In your tax app, put all of them on one partner's return: Schedule 9, line 34900.
3. Leave them off the other return, so nothing is claimed twice.
4. Give by Dec 31 for it to count on your 2026 return.

THE CATCH: it's a non-refundable credit, so it only helps if the partner who claims owes at least that much federal tax. If they owe little, claim on the other return, or carry the gifts forward (up to 5 years). If one of you earns in the top federal bracket, part of the claim can get 33%. Your province or territory adds its own donation credit on top, at its own rates. The yearly limit is 75% of net income.

Who qualifies: married or common-law couples, with official receipts from registered charities.

Do this: Claim both receipts on one return.

Send this to the partner who keeps the receipts.

Education only, not financial advice.

Follow for one money rule a day, in plain words.

Holiday gifts? Set a $300 cap first. The habit: before you buy anything, write every name with a dollar amount, and make them add up to one total.

Rich Habits, Decoded No. 8. Each episode takes one money habit and shows you how to do it on a normal paycheque.

WHY IT WORKS: holiday spending happens one "it's only $20 more" at a time, in many stores and apps. A total you pick in advance turns lots of small decisions into one. Canada's Financial Consumer Agency says to plan for big purchases and life events inside your budget, and the holidays are one.

HOW:
1. Pick the total you can pay in full by January, without a balance on your card. (We used $300. Made up for this post.)
2. Write every name and give each one a dollar amount: Mom $70, Dad $70, sister $60, best friend $60, office swap $40.
3. Before each purchase, check the list. Over on one name? Take it from another, never from outside the total.
4. Cross off each gift with what you really paid.

THE CATCH: the list only works if it includes everything: wrapping, shipping, the extra host gift. Add a small "extras" line if you need one.

Do this: Write the names and amounts tonight, before you shop.

Send this to the friend who starts holiday shopping in November.

Education only, not financial advice.

Follow for one money rule a day, in plain words.

#personalfinance #budgeting #moneyhabits #richhabits #holidaybudget

posts.caption:
Babysitter at 6 and it's all still in your head? Paste the messy brain dump into AI and ask for a fridge note sorted by time.

WHY IT WORKS: you remember things in the order they pop into your head; a sitter needs them in the order the evening happens. AI works from what you paste, so it reorders your facts instead of inventing new ones.

THE REAL TEST: we made up a family and asked Claude (Anthropic) on Nov 5, 2026: "Our babysitter comes at 6 tonight and I haven't written anything down. Here's my brain dump, in no order: the kids are Maya (7) and Leo (3). Mac and cheese is in the fridge, heat it for 2 minutes. Leo goes to bed at 7:30 with his stuffed rabbit. Maya goes to bed at 8 and can read for 20 minutes first. No screens after 7. We're at a restaurant 10 minutes away and back by 10:30. Call, don't text, if anything comes up. Turn this into a short note for the fridge, sorted by time, one line each. Leave blanks for our phone numbers."
A few lines, word for word: "7:30: Leo to bed with his stuffed rabbit." · "7:40: Maya can read for 20 minutes." · "8:00: Maya to bed." It worked out the 7:40 itself.
And it flagged the one gap it could see: "You didn't give a dinner time, so I left it without one. If you want a time on it, "6:15" would fit well."

HOW: open ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini, type everything in any order, ask for a note sorted by time, one line each, then read every line before you print it.

THE CATCH: AI can't add what you never mentioned. Add these yourself: allergies and medicines, emergency numbers (911 and a neighbour you trust), your phone numbers and your home address.

PRIVACY TIP: first names are enough. Write your address and phone numbers on the printed note by hand, not into the chat.

Family made up for this post.

Do this: Paste your brain dump. Ask: sorted by time.

Send this to whoever has a sitter booked this week.

Follow to learn one real AI trick a day.

#ai #learnai #claude #parenting #babysitter

posts.caption:
4 roommates and nobody knows whose turn it is? Tell AI the chores and who's busy when, and ask for one friendly group text with a fair rotation.

AI, for real · Day 15. One real test of what AI can do, with the output shown.

WHY IT WORKS: chore fights are rarely about the dishes, they're about feeling blamed. A text that proposes a plan ("so nobody has to guess whose turn it is") talks about the system, not the person. Telling AI who's busy when lets it work around real schedules: it gave Theo, who works weekend nights, Monday and Tuesday dishes.

THE REAL TEST (names made up for this post), Claude (Anthropic), Nov 5, 2026:
Prompt: "I live with 3 roommates (Sam, Ana and Theo) and the kitchen is a mess because nobody knows whose turn it is. The chores: dishes every night, trash and recycling out on Tuesday night, counters and stove once a week, bathroom once a week. Theo works night shifts on weekends. Write a short, friendly text for our group chat that proposes a fair weekly rotation, so nobody feels blamed. Under 80 words."
Slide 2 shows what we told it and its text, word for word (66 words, counted).

THE CATCH: check the maths before you send. It gave "me" (you) 1 dish night plus the Tuesday trash, and left "me" out of the weekly counters and bathroom, while the other three each get 2 dish nights and share the weekly jobs. Friendly, but not quite fair. Ask it to even things out, or fix it yourself, before it goes to the group.

PRIVACY TIP: first names are enough. Don't paste your old group chat, anyone's work schedule details or your address; "works weekend nights" is all it needs.

Do this: in ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini, list the chores and who's busy when. Then ask: "Write a short, friendly text for our group chat that proposes a fair weekly rotation, so nobody feels blamed."

Send this to the group chat that needs it.
